paragraphs.text: "The book of the generation": that is, a genealogical table, taken from the genealogical tables that the Jews took care to preserve while awaiting the coming Messiah. These tables were lost when Jerusalem was destroyed in AD 70 at the hand of Titus, the Roman commander. God ordained their concern for these tables so that this would be proof that Christ is the son of David, so that they might believe in Him.

There are two genealogical tables of Christ in the Holy Bible. One is in Luke (Lk 3:23-38), who addresses the Gentiles, so he records the legal lineage, that is, the males whom the Law regards as fathers: if a man died without having children, his brother would marry his wife, and the offspring would be reckoned to the one who died (Deut 25:5-6). Some of the sons mentioned are therefore sons by adoption, to proclaim to the Gentiles that they are sons by adoption and have salvation just like the Jews. As for Matthew (Mt 1:2-17), because he addresses the Jews, he records the natural fathers, because they are the people of God, descended in sequence from their natural fathers, that is, the Jews.
So we see that Joseph, the betrothed of Mary, has a legal father, Heli, who is mentioned in Luke, who died without having children.
As for Jacob, who is mentioned in Matthew, he is his natural father, as St. Severus of Antioch says. As for John (Jn 1:1-2), he wrote His divine lineage.
"Jesus Christ": Jesus is the human name of Christ, and its meaning is Savior.

As for Christ, it means the One anointed by God for this service, that is, the redemption of mankind. In the Old Testament the prophet, the priest and the king were anointed, and these three were united in Christ; and the anointed one has authority from God to carry out his work.
"The son of David, the son of Abraham": He is the son of David the king, as the prophecies mentioned (Isa 9:7), and the son of Abraham, as God promised him (Gen 22:18).
It was known to all the Jews that the awaited Messiah would come from the seed of David and Abraham.

A) It is noticed in this series that the genealogy descends from Abraham to Jesus, since Christ bears the sins of mankind, redeems us and saves us, because this series carries many sinners, such as Rahab the harlot, Tamar who put on the garment of a harlot, and the wife of Uriah, with whom David committed adultery. Whereas St. Luke ascends in his genealogy from Jesus to Adam, raising all mankind to God, the Father of Adam, because Luke addresses the Gentiles.
B) Matthew speaks in the genealogy of the natural fathers of Jesus, who were begotten by physical procreation, whereas Luke mentions the legal fathers.

C) The genealogy ends with Joseph and not the Virgin, although Joseph did not physically beget Christ. But the Jews recognize only men in genealogies, so, to protect Christ before Jewish society, Joseph was regarded as His father, as the angel informed him (vv. 20-21).

At the same time, the Virgin too is of the seed of David, for when they wanted to send her out of the Temple on reaching the age of twelve, they brought men from the seed of David, and God chose Joseph to be her betrothed.

There is another opinion, which is that Luke recorded the lineage of Christ through Mary His mother, so he mentions Heli, who is the father of Mary and is also called Joachim, and he attributes Joseph's lineage to him; and it was known among the Jews that a man could be reckoned to his father-in-law.
In any case, the two genealogical tables of Christ in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke were among the tables accepted by the Jews, as is proved by their not objecting to them.
D) Among the grandmothers of Christ were Rahab the Canaanite and Ruth the Moabitess, so that Christ might proclaim that He came for the salvation of the whole world, Jews and Gentiles.

E) Matthew the Evangelist mentions that the genealogy is divided into three parts, each part of 14 generations. It seems that the Jews tended to use certain numbers for blessing, such as the number 7, and the number 14 is double the number 7.

It seems that this series was written down and known among the Jews, for although it has abbreviations, these tables omitted names, such as King Joram, who did not beget Uzziah but begot Ahaziah, who begot Joash, and Joash begot Amaziah, and Amaziah begot Uzziah.

So Matthew abridged these names to reach his goal, which is that the Messiah is of the seed of David and Abraham. And although the first series began with Abraham and reached David the great, the second series descends through those who were in captivity because of the sins of the people, and then the third series rises to reach Jesus, the Savior of the whole world.

F) The series of Matthew differs from that of Luke, and this confirms that neither of them looked at the other's book, but each wrote it truthfully by inspiration of the Holy Spirit, to inform us of more details about Christ.

If Christ was not ashamed to mention His wicked and Gentile ancestors, then we should honor our fathers and relatives, even if their social standing was low, and appreciate their labors and virtues. Nor should we forget that our most important lineage is to Christ and the Church in which we were born through Baptism, so we have confidence in ourselves and are distinguished from those around us by this great grace, and we do not despise anyone of lowly lineage, for he may be better than we are in the sight of God and will have a greater place in heaven. Let us respect and honor every person and look for his virtues so that we may benefit from them.

entries.section: (2) Joseph's first dream and the Mother of Christ

paragraphs.text: "Espoused": that is, joined to a man, so that when she bore Jesus He would be ascribed to a man, namely Joseph, before Jewish society, and she would not be counted an adulteress.

Betrothal among the Jews meant a marriage contract, and the betrothed woman was called the wife of the betrothed; but after the period of betrothal, physical union took place, as happens now among our Muslim brothers in the signing of the contract and then the consummation. So after the betrothal was completed, when Joseph received Mary from the Temple, he took her to his house and kept her as a betrothed in purity and did not approach her. But he was surprised to find her with child before the marriage was completed, and he was disturbed, and was perplexed between her innocence and the pregnancy that he saw with his own eyes. And Matthew's saying, "before they came together," that is, during the betrothal, in no way means that they came together afterward, for the Virgin is ever-virgin.

entries.section: (2) Joseph's first dream and the Mother of Christ

paragraphs.text: It was open to Joseph to hand Mary over to the priests so that they would stone her, or to divorce her and send her out of his house secretly, without scandal. And because he was righteous, he wanted to cover for her and let her go without punishment, so that he would not be a partner in the crime of concealing a sin.

The more you love God, the more your love appears toward those around you, even if they are mistaken in your sight; so do not condemn them but cover for them, because "love covereth all sins" (Prov 10:12). And as God covers for you, be merciful to others as well.

entries.section: (2) Joseph's first dream and the Mother of Christ

paragraphs.text: "Joseph, thou son of David": the angel reminds him of his lineage from David, from whom Christ would come.

Because Joseph was a righteous man who quickly understood the revelations of God, an angel appeared to him in a dream and informed him of the truth of the Virgin's conception, that it was of the Holy Spirit and not of man, and encouraged him to take her, that is, to keep her in his house, and to look after her and the One to be born; indeed he told him the name of the One to be born, which is Jesus, meaning Savior, because He saves those who believe in Him from their sins.

"He shall save his people from their sins": He is a Savior, not from the Roman occupation as the Jews thought, but a spiritual Savior who lifts them out of their sins so that they may live in righteousness.
If you are perplexed between two difficult matters, God is able to guide you to the better solution, as the angel guided Joseph, if you pray to Him.

entries.section: (2) Joseph's first dream and the Mother of Christ

paragraphs.text: Matthew reminds us of the prophecy of Isaiah (Isa 7:14); this is the word of Matthew and not of the angel, as he tells us of the conception of the virgin, who is Mary, and explains to us the meaning of "Emmanuel", that is, that God becomes incarnate and becomes man among us, and redeems us, and is with us and dwells in us.
If God proclaims His name Emmanuel, that is, God with us, then in His love He wants to draw near to us and be with us in order to save us from all our sins and troubles.

entries.section: (2) Joseph's first dream and the Mother of Christ

paragraphs.text: Joseph's righteousness appears in his obedience to God, for he rejected his first idea, which was to send her out of his house, and even declared his responsibility for her, and believed the word of God although it is beyond the grasp of the mind.

entries.section: (2) Joseph's first dream and the Mother of Christ

paragraphs.text: Joseph took care of the Virgin until she bore the Child, and he called Him Jesus as the angel had declared, and he continued to care for her throughout his life.

And when Matthew mentions that he "knew her not till she had brought forth", it does not mean that he knew her after that, but that he did not approach her physically and cared for her as a father. The word "till" comes with this meaning in many places in the Holy Bible, as the Psalm says: "So our eyes wait upon the LORD our God, until that he have mercy upon us" (Ps 123:2); it does not mean that after He has mercy on us we do not lift our eyes toward Him.

Likewise, when Noah sent forth the raven from the ark, the Holy Bible says: "which went forth to and fro, until the waters were dried up from off the earth" (Gen 8:7); the word "until" does not mean that after the earth dried the raven returned to the ark, but that it remained on the earth.
And Jesus is described as "firstborn", not because the Virgin bore other sons after Him, but because the first one born is called firstborn even if no one is born after him.
And by logical deduction, it is impossible for righteous Joseph, whom God chose for this holy task, to defile the womb that the Holy Spirit sanctified.
The visit of the Magi, the flight to Egypt and the return to Nazareth

The Magi were the astrologers who were concerned with the study of medicine and astronomy; they were scholars in their country and were also regarded as priests, and they had a great standing that their gifts show. They came from the east, most likely from Persia or Iraq. Their number is not mentioned, but at least three of them were prominent, and they may have had a large following; and they had heard prophecies from their forefathers about the appearance of a star that points to the birth of a great king. Balaam the son of Beor the prophet said this, and he was from the east where they live: "I shall see him, but not now: I shall behold him, but not nigh: there shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel, and shall smite the corners of Moab, and destroy all the children of Sheth" (Num 24:17). They may also have understood this from Daniel, who was chief of the Magi, from his prophecy about the birth of Christ: "Know therefore and understand, that from the going forth of the commandment to restore and to build Jerusalem unto the Messiah the Prince shall be seven weeks, and threescore and two weeks: the street shall be built again, and the wall, even in troublous times" (Dan 9:25).
The star that they saw was not an ordinary star; it was either an angel who appeared in the form of a star, or a special spiritual star that God sent, and this appears from the following:
A) The stars move from west to east, but this one moved from east to west.
B) This star appeared in the daytime while the sun was bright, and not only at night.
C) It sometimes appeared and sometimes disappeared (as happened when they asked Herod).
D) It traveled high in the sky, then came down over a lowly house where Christ was born.

So when the star brought them from the east as far as Jerusalem, they were certain of the prophecies, and that He was the king of the Jews, and they supposed that He would be born in the royal palace, so they asked those in the palace.

This Herod is the one called Herod the Great. He was of Edomite origin, an intruder upon the Jews, and he had seized the kingship by force. He was marked by violence: he killed his wife and some of his sons, and he was at that time seventy years old, so he feared the new King. The news spread in the palace and throughout Jerusalem, and they were troubled and bewildered as to what surrounded the birth of the new King, and whether conflicts might arise between Him and Herod!
And this Herod is the father of Herod Antipas who killed John the Baptist, and the grandfather of the Herod who killed James the son of Zebedee and imprisoned Peter.

Herod understood that they were speaking about the awaited Messiah, and he feared that the kingdom would be taken from him, so he gathered the chief priests, that is, the present high priest and the former high priests, and all the heads of the priestly divisions, and the scribes of the Law who studied it, to inform him where Christ was to be born so that he could kill Him.
However great a person's greatness and authority, he cannot keep his peace as long as he is in sin, far from God, for peace is enjoyed only by the children of God.

"Bethlehem": it is a small village southwest of Jerusalem, about 8 km away from it, and it is also called Ephratah (Mic 5:2), or the city of David because he was born in it (Lk 2:4), and Micah the prophet prophesied about it (Mic 5:2). It is in Judea, to distinguish it from another city called Bethlehem in Galilee, and it is clear from the prophecy that it was small and lowly, but it became very great through the birth of Christ in it.

Note how the priests and their chiefs did not take care to search for the awaited Messiah, of whom the prophets had spoken and to whom the types pointed, because they were occupied with their positions and their wealth. Whereas the Gentiles, those far from Him, in the form of the Magi traveling from a distant land, searched for Him, so that the Holy Bible might confirm that Christ came for the salvation of the whole world, and He draws every person to Himself in the way that suits him (the Jews by the prophecies, and the Magi by the star because they were astronomers); what matters is that a person respond to the voice of God.
So however weak or lowly you are, you are turned into the greatest of people by Christ's dwelling in your heart.

After Herod learned the place of Christ's birth, he asked the Magi about the time when the star appeared to them in their country, and he calculated the time until their arrival from Persia in Judea, and it was more than a year, in order to know the age of the new King.
"Privily": because he felt his own wickedness, as he intended to kill Christ, so that his plan to kill the children of Bethlehem, with which he would take the Jews by surprise, would not be revealed.

Herod hid the cruelty in his heart and his desire to kill the new King, and showed himself in innocence to the Magi, as though he wished to worship Him as they did, so he asked them to find out the place with care and then tell him. It seems that, in his agitation, he did not send anyone after them to learn the place of the Child.

The Magi relied on their own reasoning, so they asked in the royal palace where they supposed the new King would be born, and no one guided them; then they went out and found that the star had disappeared from them. And after they failed to learn His place, the divine star appeared to them and they rejoiced greatly, and it led them to Bethlehem and then to the house in which Christ was born.

Hold fast to God's commandments so that they may guide you on the path of your life, and likewise the guidance of your father of confession above all your thoughts and reasoning, lest you stray from Christ.

So do not be hindered by the cares of the world and its reasoning from your goal, which is the love of God, and the measure of your holding fast to God's commandments will continue to guide you; but if you neglect it you will be perplexed and ask: how can I hear the voice of God?

When they saw the child Jesus with His mother the Virgin and Joseph the carpenter, they felt great reverence, and they worshiped Him with hearts full of joy, then presented to Him their gifts, which were gold, frankincense and myrrh, and these point to the offices of Christ: gold because He is King; frankincense, that is, incense, because He is a Priest by the sacrifice of Himself on the Cross; and myrrh is a reference to His sufferings and death. Perhaps these gifts were a help to the Holy Family in some of the costs of the journey to Egypt.

The greatness of the Magi's faith in Christ appears here, that He was in a lowly form; and note also the Jews' lack of concern to glorify their King, whereas they believed according to God's guidance to them by the star.

The Magi did not understand the wicked intention of Herod, but God, after their visit to Christ, informed them in a dream not to return to Herod because he was wicked, and guided them to another way by which they returned to their country. It seems that this dream came to them right after seeing Christ so that they might hasten their departure to their country, before Herod noticed and carried out his plan to kill the children of Bethlehem.

If you have enjoyed sitting with Christ, do not return to wicked Herod, that is, your former evils, but return to your first homeland, which is Paradise where Adam was created of old, that is, lift your heart to heaven, continuing in a spiritual relationship with God.

The Magi told the Holy Family what God had said to them in the dream, and they understood that Herod was seeking Jesus to harm Him, but they were not troubled, and waited for God's guidance. Then God's care for them and His mocking of wicked Herod appeared: the angel of God appeared in a dream to Joseph for the second time and asked him to take the child Jesus and His mother Mary and flee with them to Egypt, and to be there until he told him.
And Egypt is the nearest place to Judea and is not under the authority of Herod.
In this, God declares to us fundamental matters in our spiritual walk, which are:

A) The necessity of enduring sufferings so that a person may be proved; how hard it was for old Joseph, young Mary and the child Jesus to bear the hardships of travel and of living in a foreign country.
B) The confirmation of Christ's Incarnation, and His bearing all the suffering of mankind from His childhood, not using the power of His divinity to ease Himself.
C) Not resisting evil but fleeing from it.
D) The blessing of Egypt, that it might be a center of spiritual work through the generations by its scholars, its monks and its saints.
Joseph the carpenter obeyed the angel's word, not excusing himself because of his old age, or the smallness of the Child, or his not knowing Egypt, and he arose by night to travel to it.

"By night": most likely on the very night in which he saw the dream, to hurry in the flight before Herod's plan was carried out; and because he was a stranger he did not have many belongings that needed preparing for the journey, and likewise no one paid attention to him, for he was not from the people of the place.

The Holy Family moved to Egypt, passed through many places and blessed them, and stayed there about two years until Herod died, and by this the prophecy of Hosea the prophet was fulfilled about the Messiah's return to the land of Israel: "Out of Egypt have I called my son" (Hos 11:1). This prophecy was about the exodus of the children of Israel from Egypt, and also about the return of Christ from Egypt to the land of the Jews.

entries.section: (4) The slaughter of the children of Bethlehem

paragraphs.text: Herod was greatly enraged because of the Magi's disobedience to him and regarded it as a great insult, and his fear of the new King increased, so in hardness of heart he decided to kill all the children of Bethlehem, among whom was the new King. And to make sure of killing Him, he asked the soldiers to surround the place, so that no one would escape from all the borders (boundaries) of Bethlehem.

And according to his expectation of the age of the new King, that He would be about a year old or more, he asked that all the children up to the age of two years be killed, to make sure of getting rid of Him, lest the soldiers err in estimating the children's ages; and he likewise ordered the killing of all those around Bethlehem, and also those older than the age of the Child, so that he would have done away with Him, and this shows Herod's brutality.

entries.section: (4) The slaughter of the children of Bethlehem

paragraphs.text: By this the prophecy of Jeremiah, referred to previously in (v. 8), was fulfilled, which expresses what happened during the captivity, and also what happened in the massacre of Bethlehem, where the news spread throughout Jerusalem and its surroundings, since the city of Ramah lies north of Jerusalem, and they heard the weeping and wailing of the Jewish mothers (who are symbolized by Rachel) for the loss of their children. Also Rachel, the wife of Jacob, who is buried in Bethlehem, wept first for those who were killed in the days of the Babylonian captivity, and weeps also for the children killed in the days of Herod. All this is a symbol of the grief that prevailed, not only in Bethlehem but in all the lands surrounding Jerusalem.

Hardness of heart makes a person not feel those around him, so he wrongs them while he is absorbed in achieving his own aims. May you put yourself in the place of others so that you feel for them, and may your achieving your aims not be at the expense of people's comfort, but may you seek their comfort before your own, as Christ did when He died for our redemption and salvation.

After the Holy Family had stayed about two years in Egypt, waiting for God to permit them to return to the land of Israel, the angel appeared to Joseph for the third time and informed him of the death of Herod and of his son Antipater, who had wanted to kill Jesus (for Herod killed his son five days before he died, after he had completed 37 years in the kingship, and that was in 4 BC). And the angel commanded Joseph to return.

Joseph obeyed, and did not ask to remain in Egypt, excusing himself because of his old age or to keep away from the wicked in Judea, for the virtue of obedience is above all reasoning, so that God may lead the life of the one who obeys Him.

When Joseph reached the borders of the land of Israel, he heard that Archelaus, the son of Herod, had reigned in his place, and he was known for cruelty like his father, so he feared to return to Bethlehem near Jerusalem, where he had supposed it to be a suitable place for Christ to live, near the Temple and the priests of the Jews. And he asked God what to do. Then he was "warned of God in a dream", perhaps by an angel as in the previous times, to go to Galilee, which is in the north of the land of Israel, where Herod Antipas, the brother of Archelaus, reigned, and there were problems between them, in addition to his being gentle.

When he reached Galilee, he went to the city of Nazareth, where he had lived at first, for it was his original home, and by this the prophecies of the prophets were fulfilled that He would be called a Nazarene.

And the word "Nazareth" means a branch, and Isaiah, Jeremiah and Zechariah prophesied that Christ would be called the Branch (Isa 11:1-2; Jer 33:15; Zech 3:8), and this is the fifth time that St. Matthew cites the prophecies.

And Jesus lived in Nazareth about 28 years until He reached the age of thirty, and He worked with Joseph the carpenter in carpentry. Not much is recorded about this period except that He was obedient to His mother and Joseph, and was growing in stature and grace, and visited Jerusalem at the feasts to fulfill the worship according to the Law. God leads your life, so do not be troubled by the wicked however much they threaten you, for Herod and his son Antipater have died, and as for Archelaus, God took His Christ away from him when He settled in Galilee. The power of the wicked is worthless before God, so walk in calm and reassurance, occupied with God, and He protects you from every evil.
E The preaching of the Baptist and his baptism of Christ

entries.section: (1) The person of John the Baptist

paragraphs.text: "In those days": that is, when Christ drew near to the age of thirty, and precisely six months before it, John the Baptist appeared, who was six months older than He.

"John the Baptist": he is John the son of Zacharias the priest, who became famous for baptizing the Jews, and so was called the Baptist, and who lived about thirty years in the wilderness in a life of asceticism, as a model of monasticism in the Old Testament and of the love of prayer and solitude. This was a spiritual period in which he was prepared for the greatest service, which was preparing the way for the proclamation of Christ and His redemption.

"Preaching": he began his preaching after thirty years of silence, and called the people to repentance and to return to God. "The wilderness of Judaea": it lies east of Jerusalem, near the Dead Sea (the Sea of Lot).

entries.section: (1) The person of John the Baptist

paragraphs.text: His preaching was of repentance, that is, the purification of the heart from sin, and a change of direction from evil to life with God.

"At hand": because after six months the preaching of Christ would begin, who reigns over hearts with a heavenly kingship. His warning was clear, namely the nearness of the Kingdom of Heaven, that is, the reign of Christ over hearts, which is a heavenly, spiritual reign, and not an earthly one as the Jews imagined, to rescue them from the cruelty of the Romans. He preached the Kingdom of God over the heart, so that a person may be made fit to dwell in heaven and reign with God forever; and God cannot reign over a heart that clings to sin and refuses repentance.

entries.section: (1) The person of John the Baptist

paragraphs.text: In this verse Matthew the Evangelist, who addresses the Jews, cites the prophecy of Isaiah, who was famous and well known among the Jews, to confirm the preparing of the way of the expected Messiah (Isa 40:3). It is said of John that he is a "voice", to distinguish him from Christ, who is the Word Himself. And in his preaching he was strong, like one who cries out and proclaims the preparing of the way of God in the heart, that is, by repentance and the good conduct that results from it.

"Prepare ye the way of the Lord": to remove the obstacles, as the herald used to cry out to prepare for the passing of a king or a great man; what is meant here is the removal of sins and pride from the heart.
"Make his paths straight": by keeping away from hypocrisy and evil, that is, correcting what is crooked, so that the heart is upright and God may pass through it and fill it with ease.

entries.section: (1) The person of John the Baptist

paragraphs.text: He describes the ascetic life that John the Baptist lived: his clothing was of coarse camel's hair, and not soft garments. As for the girdle that he wore about his loins, that is, his waist and belly, it was of leather, and not an expensive, decorated one.
As for his food, it was locusts, the well-known insect, though there is another opinion that it was a wild plant, in addition to wild honey which bees make in the clefts of the rocks.

The meaning of this is that he was content with necessary clothing and food, because his heart was occupied with heavenly things and the service of God. He is an image of the monastic life in the Old Testament, like Elijah the prophet.

entries.section: (1) The person of John the Baptist

paragraphs.text: In view of the depth and spirituality of John's preaching and its strong effect on hearts, most of the inhabitants of Jerusalem went out to him, and indeed all the region of Judea and all the lands surrounding the river Jordan; and he said "all" as an indication of the majority.

entries.section: (1) The person of John the Baptist

paragraphs.text: And being moved by his sermons, they came forward to be baptized, each one of them, in the river Jordan, confessing his sins. This was a baptism of repentance, and a clear indication of the sacrament of confession at the hand of the priest in the New Testament. Baptism was known among the Jews, for they used to baptize proselyte Gentiles when they joined them. So baptism was familiar to them, but the addition here is repentance and confession. As for the baptism of the New Testament, it differs from the baptism of John in that it is by the Holy Spirit, to change human nature, so that it becomes pure from every sin.

It is clear that the baptism of repentance is a preparation for the baptism of the New Testament. And this is what takes place now, when a person confesses his sins, if he is an adult, before receiving the sacrament of Baptism.

Repentance is your way of preparing your heart so that Christ may dwell in it. So do not neglect the voices of God crying out to you for repentance through the Holy Bible and the teachings of the Church, and also through those around you and their rebuke of you, but hasten to repent before God every day, and then at the hand of the priest, to receive forgiveness of your sins.

The Pharisees: a party that appeared in the second century BC in Jewish society, holding to the Law literally, and they were regarded as the leaders of Jewish thought; the meaning of their name is "the separated", that is, those chosen by God. They trusted in their righteousness, and said: if two enter heaven, at least one of them is a Pharisee. The Sadducees: a party that objected to the authority of the Pharisees and denied eternal life and spirits. They shared with the Pharisees in the spiritual leadership of the Jews, and were regarded as the rich aristocratic class, and they were descendants of Zadok the priest.

They came to John not for repentance, but to get to know John, who had drawn the crowds away from them. Perhaps they were seeking a position of leadership behind this new leader to whom all the Jews had gone out. John the Baptist was strong, and confronted them with the crookedness of their hearts, since in appearance they sought repentance while inwardly they were far from it, so he rebuked them, describing them as a "generation of vipers", a kind of snake marked by great cunning and craftiness, and whose young eat their mother's belly and kill her in order to come out to life; that is, he described them as selfish and hard-hearted.

"The wrath to come": that is, the judgment of God on the last day, before which they must stand, and he marveled at their neglect of repentance and of preparation for eternity, though they were the teachers of the Jews, by his saying: "who hath warned you".

John calls them to prove their repentance by doing the works of repentance, that is, forsaking sin and doing what is good; for without fruit, however much they speak about repentance, it profits them nothing, and likewise their baptism would be of no benefit to them.

He also rebukes them for their pride, since they supposed that by their claim to descent from Abraham, the man of the promises, they would receive the promises. But God requires the one who walks in the righteousness of Abraham, to be a true son of his. "These stones": he points to stones that were before him. Just as God created Adam from dust, He is also able to create children for Abraham from stones.

He also means that God is able to raise up children to Abraham from the stones, that is, the stony, hard hearts of the Gentiles who worship idols of stone, who, if they believe and walk in righteousness, become true children of Abraham.

Do not rely on being a Christian, but repent and do good, so that you may enjoy God's care and the Kingdom of Heaven. The name condemns you if you do not live by it, and likewise the honor of your family and your kinship to spiritual people does not benefit you, but calls you to imitate them, so that you live a life of repentance and do good like your Christ.
This "axe" is the wooden Cross, or the word of God, which condemns everyone who does not believe, and cuts him off from his root and destroys him, because he did not believe in Christ the Savior.

And the laying of the axe means the nearness of judgment, so repentance is necessary and presenting its proof, which is the fruits of righteousness; and if a person does not bring forth fruit, he should expect nothing but the eternal fire.

John distinguishes between the baptism of repentance and the baptism of Christ, God the Word, which is by the Holy Spirit, to renew human nature; and although he is the leader of the baptism of repentance, yet in relation to Christ he is not worthy to be the least slave in His service, to whom the carrying of the sandals is entrusted.
The humility of the Baptist appears from this, for although he was the strongest of the prophets, he denied himself, giving glory to Christ.
"The Holy Ghost and with fire": he means the baptism of the Holy Spirit which renews nature, and the fire burns up evil and the nature inclined to sin, to renew a person for life with God.

In the end John the Baptist proclaims Christ the Judge, and likens Him to the farmer who separates the grain from the chaff after the process of threshing, using for this the winnowing fork, that is, the pitchfork, which is a shaft with wooden fingers by which the grain mixed with straw is lifted, so the grain falls quickly, while the chaff or straw flies off and falls far away. In this way the grain is gathered by itself, and the straw by itself, and this is done in a wide place beside the field called the threshing floor. Then the grain is gathered into sacks and put in the granary, while the straw is burned with fire since it is not needed.
The winnowing fork: it is the word of God, or the Cross, by which God judges the unbelievers and the unrepentant. The threshing floor: it is the end of the world, and the day of judgment.
The granary: it is the Kingdom of Heaven or the Church.
The fire: it is the eternal torment.
The chaff: they are the wicked.

The wheat: they are the believers who will be glorified with Christ in the heavens, and he says of them "his wheat", that is, those joined to Him who remain with Him in the Kingdom, unlike the chaff, that is, the wicked, of whom he does not say "his chaff" because they have separated from Him.

Christ lived His childhood and youth until the age of thirty in Nazareth and the region of Galilee, then turned south to Judea at the river Jordan, where the crowds had gathered around John the Baptist. And He came forward as a representative of mankind to be baptized with the baptism of repentance, though He is without sin, but bearing our sins, offering repentance on our behalf. "Then": he means the period in which John the Baptist was preaching, which was six months.

"Cometh": that is, He appeared openly among the crowds to share with us and to fulfill all righteousness on our behalf, though He has no need of repentance. "Jordan": he means the river Jordan, which extends about two hundred miles from the north of Israel to its south.

John knew by the Spirit that this was the expected Messiah, and he marveled at the humility of Christ, so he said to Him humbly that it was he who needed to be baptized by Him, so how could he baptize Him? And Christ replies with gentleness and greater humility, asking John to permit it and baptize Him, to fulfill all righteousness on behalf of sinful human beings, who were unable to fulfill it because they kept away from repentance and the righteous life.

Contemplate this wonderful love, so that you too may be humble, not only before those greater than you, but before those lower than you in position or age, and ask yourself: do I speak with gentleness and humility to every person?

Jesus went down into the river Jordan and was immersed in the water, then went up and came out of the water. For this reason the Church holds to the rite of immersion in the water of Baptism, because it means burial with Christ, then resurrection also with Him, as the Holy Bible says: "Buried with him in baptism, wherein also ye are risen with him" (Col 2:12). And for the first time God manifests His three hypostases in full clarity: Christ the Son in the water, the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove upon His head, and the Father, whose voice they heard from heaven.

This was clear before John, who baptized Christ, and all those present. For this reason the Church celebrates the baptism of Christ, and calls it "the Feast of Theophany (Immersion)", because He was immersed in the waters of the Jordan. And she also calls it "the Feast of the Divine Manifestation", because He manifested His three hypostases on that day, that is, His essential personal attributes in which the divine Being subsists, and these hypostases are one God.

And with this divine manifestation, and the appearance of the Spirit in the form of a dove upon His head, the ministry of Christ on earth begins, just as kings, prophets and priests of old were anointed with oil, which is a sign of the anointing of the Holy Spirit, and then began their ministry; and this is what takes place now in the sacrament of the priesthood in the New Testament.

"My beloved Son": He is the Son of God in essence and nature from eternity, which is different from our sonship to God by adoption. "In whom I am well pleased": because He fulfills God's will in the Incarnation, and afterward in redemption for the salvation of mankind.

Christ fulfills all righteousness on our behalf in order to teach us to love one another, that we may make up for one another's shortcomings and cover over sins, and so learn humility and service in secret.
The temptation on the mountain; the calling of the disciples

"Then": that is, after His baptism in the Jordan, He went forward to meet the temptations and overcome them, so that He might give us the power to be victorious. He did not enter into temptation by Himself, in order to teach us not to throw ourselves into it as Lot did by going to Sodom. But if God allows it to us, we strive with His help and overcome it.

The Holy Spirit dwelling in Christ led Him into a wilderness near the river Jordan, and He met Satan, because it was familiar in ancient times that demons dwell in the wilds and wastes (deserts), and not in holy places where righteous people are. And He went in order to overcome him, to give us strength and confidence that we will overcome Satan if we fight.

And the Lord Christ permitted the devil to tempt Him, to make us feel that He is near to us and feels our temptations, as the Holy Bible says: "For in that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able to succour them that are tempted" (Heb 2:18), and in order to confirm that temptations must come, so that we may be confident that we shall overcome them, and even receive spiritual blessings from them. But God does not permit him to tempt us except to the extent that benefits us, and He gives us the divine help by which we overcome.

In the quiet of solitude, Christ remained forty days in fasting and prayers, to proclaim the importance of being alone with God, even if this is accompanied by the feeling of physical hunger, because being filled with God and enjoying Him is the goal of our life; and this provokes the devil, who dwells in the soul far from God. But when the soul is filled with God, and he tries to fight it, he is defeated.

Christ fasted forty days continuously without eating, like Moses and Elijah, so as not to go beyond the limits of human beings, lest people think that He was not an ordinary man, and "afterward he was an hungred" to confirm His humanity. The number 40 is the number 10 multiplied by 4, and the number 10 points to perfection, like the Ten Commandments, and the number 4 points to the four directions of the world; so the number 40 represents the perfection of striving in all directions. Christ accomplished this for our sake, though He had no need of fasting, but as an example for us, to sanctify our fasts.

After the devil heard the testimony of heaven about Christ, that He is the Son of God, when He was at the river Jordan, he marveled when he saw Him hungry, and doubted His sonship to God, so he took courage to tempt Him as a man, asking Him to prove His sonship to God by satisfying His hunger by turning the stones into bread. He did not say delicious foods, but merely bread, Satan thereby trying to persuade Him of the necessity of eating lest His body faint. By this temptation he meant to make Him fall into the sin of not relying on God, instead of trusting in His care and that He would provide for Him the food He needed. Christ did not use His divinity for His own comfort; He used it to feed the multitudes (ch. 14:13-21, ch. 15:32-39), to teach us to labor for the comfort of others, and to rely on Him for our needs, confident of His care, fulfilling our duties faithfully.

"If thou be the Son of God": a question of doubt, by which he means to make a person doubt himself, and this is the devil's habit in his war with us. It is a provocative question to push us to do what he wants, so that we fall into sin. Therefore we should not hasten to carry out what comes to our mind, for it may be thoughts from the devil, and we should test them by prayer, especially if they concern important decisions, so we take sufficient time for prayer, and we can join it with fasting, that God may guide us and expose the devil's scheme.

Christ answered the devil with a verse from the Holy Bible (Deut 8:3), which declares that spiritual satisfaction from the word of God is the foundation, and not only concern for material satisfaction. He did not answer his question about His sonship to God, and declared that the spiritual person is occupied with the word of God before being occupied with his material needs, relying in this on the guidance of the Holy Bible, with which he repels the devil's thoughts.

This is the first temptation, and many temptations may have preceded it, but in these three temptations the devil was manifest, for he came forward and confronted Christ; for it is written that he was tempting Him forty days, and not only at their end (Mk 1:13).
"Taketh him up": by agreement with Him and not by force, because Christ was willing to be tempted by His own will, to teach us how to overcome the devil.
"The holy city": that is, Jerusalem, where the Temple of God is, the holiest place, for the devil fights in every place, even in holy places.
"A pinnacle of the temple": a very high place rising above the ground about 200 meters.

The second temptation: the devil took Him to the highest place in the Temple, which is its pinnacle, to cast Himself down from above, and the angels would come and bear Him up, and He would descend into the great court carried on their hands, and so would dazzle the gathered crowds, and everyone would know that He is the Son of God, and by this He would begin His ministry.

And the devil relied on a verse, to deceive Jesus into thinking that by this He would be fulfilling the word of God, for the divine promise is that He keeps His children by His angels (Ps 91:11-12). It is clear that the devil was still perplexed: is Christ the Son of God, or an ordinary man?!

"It is written": the devil resorted to using the word of God in his war, to persuade Christ and make Him fall into temptation, as he does with us, using verses of the Holy Bible and interpreting them according to his wickedness.

And the error here is a person's throwing himself into temptation, for God cares for us and rescues us from temptation if it comes upon us, but it is not right for us to throw ourselves into it and then ask God to deliver us.

Christ replied to him that God cares for His children, but it is not right for a person to doubt this care and try to test it to make sure of it, nor to throw himself into temptation. But if he falls into temptation, God protects him (Deut 6:16).
In this, Christ fled from vainglory, to teach us to work and serve in humility, indeed in secret as far as we are able.

The third temptation: the enticement with the glories of the world and its pleasures, and the easy way to reach one's needs, instead of suffering and carrying the cross. So he took Him up into an exceeding high mountain, which points to pride, and there he offered Him the love of possessing the kingdoms of the world, with all the desires and pleasures they carry.
"The kingdoms of the world": they are the cities and villages of Judea, which are a sample of the cities of the world with all the glories they carry.

The lying devil claimed ownership of all the kingdoms of the world, or perhaps he means his authority over the evil desires with which he entices Jesus, and the condition for obtaining them is submission to him, and the proof of it is worshiping him. The temptation here is the love of possession and leadership, and he offers Christ a solution in place of His coming toil and sufferings, that He would become king over the whole world, and by this free His Jewish people from the Roman occupation, but the condition is submission to the devil and worship of him.
"Get thee hence": He clearly declares His rejection of the devil's word and thoughts.
"Satan": that is, the adversary.
"Him only shalt thou serve": He reserves worship for God alone, and therefore forbids offering worship, not only to idols, but every attachment and preoccupation with the desires of the world.

Jesus Christ, the second Adam, did not have love of the world in His heart, so He was not affected by the devil's enticements, in addition to His attachment, as man, to the love of God and submission to Him. And He answered him with what is written, that worship is for God alone (Deut 6:13).
If the heart submits to God and fears Him, it does not accept the evil desires of the world.

Since the devil was defeated by Him, he left Him, but only for a time, to return and fight Him again, as will happen in the attempt of the Pharisees and Sadducees to make Him fall into error. Then the angels came to Him to bear the crowns of His victory up to heaven, for the angels strengthen us and guide us and bear our prayers and our victories up to heaven, that we may be crowned for them in eternity.
And Christ faced the temptation alone, so that the victory might be His and not due to the help of the angels.

"Leaveth him": this means that every temptation has an end, so that God gives us an opportunity for calm and growth in His love before a second temptation comes, and in this way we are strong before the temptations to come.

Christ remained a few months in Judea; John the Evangelist mentioned what happened in it in the first chapters of his Gospel, and during it John the Baptist was completing his preaching and his witness to Christ. Christ stayed this period in Judea to show His agreement in preaching with John the Baptist. During this, many of John's disciples joined Christ. Then after John the Baptist finished his preaching, Herod arrested him and cast him into prison.
"Galilee": it is the northern part of Israel, and extends eastward from the river Jordan to Acre in the west on the coast of the Mediterranean.

Jesus returned to Galilee, where He had lived in Nazareth in His first years until the age of thirty. But He did not dwell in Nazareth, but went to Capernaum, a well-known city in Galilee, situated on the Sea of Galilee, that is, the Sea of Tiberias, in the places owned by the tribes of Zabulon and Nephthalim (Naphtali).
Isaiah prophesied (Isa 9:1-2) about the preaching of Christ in Galilee, and this is the sixth prophecy that St. Matthew mentions about Christ.
"The land of Zabulon and the land of Nephthalim": they belong to two tribes of Israel (two sons of Jacob), and lie west of the Jordan and north of the Sea of Galilee.
"By the way of the sea": he means the Sea of Galilee.
"Beyond Jordan": that is, the land that lies west of the Jordan.

"Galilee of the Gentiles": the Jews mixed with the Gentiles in the region of Galilee, therefore it was called "Galilee of the Gentiles", and pagan worship was mixed with Jewish worship, and for this reason the people of Judea despised the inhabitants of this region for their mixing with the worship of the Gentiles. The region of Galilee included the twenty cities that Solomon gave to Hiram because he helped him in building the Temple (1 Kgs 9:11).
"The people which sat in darkness": the inhabitants of this land accepted sin and lived in it, which is symbolized by darkness.
"Saw great light": light points to the new life with God and to purity, and what is meant here is the proclamation of Christ and His call to them to repent and return to God.

"The region and shadow of death" (Ps 107:10): the sins in which the inhabitants of these lands were immersed have death as their punishment. And the word "shadow" means everything connected with death, the evils that lead to it.
"From that time": that is, after the arrest of John, Christ began His preaching in Galilee.

The preaching of Christ was the same as that which John the Baptist proclaimed, which is quick repentance because of the nearness of the Kingdom of Heaven, that is, the reign of God over hearts, the spiritual reign, which was accomplished by the Resurrection of Christ, and then this Kingdom is completed in the heavens.

God seeks you even if you are immersed in sin and mixed with the wicked, and He is ready to purify your heart and renew your life and dwell within you, and even transform you to holiness. So respond to Him by accepting the call to repentance and return to Him, and He will help you and support you and make you prosper in all your steps.
"The sea of Galilee": it is a lake with fresh water, 12 miles long and 10 miles wide and about 50 meters deep, and it is the one called the Lake of Tiberias or the Lake of Gennesaret.

And as Jesus was walking by the shore of the sea, He found two brothers, Simon, whom He afterward surnamed Peter, that is, Cephas or the Rock, and Andrew his brother, the two sons of Jonas. They were casting their net into the sea, for their trade was catching fish.

Christ called them to follow Him and become His disciples, to do a better work, which is catching souls for the knowledge of God, and they obeyed. And this is an extraordinary act, that a person should love God so much that he leaves his necessary work.

And obedience is the giving up of human will and reasoning out of love for God. Christ chose His disciples unlettered, and from a region despised in the eyes of the Jews, which is Galilee, to work through them, so that the glory might be to God, and not to human abilities; and the condition for God's work in us is obedience.

"Straightway": an indication of quick obedience. It seems that their earlier acquaintance with Christ, mentioned in (Jn 1:40-42), helped them to follow Him, but this shows their being moved and their strong response to the word of God.

"They left their nets": the meaning is preferring to follow Christ over their work and their private life, for their love was so strong that they left everything, even the nets and the work by which they lived.
"Zebedee": the husband of Salome, who afterward followed Christ (ch. 27:56), and it seems that he was rich and had workers who helped him and had a position in society (Jn 18:15).

A little later, as Christ was walking by the shore of the sea, He found two other brothers, James and John the sons of Zebedee, who were partners of Simon and Andrew in catching fish, as their cooperation with them appears in the catching of the great number of fish, after which Jesus called them (Lk 5:6-11); so they left the nets, which they were mending with their father, and followed Jesus.

Following God is better than necessary work and the relationship with parents, and this does not mean neglecting our work and not honoring our parents, but that obedience to God is above everything. So be ready to give up some of your comfort and pleasure in order to hold fast to your spiritual life, and then you will enjoy fellowship with God and inner peace.

Jesus went out from Capernaum on many journeys in the region of Galilee, about nine journeys, passing through most of its cities and villages, which number more than 200 cities and villages, each of which held on average 15 thousand people, that is, the population of Galilee was about 3 million, and He preached to them repentance and the nearness of the Kingdom.

"Their synagogues": places of worship that appeared in the days of the captivity and continued afterward, in which they pray and read the holy Scriptures and deliver spiritual sermons. They were spread throughout the land, because the Temple was only in Jerusalem; and Christ made use of these synagogues in preaching the salvation that He offers to mankind.
And Christ was compassionate, healing their diseases to proclaim His love for mankind. Through these miracles hearts were attached to Him, and He spoke to them His deep spiritual words.
"All manner of sickness": that is, bodily troubles of which people complained.
Because of His miracles and His moving teachings, His fame spread, not only in Galilee, but to many other regions, which are:
(1) Syria: a large Roman province lying east of Galilee.

(2) Decapolis (the Ten Cities): cities distinguished by Roman privileges, lying east of the Jordan, and now called the Golan. (3) Jerusalem: a well-known city because the Temple of God was in it, lying in the southern part of the land of the Jews. (4) Judea: a region comprising the southern part of the land of the Jews, with the city of Jerusalem inside it, and including many cities and villages.
(5) Beyond Jordan: a region lying south of the ten cities.

"Those which were possessed with devils, and those which were lunatick, and those that had the palsy": he mentioned these diseases because of their difficulty compared with others. The insane and the epileptics are either afflicted by the works of demons in them, or by nervous diseases that make them unbalanced, or they may sometimes faint and fall to the ground. As for the paralytics, they are those who suffer paralysis in a part or most of their body.

May you accustom yourself to do good in every place, helping every needy person and everyone who suffers from weakness, whether he asks you or not; and as they are moved by your love, they readily accept your word about Christ and repentance and returning to God.
Chapter 5 The Sermon on the Mount The Beatitudes The completion of the Law

entries.section: (1) Introduction to the Sermon on the Mount

paragraphs.text: The crowds multiplied behind Christ, so He went out with them to the mountain to speak to them with His life-giving words.

The mountain points spiritually to rising above material things, and to spiritual strength and steadfastness. He spoke to them in a long discourse that took up three chapters, and it is regarded as a constitution of Christianity containing its most important teachings. His disciples drew near to Him because of their love for Him.

"Went up": there were many crowds following Christ, those mentioned at the end of the previous chapter. So that they might hear Him and see Him clearly, He went up a short distance on the mountain and sat down, and His disciples came to Him. As for the rest of the crowds, they sat before Him on the ground in the wide valley; and this mountain is one of the mountains near Capernaum in Galilee.

entries.section: (1) Introduction to the Sermon on the Mount

paragraphs.text: Christ began to speak and teach the crowds in direct words, and this sermon is one of His most famous. He may have repeated some of its meanings on other occasions, but because of its importance it is regarded as a constitution of Christianity. His sermon served as an interpretation of the Law, adding to it the perfection of the Christian life, for He did not come to destroy the Law but to fulfil it (v. 17).

entries.section: (2) The Beatitudes, which are the blessings

paragraphs.text: Christ began His discourse by encouraging His children and praising them, so that they would strive in their spiritual life, so He showed them the reward, that they might be zealous for spiritual work.

The first praise was for "the poor in spirit", that is, the humble, because humility is the foundation of every virtue, just as pride is the first sin that made Adam fall, and Satan also. Consequently, the humble person is assured of the eternal Kingdom of Heaven by God's dwelling in his heart with His spiritual Kingdom, so he rejoices and enjoys it at all times.

entries.section: (2) The Beatitudes, which are the blessings

paragraphs.text: Then He praises those who mourn for their sins, that is, the penitent, and those who grieve over the sins of others and so pray for them, because God gives them peace in their hearts in this life, and then heavenly comforts and glories in eternity.

For this reason the children of God loved tears and remorse over sin, so that they might live in righteousness with tender hearts that feel God's compassion and forgiveness and thank Him at all times. This mourning is of course different from grief over the loss of material things, or not obtaining them; that is vain grief from which one must be freed.

entries.section: (2) The Beatitudes, which are the blessings

paragraphs.text: When a person is adorned with repentance, his soul grows calm, so he becomes meek within, not stirred by any gain or loss. In proportion to the strength of the spirit's relationship with God, the body grows calm and its energies are disciplined; and Christ presented Himself as the highest example of meekness for us to learn from Him.

Some think that the meek person loses his rights in this life, but God promises the meek that they shall inherit the earth. What is meant by "the earth" is not only the new earth in the Kingdom of Heaven, but also the earth on which we live, for the meek person is loved by everyone and God's blessings to him increase, material as well as spiritual, so he lacks nothing material.
The earth also signifies the body, which submits to the spirit and becomes a temple of the Holy Spirit.
The earth also signifies the wicked, who turn from their evil nature through contact with the meek, and in this way they are won for Christ.

entries.section: (2) The Beatitudes, which are the blessings

paragraphs.text: "Righteousness": it is goodness and good works, and all life in God. The perfection of righteousness is Christ, so hungering and thirsting after Him is the feeling of constant need to be filled with Him. Just as the children of Israel in the wilderness had their hunger satisfied by God with manna from heaven and their thirst quenched with water from the rock, giving them life in the barren wilderness, so Christ is our life, which we cannot live without Him. And whoever seeks Christ will surely be filled and full of joy.

This hunger and thirst drives a person to grow in the spiritual life through aspiration and increasing nearness to God, and seizing every opportunity to know Him through prayer, reading and meditation, and above all enjoying the Holy Sacraments.

entries.section: (2) The Beatitudes, which are the blessings

paragraphs.text: Mercy is feeling for the other and putting yourself in his place, so you give him, not only material or emotional needs, but participation, so you eat and move and think with him, as Christ did when He became incarnate and shared with us all of our nature except sin alone. And remember that Christ is the one with whom you are doing mercy, because He called the needy "His brethren", and what we do for them is as though we had done it for Him. The reward of mercy is that we obtain God's mercies in our life, especially in tribulation, and then in eternal bliss (see ch. 10:42, ch. 25:34-46).

entries.section: (2) The Beatitudes, which are the blessings

paragraphs.text: "Heart": it represents the inside of a person, his depths, feelings and intentions, and its purity means its being stripped of every evil desire and every worldly preoccupation that distracts from the love of God, for the heart becomes prepared for God's dwelling through purity, and is able to see God and feel that He is within it and with it in everything, not by sensory sight or hearing, but by spiritual perception, because it is deeper than sensory things, and very satisfying to the soul; and all the preceding qualities come together to qualify the soul for the purity by which we see God.

entries.section: (2) The Beatitudes, which are the blessings

paragraphs.text: "Peace": it is the steadiness of the heart, its rest and joy. Making peace begins with oneself, so I live in peace, and this requires giving up everything that disturbs, of bad desires and earthly greed, indeed being ready to give up all rights and keep the most important right, which is inner peace.

And if we have gained our peace, we can make peace with others through love and prayers for them, and helping them out of their troubles, even if we bear with them much because they are poor souls who have lost their peace. Peace is submission to God, the God of heaven, who grants it as a gift to those who love Him. And He made peace between earth and heaven, and a reconciliation between them, by His blood on the Cross. If we strive to seek peace, we are truly His children.

entries.section: (2) The Beatitudes, which are the blessings

paragraphs.text: The eighth and last beatitude results from all the seven preceding qualities, and it is enduring persecutions for the sake of the pure life and faithfulness, and for the sake of obeying Christ and His commandments. And the Lord promises us, in return for the limited sufferings of this life, the glories of the Kingdom of Heaven which never end. "Righteousness": that is, goodness and works of good and life with God, and this is a condition for the heavenly reward, because if people wrong us not for our righteousness but for mistakes that we made, this is our natural recompense.
"Revile": that is, mock you and your Christ and all your beliefs and upright conduct.
"All manner of evil": these are false accusations that the wicked claim against you, as they did in the days of the Roman persecution, and in every generation.
"Rejoice, and be exceeding glad": because you have shared with Christ in His sufferings, and because of the heavenly glories that await you in return for all that you endured.
"Great": to show the measure of the heavenly blessings that cannot be expressed.

And He calls us to confidence in our righteous conduct, whatever doubts and claims of the wicked we endure, knowing that they are our way to receive our heavenly reward, especially as all the prophets and saints endured for God's sake, for endurance is an essential condition for obtaining the Kingdom.
And the texts of these beatitudes are the qualities of the Christian person, none of which can be dispensed with in order to obtain the eight rewards.
And before us is our highest example, Christ, so that we may find the practical application of all these qualities in Him.
If you seek happiness and long to reach the Kingdom, you must acquire virtue, and labor to acquire it, and so rejoice in Christ's dwelling in you.

Examine your life, to know the recurring sin that you suffer from, and strive to acquire the virtue that is the opposite of your sin. If you suffer from pride, learn humility. If you are fought by impurity, you need purity ... and the guidance of your father of confession will benefit you greatly in this matter.

Christ likened His children to the salt that salts the earth, that is, earthly people bound to the world. Salt is distinguished by dissolving in food, giving it a better taste without canceling its original flavor, like the Christian who influences others so that they come to a better life without losing their own personalities.

Salt is cheap and spread easily throughout the whole world, like the humble Christian whose service spreads to every person. Salt is white in color, so it signifies purity and chastity. It is also used to preserve foods from corruption, just as the Christian preserves himself and those around him and establishes them in life with God.

The real problem is that the salt on which we rely to set everyone right should spoil. And when does salt spoil? (1) If it is mixed with foreign substances, so that its effect weakens, like the Christian's mixing with the wicked and being influenced by them. (2) If moisture enters it and weakens its saltiness, and this signifies luxury and indulgence in bodily ease and the desires of a corrupt life.

(3) If it is mixed with water and an electric current passes through it, it turns into harmful substances such as caustic soda, and this signifies the Christian's submission to the evil powers of the world, such as attachment to the love of money and various desires, which fill his heart and change him from his nature, and he becomes harmful and corrupting to those around him who see him as an example, and so he becomes a stumbling block to them.

Then a problem appears, namely: with what shall we salt or set others right? And from another side: what shall we do with this spoiled salt? It has lost its work and the purpose of its existence in life, and nothing awaits it but to be cast out of the Kingdom, and to suffer the pains of being trodden underfoot, that is, eternal torment, and a crushing that never ends.
He likens the Christian to the light whose function is to give light to others, and it is distinguished by the following:
(1) It guides others on the path of their life.
(2) It reveals to them evil and everything that harms them so that they may keep away from it.
(3) It helps them to do good, for work is done in the light and not in the darkness.
(4) Light is strong, it does not fear the darkness, that is, evil, but rather the darkness flees from it.

So the Christian must be in the loftiness of a spiritual life like a city built on a hill, whose light cannot be hidden, like the moon which lights the world with its light that reflects the light of the sun, which is God; He asks us to give light to the whole world by our good life.

He also likens the life of the Christian to a lamp (a light or oil lamp) in a house, whose purpose is to light this house, and it is placed on a lampstand or a high place so that its light reaches all parts of the house; and it is illogical to put a measure over the lamp to hide its light.

"Bushel": it is a vessel with a narrow mouth and a larger base, used to determine the volume of grain when it is sold, and if it is placed over the lamp it hides its light completely. It signifies material things, mental measurements, and the cares of the world that prevent the light, "the light of the work of the Holy Spirit in us", from going forth to shine for others.

He asks us to be an example to others in good works, so that they may see Christ in us, and the work of His Holy Spirit, and so glorify God and be drawn to life with Him; and our purpose in good works should not be pride and the praise of people and our own glory, but we walk in righteousness for God's sake as an example to others, and so draw hearts to the love of God.

You have an essential role in the world, which is showing Christ in your words and your conduct in every place you go to or are in. So ask yourself at the end of every day: have I shown Christ in my home and my work and every place I went? so that you repent of your sins and are careful in your conduct, and so gain yourself and those around you.
Christ is God, the giver of the Law. Consequently, it is unreasonable that He should destroy what He established, but He became incarnate to fulfil it; how?
A) In Him all the types and prophecies in the Old Testament are fulfilled, as Matthew the Evangelist mentions this phrase: "That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophets"...
B) He Himself fulfills every law on our behalf, since we were unable to fulfill it, as He says to John the Baptist: "it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness" (ch. 3:15).
C) He fulfills the Law in our lives by the power of His Holy Spirit, for if we were unable by our own strength to fulfill it, the Holy Spirit supports us and strengthens us.
D) He completes the details of the commandments, giving their causes and roots so that we may avoid them; murder, for example, begins with anger, and adultery begins with an evil look.
"The law or the prophets": by these he means all the books of the Old Testament.
"Verily": it means "Amen", and what is meant is the establishing and confirming of what He will declare in the verse.
"Heaven and earth": an expression for the most stable things in the world, to make clear the steadfastness of God's word in the Holy Bible until the end of the ages.
"One jot or one tittle": that is, the smallest teaching cannot change.

"Till all be fulfilled": until God's plan for the salvation of His children is completed on the day of judgment, and the application of the whole Law is completed, by the glorification of God's children and the torment of the wicked.
The scribes and Pharisees kept the Law literally, but they broke it by their deeds.

For despite the importance of the letter, what is more important is carrying it out in practice. Whoever neglects the smallest commandment, and knows it, will be the lowest and least person in the Kingdom of the New Testament, that is, the Church, and he must repent quickly so as not to lose his eternity. For whoever breaks one of the commandments and rejects it deliberately has rejected them all. But as for the one who sins through his weakness, repentance wipes away the sins in the sacrament of confession.
But whoever joins his teaching of the commandments with doing them in his life, he is called great in the Church and the eternal Kingdom.

Then Christ calls His followers to let their righteousness exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees, so that they not be content with keeping the letters of the Law, but must apply its commandments practically in their lives, because if they do not apply the Law they will not enter the Kingdom of Heaven.

"The least commandments": they are those that concern keeping away from something, or paying careful attention to something small. They are as important as the great commandments such as the Ten Commandments.

The scribes and Pharisees: the Jews thought that because of the abundant knowledge of these two groups, they were the greatest example of life with God, so Christ made clear the necessity that the righteousness of anyone who wants to be saved must exceed this theoretical righteousness.

May you apply in your life what you say to others before you teach it to someone else, so you experience it and receive its blessing, and your words are more effective on your hearers. All your spiritual knowledge, God gave to you first before you teach it to others. So accept everything you read or hear for practical application, and so you save yourself and those who hear you, for an upright conduct appears in your life that becomes an example to others without your being aware of it.

If the Beatitudes spoke of the positive qualities in the Christian person and their rewards, Christ now mentions the negative sins and how to treat them, and takes for example a difficult commandment, which is "Thou shalt not kill", and so He brings its root, which is the sin of anger, because if we keep away from anger, we will of course not kill anyone. The scribes, Pharisees and elders of the Jews used to punish whoever killed deliberately, while the one who killed unintentionally fled to the cities of refuge. They gave no attention to inward anger, but were content with carrying out anger outwardly in murder. And in order that Christ might make clear the seriousness of anger, He said: "Whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause", that is, because of vain, passing material things, "shall be in danger of the judgment", the judgment of the small courts that were set up throughout the Jewish land, in which 23 judges from among the elders ordinarily sat, and this judgment could be appealed or reviewed in the higher courts, the greatest of which was the "Sanhedrin" council in Jerusalem, which consisted of seventy of the great elders of Jerusalem, the heads of the Jews, and for this reason it is also called the council of the seventy, and it is the highest council to which all the subordinate councils belong. It was also the greatest Jewish authority making decisions in the religious matters of the Jews, and many of the scribes were also members of this council.
What is meant by anger here is inward anger of the heart, without showing any expression of it.

As for "whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca", which is a Syriac word expressing contempt joined with anger, this deserves trial by "the council", that is, the Sanhedrin council, which consists of the great elders of Jerusalem.
But if a person goes further in his anger and describes his brother as foolish and stupid, he deserves "hell fire".

"Gehenna": taken from the valley of Hinnom, into which the remains of sacrifices were thrown, and worms spread in them, and they burned them with fire, so the fire was never put out in this valley. For this reason God likened eternal torment to the fire that is not quenched and the worm that dies not, in the valley of Hinnom, but in a spiritual way that is more tormenting and severe. And here Christ shows His rejection of anger and its seriousness, for even inward anger deserves judgment before God, and consequently any expression of it will lead a person to eternal perdition.

Christ declares clearly that prayers and gifts offered to God are not accepted from the angry person, or the one who wrongs others, or the quarrelsome, because God wants the prayers offered from a pure heart full of love.

If one of the Jews offered his sacrifice as a gift to God, and then remembered and noticed that there was a quarrel between him and someone, he should not complete the offering of his sacrifice, but first be reconciled with his brother, then return and complete the offering of his sacrifice, so that it may be accepted by God. "Thy brother hath ought against thee": He did not say that you have something against him, so call yourself to account for your duties before your rights.
"Leave": it makes clear the importance of reconciliation and offering love before worship, because if the heart is purified by love it is acceptable to God, and so is the worship it offers.

"Go thy way": that is, take care to reconcile with your brother even if he has wronged you, as Christ Himself commands, saying: "If thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault" (ch. 18:15).

It is necessary to purify the heart of all anger before prayer, whether in the closet of your house or in the church, and especially when partaking of the Holy Sacraments, because your prayers are not accepted if you have not purified your heart.

So hasten to reconcile with others, even if they have wronged you, and so win them by love, and do not be troubled by their pride or harshness, but pray for them that anger may be removed from their hearts, and care for your peace before everything.

Your "adversary" is the commandments of God, or your conscience which reminds you of God's word, or the Holy Spirit dwelling in you, since you have come into a quarrel with Him because of your falling into evil.

"The way": it is this life. If you submit to the voice of the Holy Spirit and the conscience, and obey the commandment, keeping away from anger, malice and all evil, you save yourself and are reconciled with this adversary; but if you are not reconciled with him by submitting to him and repenting, he delivers you to "the judge", who is God the just Judge on the day of judgment, and he sentences you to eternal perdition, and delivers you to "the officer", who are the angels who cast you into prison, that is, eternal torment, and "Thou shalt by no means come out thence, till thou hast paid the uttermost farthing" (all your debts down to the smallest coin). And because your sin is unlimited, since it is against the unlimited God, its punishment is unlimited, and consequently you remain in eternal torment.

May you guard against the sin of anger, and not give yourself excuses to persist in it, but have compassion on others however great their faults, so you protect yourself from the evil results of anger, and regain your peace, and return to your spiritual way that leads to the Kingdom, and win the souls of those around you.

Adultery is looking with the intent of lust, and this gives rise to delight in lust in the thought, which leads to falling in deed in its various degrees. Therefore Christ wanted to cut off the sin from its root, which is looking, making clear that it is counted as adultery, so that no one may be lax about his look or thoughts or feelings and think this ordinary, otherwise he will go further and regard even evil touches as ordinary. And if he falls into complete adultery, he may excuse himself, and so the door of repentance is closed before him, because of his laxity and justification of the sin.
As for you, O man of God, flee from looking needlessly so that you do not fall into evil sights, as a person flees from a snake or a scorpion.
Since a person, because of his weakness, is exposed to falling by looking or by deed, Christ says:

If you have fallen into an evil look, pluck out your right eye which has offended you and made you fall into the sin of adultery. And if you have stolen, cut off your right hand which has offended you.

What is meant here is not the literal meaning, for what is the difference between the right eye and the left? Rather the right signifies strength and importance, and so it points to the very close friend, or the beloved desire, or anything dear to you like the eye or the hand, which you must keep away from and give up attachment to, so that you do not fall into sin, and your end be eternal torment.

Examine, my brother, the sources of your falling into sin, whether adultery or any other sin, and give them up and keep away from them however dear they are to you, so that you gain the salvation of your soul and your eternity.
"A writing of divorcement": the husband sits with one of the scribes and has a record of divorce written, which gives the wife freedom to be joined to another.

The pagan world allowed divorce for any reason, especially the Greeks among whom debauchery and adultery in their temples had spread. As for the Jews, he had to reconsider and write a bill of divorce, perhaps so that he might go back on his decision, if he felt that his wife would belong to another, and his anger and distress would calm down.
