As for Christ, He shows the greatness of the sacrament of marriage, that it is a union that cannot be separated, unless one of the parties is joined in adultery, for then he has separated himself from the other and divided this union. But whoever divorces his wife for any other reason makes her commit adultery if she is joined to another, because she is still his wife before God, and the new husband is counted an adulterer because he married another man's wife.

And Christ here does not oppose the Law of Moses written in (Deut 24:1) permitting divorce and writing a bill for it, but returns matters to their origin. Moses was compelled, as a result of his people's mixing with the Egyptians and their becoming accustomed to divorce, to set limits for them, that a person should reconsider and write a certificate of it. But this was not God's intention when He created man to be united with the other in the sacrament of marriage, when He said: "Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh" (Gen 2:24), and He gave no permission for divorce except in the case of adultery, because it separates the two bodies of the spouses when one of them is joined to another body. Let us sanctify the sacrament of marriage, to rise above the causes of disputes, and try to resolve them by spiritual guidance, repentance, and clinging to the Church.
(8) Al-Qa

33- "Again, ye have heard that it hath been said by them of old time, Thou shalt not forswear thyself, but shalt perform unto the Lord thine oaths: 34- But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God's throne: 35- Nor by the earth; for it is his footstool: neither by Jerusalem; for it is the city of the great King. 36- Neither shalt thou swear by thy head, because thou canst not make one hair white or black. 37- But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil."

God permitted His people of old to swear (take oaths) by His name, in order to direct their hearts to His worship, and not to swear by the pagan gods. What He forbade them was forswearing, that is, swearing falsely. The meaning of that is carrying out what they swore, like vows which must be fulfilled when a person utters them, and he promised God to fulfill them.

And the scribes and Pharisees used to teach that the oath by the name of the Lord is the one that must be fulfilled, while an oath by anything else can be retracted. This is of course a wrong teaching which Christ opposes here, and corrects in the following verses, teaching not to swear or take oaths at all.
In the New Testament the Law is fulfilled by forbidding oaths, because God's name is too exalted to be said for material dealings, but is to be mentioned for worship and for blessing our life.
"God's throne": heaven signifies the presence of God because of its loftiness and height, so it suits His exaltedness.
"His footstool": the earth and earthly things are lower than heaven, therefore it was called a footstool for God's feet.
From another side, we do not own anything in the world, but we are stewards over it, so how do we swear by something we do not own? God alone is able to swear, because He owns everything.
And Christ makes clear that we do not own even one hair of our heads, and are unable to change its color.

Consequently, it is not right to swear by the life of a person or anything of the creatures in the world; therefore He asks that our speech be simple, free of oaths, that is, we do not need to prove it by an oath, and our answer to others is only yes or no.

"Yea, yea; Nay, nay": that is, we do not use the oath, and we declare facts or our agreement with what others say with the word yes, or forbid and refuse what does not suit us with the word "no", without needing to prove that with the words of an oath. "Of evil": that is, the use of the oath is the work of Satan the evil one, for he is the one who brought about lying and deceit, and calls people to swear to prove their lies.

Forbidding the oath restrains anger, so that it does not go on to binding decisions, and it is a mark of Christians in their innocence. An oath is not a proof of truthfulness, but the wicked use it in lying to reach their aims. Be careful with your words, so that God's name is in them for blessing, and keep away from lying, and consequently you do not need to prove your statements with false oaths. And do not make light of God's name, or the lives of people, by swearing by them carelessly merely out of the habit of repeating them.

In the Old Testament God wanted to establish the idea of divine justice, and the need for redemption, that if a person sinned he needs a man like himself to redeem him. The eye is redeemed by an eye, and the tooth (singular of teeth) is redeemed by a tooth like it. And because sin is unlimited, since it is against God, it needed an unlimited redemption, that is, by the death of God incarnate, Christ our God.
He also wanted by this commandment "an eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth", that a person should not repay evil with greater evil, but it is enough to repay with evil like that which befell him.
These are the commandments of the Old Testament, because the level of understanding of the people could not bear more than this.
And a person in his spiritual maturity progresses through six degrees before the evil that befalls him:
(1) Assaulting others with evil, and this is the barbaric way.
(2) Meeting evil with greater evil, because the other began with evil.
(3) Meeting evil with evil like it, and not more, as in the Jewish Law.
(4) Meeting evil with lesser evil, and this has self-control in it.
(5) Not answering evil, but keeping silent, and this is complete self-control.
(6) Meeting evil with good, and this is the Christian level, the highest of the degrees.

Christ warns us not to let the heart be agitated so as to answer evil with other evil, because if the heart is filled with love, it finds an excuse for the other, and is not disturbed by outward insult to the body, that is, the slap. The literal meaning in the slap is not what is intended, because a person is slapped on his left cheek and not the right, unless the striker is left-handed, that is, uses his left hand, so the slap falls on the right cheek. But the spiritual meaning is what is intended, which is forgiveness and endurance, indeed continuing to endure by accepting a second slap, that is, a second insult.
He gives another example in endurance and forgiveness, which is if a quarrel occurs and the other tries to seize your coat.
"Coat": it is the inner garment like a robe, and the Law ordains that no one take it because it is the covering of the poor (Ex 22:26-27).
"Cloak": it is the outer mantle, and it is more costly.

In this way we meet injustice with love, and with a gift greater than the wrongdoer wanted, however severe the injustice, so the wrongdoer is ashamed and his anger calms. And this cannot be done except from a heart full of love and satisfied with God, who easily gives up material things, even if the other thinks at first that he gained something from him and exploited him, but he stands amazed before this wonderful love, for it is a silent proclamation you offer to the wicked so that they may repent, confident that God compensates you many times over, not only in heaven but on earth as well, because His promise is clear: "There is no man that hath left house, or brethren, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my sake, and the gospel's, But he shall receive an hundredfold now in this time ... and in the world to come eternal life" (Mk 10:29-30).
Forced labor: it is work without pay. If someone compels you to do a work, offer him a greater service, and so you win him by your love, and receive heavenly blessings.
The second mile: it is love, with which you put out the evil and injustice of others.

If you find a needy person who asks you, give to him. This is a giving up of the love of money, and a feeling for the other, and not looking at him as covetous, for his covetousness may be the result of his feeling of deprivation, so bear with him. And he may be ashamed to beg from you, so he asks for a loan while unable to repay it, so do not demand it of him, but leave it to him as a gift of love from you.

And of course, all this is according to the love that is in your heart. If you are not able to have this love, then at least bear with him and forgive him. And do not be selfish and stingy in your giving, because God said clearly: "Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy" (v. 7).

If you believe in love, you can put out all the flame of evil in those around you, for love is stronger than hatred. Have compassion with your love on the angry and the covetous, for they are sick and need the medicine which is love, whether by bearing with them and praying for them, or speaking with them gently in place of their bad words, or offering them services; and you cannot bear with them and love them unless your heart is filled with the love of God.
So care for your spiritual relationship with God, and ask His help, and you will be able to overflow with love from Him upon others.
"Thy neighbour": in the view of the Pharisees he is the Jew, but Christ's interpretation is that he is every person, as in the parable of the Good Samaritan (Lk 10:30-37).
The Law in the Old Testament commanded love of neighbor, so that a person may come out of his selfishness and love his relatives and those close to him.

"And hate thine enemy": it is an addition by the Pharisees that the Law did not decree, and perhaps they deduced it from God's command to destroy the wicked from the Promised Land, that is, to remove evil.

Yet the Law approved helping the enemy if his donkey fell under its load (Ex 23:4-5). And it also commanded that the Edomite not be hated because he is a brother, nor the Egyptian because he was a stranger in his land, though they were among the fiercest enemies who humbled them and fought them (Deut 23:7).

With spiritual maturity in the New Testament, the Law demanded love for enemies, because their nature was created pure by God, and the evil in them is an intruder upon them from the devil. So we do not look at them as wicked, but as sick people needing love and compassion, so we bless them with kind words, and the words of evil on their lips fall silent. And by doing good with them, their hearts grow calm. And we pray for them, that God may remove from them their bad thoughts, and in this way we win them for ourselves as friends in faith and love.

"Bless": love is not limited to inner feelings, but comes out in kind and encouraging words. "Do good": love is also tied to offering services and kindnesses to those who have fallen into the case of hatred toward us. "Pray": this is the lowest degree of love, or the means that cannot be prevented, because one who is hostile to us may refuse to speak with us or accept our services, but he cannot prevent us from praying for him, however much he persecutes us.

"The children of your Father": God is love, and the proof of our sonship is that we love everyone, including the wicked and those who wrong us. By this love we become like God, who loved us and died for us on the Cross, we who disobeyed Him and defied Him and crucified Him.
And God continues in His giving to all mankind, whether those who believe in Him or those who reject Him, for He makes His sun to rise on all, and His rains water all.
And He used the sun and the rain because of their benefit to all mankind, and because they are in heaven they signify God's heavenly gifts.
If God gives light to all and satisfies all, then offer your love to everyone you meet, and forget yourself, enduring sufferings for Christ's sake, however much others wrong you.
"The publicans": they are the collectors of the Roman taxes, and are marked by greed and harshness, so they were the worst group in society, and their name is tied to sinners.

Christ declares clearly that our love for those who love us is something ordinary, which the wicked share with us, who are represented by the publicans marked by harshness and greed. But our distinction as Christians is that we love and give peace, and do good to those who wrong us and are hostile to us.

"Salute": the Law decreed not saluting the Gentiles, and limited it to the Jews, and by this the deficiency of love appears, and its not being wide enough to include all mankind, so the law of the New Testament commanded love for all.
"Be ye therefore perfect": that is, strive toward perfection.

Christ confirms that this is the perfection of love, that is, love for enemies, so that we become children of the perfect God, and He calls us to strive toward the perfection which cannot be fully reached, but God rejoices in this striving because He is the Perfect One, so this is striving toward Him.
The Sermon on the Mount continued; Spiritual practices; Detachment

Christ speaks here about the basic pillars of worship, which are almsgiving, prayer and fasting. Perhaps He begins with almsgiving as an extension of His previous words about offering love and doing good to everyone, even enemies. And He sets a basic condition for the acceptance of almsgiving, which is that it be for God's sake, and not with the aim that people should see us and glorify us, because if we receive the praise of people, we have no reward with God. In ancient times the hypocrites did not give alms because of their love for God and for the needy, but gave alms for their personal glory, so they sounded trumpets so that people would gather and see the greatness of their giving and glorify them.

"Your Father which is in heaven": he means God, who is exalted above the earthly, passing thoughts of the hypocrites, and with whom we prepare to be in eternal life, and receive the reward of our righteous life on earth in the eternal heavenly inheritance.

"Hypocrites": those who show what is different from what they hold within; their appearance is the work of mercy, and their reality is pride and seeking the praise of people; and what is meant here is the scribes and Pharisees.
"In the synagogues and in the streets": where people are numerous, so that they may offer them greater praise.
The left hand: it signifies giving to win the praise of people.

The right hand: it signifies blessing and obedience to the commandment, that is, giving for God's sake. He also means that giving should be in secret, so that it is hidden even from those nearest to us, like the nearness of one hand to the other; then almsgiving is for God's sake alone, and we receive the eternal reward, which will be before all creation, and God also blesses us in our earthly life before all.

This does not mean that a person should not give if there is someone who sees him, for we do not withhold giving because it cannot be hidden, but let us have the spirit of secrecy, and not be occupied with the opinion of people.
Care for the needy who cannot ask openly, for these who are concealed may be more in need than all, and thank God who permitted you to give to Him in the form of these needy ones.
Christ did not tell us the details of individual or communal prayer, but left these details to the Church, to arrange by His Holy Spirit.

He spoke of the essence of prayer, that it be a personal bond of love between man and God. How, then, do you put it on display before people to receive their glory, whether in crowded places like the synagogues where the assembled see you, or in the corners of the streets so that those coming from the different streets see you? In this you will receive the glory of people, and lose the eternal reward.

Therefore the children of God should pray in secret, and shut the doors so that no one sees them. What is meant is the doors of the heart before the material doors, because if a person enters his closet, and his heart wishes that people know that he is inside praying so that they may glorify him, he will not receive God's blessing. This does not mean that a person should be troubled if someone sees him while he prays, whether in his own room or in the church or in any place, but what matters is that his heart not desire that people see him and glorify him.

In ancient times some, in pagan worship and then among the Jews, used to read prayers and repeat them many times, thinking that by much repetition the prayer is answered; this is vain repetition which benefits nothing. But sound repetition is persistence with God in supplication and faith, that is, the person understands what he says, and it is not merely the repetition of the lips.

And Christ affirms that God knows our needs, so repetition is of no use, as though God did not hear. All that He awaits from us is to turn to Him and open our hearts to Him. When we show our sonship and our clinging to Him, He pours out His mercies upon us; God awaits our asking, because He loves us, and knows our need, and wishes to give to us if we love Him and ask Him. If you are occupied during prayer with people's opinion of you, and they approve of your words, you have received your reward on earth, and this prayer profits you nothing before God. So open your heart in your own room, or away from eyes, to express all your feelings in words and tears and prostration, and your heart is comforted by the grace of God, who hears you and rejoices in your prayer.
Christ Himself gave us the example that we follow in all our prayers, which is the Lord's Prayer, which we recite often before, during and at the end of our prayers.

The Lord's Prayer includes three petitions for the glorification of God's name, which are petitions of love for His person and extend to find their fulfillment in eternity, then three other petitions for our material needs, to teach us to honor God and glorify Him before asking anything for ourselves.

"Our Father": this prayer begins by showing our special sonship to God, so we enter prayer with this boldness, and this Father of ours is exalted above all sin, so if we are His children, we walk in purity as heavenly beings while we are on earth. He is not exalted in the visible heaven, but dwells in our hearts, which are purified by repentance and by His love, and so become a heaven. "Hallowed be thy name": God's name means all of God, for a person's name indicates all that is in him. We do not ask for God's holiness because He is holy in Himself, but for His being hallowed in our sight and in our life, that is, that our hearts be pure and consecrated to Him, so that they are fit for His dwelling, so we reject all evil by repentance, and prepare our hearts for prayers, meditations and every good work.

"Thy kingdom come": God is the owner of everything in the world, but we ask that He reign over our hearts, so that we may enjoy His fatherhood, care and love. In this we drive out every sin that has control over us, and every earthly attachment. It also means our longing for the heavenly Kingdom in eternity, where God reigns without hindrance over our hearts and completes our joy.

"Thy will be done": we, as children of God, ask for His will and not our will, because our will is liable to error, but His will is always good for our benefit. And He, in His fatherhood, seeks our good and our arrival at His blessed eternity. "In earth, as it is in heaven": the angels in heaven submit to God, and we wish to obey His word on earth as they obey Him in heaven, for there the conflict between body and spirit ceases, and a person lives in constant enjoyment of God. Therefore we wish that our earthly life be turned into a heavenly life, in which the body agrees with the spirit in the love of God and service of Him.
Heaven also signifies holiness, so as the saints live seeking God's will, we also wish to be like them.
And heaven points spiritually to faith, where the faithful are happy with life with God; so we ask that all the earth believe in God and become a heaven.
"Our daily bread": it is sometimes translated "our bread for tomorrow" or "our coming bread" or "our essential bread".
"Daily" (sufficient): the bread that suffices us today, and we are not anxious or occupied with the future.
Our bread for tomorrow or the coming bread: that is, the heavenly spiritual food, which we need to taste from now on earth.
Essential: that is, the spiritual food, which is the most important, to distinguish it from the passing material food.
All these translations mean one spiritual idea, which is: give us our necessary bread, that is:

(1) Our necessary material needs that suffice us today, and we do not care about tomorrow since we trust in Your care, and that You will always supply our needs, so our heart is occupied with soaring in Your love.
(2) The word of God through the Holy Bible, and prayer and the Midnight Praise (Tasbeha), for they satisfy us more than material food.
(3) Partaking of the Holy Mysteries, whether by partaking daily, or by feeling it if we partake at longer intervals (weekly, for example).

We learn from all the preceding meanings, whether the material bread whose sweetness we feel because it is God's heavenly gift to us, or the sense of Christ with us daily through the means of grace and the Holy Sacraments, that all these are a pledge of the Kingdom which we taste on earth so that we long for heaven.
The petition for forgiveness of sin is a clear confession that we are sinners offering repentance before God, confident of His forgiveness and His love that does not reject us.

It also means our weakness and constant need for forgiveness, because, although our nature was renewed in Baptism, we are liable to fall into sin every day, so we receive forgiveness in the prayer of repentance and the sacrament of confession. The Lord's Prayer sets a condition for obtaining forgiveness, which is love for others and forbearance and forgiving their sins, because it is unreasonable for the hard-hearted, unforgiving person, who is a judge of others, to obtain forgiveness from God. If God is ready to forgive our sins against Him, which are unlimited sins since He is unlimited, then all the more should we forgive our brethren their sins against us, because they are limited sins, since we are limited. So when you forgive another you gain the greater thing, which is God's forgiveness of your unlimited sins. And this forgiveness of yours to your brother purifies your heart so that you are worthy of God's forgiveness, but he needs to repent in order to obtain God's forgiveness.

"Lead us not into temptation": a phrase that means a person's humility and his feeling of his weakness, so he asks God to keep temptations away from him. But if God's will allows a person to pass through a temptation, let him ask God, saying: "But deliver us from evil": that is, do not allow the devil to dominate us, and do not forsake us so that we fall into temptation, but with Your help we endure it and come out of it pure, and even increase in virtue. For real temptation is not merely tribulation, but falling into sin and departing from God, and this is what we ask God to protect us from. Then He concludes the Lord's Prayer with the glorification of God, confessing, saying: "For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen."
"The kingdom": that is, He reigns over the heart as was asked previously.
"The power": a confession of God's power that is able to answer our prayer.
"The glory": He is worthy of glorification and honor at all times.
And this confession means submission to God, not by the lips only, but by deed as well.

The last three petitions concern our life on earth, because in heaven we do not need material food, or a pledge of the Kingdom, because we will have reached it, and there is no sin, so we do not need forgiveness, and there is no temptation or Satan to fear.
Because of the importance of loving others, God repeats the necessity of forgiving them and being forbearing with them, otherwise we lose all the blessings of the Lord's Prayer and God's love for us.
And because of its importance, He repeats it twice in these two verses.

May you be aware of the meanings of this prayer when you recite it every day, so that you enter into God's presence with the boldness of sonship and seek His glory, and declare your longing for Him. Then, with the need of a son, ask all that you want, confident of His love.
"When ye fast": just as almsgiving and prayer are necessary, so also is fasting.
And He speaks here about its manner, while the arrangement of communal fasts He left to the Apostles and the holy Fathers in the first generations.
"Of a sad countenance": the scribes and Pharisees, when they fasted, did not wash their faces, and put ashes on their heads so as to appear fasting before people, and so receive their praise.
"They have their reward": that is, their fasting is worthless before God.

On the contrary, Christ showed the importance of hiding the fast, because it is a personal bond of love between man and God, for he leaves something for His sake. Therefore He asked that the person's appearance be ordinary, not sad, that is, his face washed and his hair anointed.
And from the spiritual side, washing the face signifies purity from sin by repentance, and anointing the hair signifies joy in fellowship with God and in the spiritual practices during the fast.
He affirms here the importance of the divine reward for those who fast, with blessings on earth, then eternal life, as happens with those who pray and give alms.

And if your grumbling appears over the fast or any spiritual worship, you have lost your heavenly reward. So take care to hide your fast as much as you can, because it is a bond of love between you and God. But if someone knows that you are fasting, do not be troubled, because you did not seek that.

Christ warns us against placing our hope in earthly things, so that we fall into the love of possessing, because all possessions are exposed to corruption, either by insects and rust and the forces of time, or they are exposed to theft by robbers, so they are changeable and passing; how then can a person's hope be changeable and passing?! And on the other, positive side He calls us to have our treasures in heaven, far from any change or passing away, and that by exerting effort in holy worship and works of mercy.
This does not mean that saving and providing for a person's needs and various projects is regarded as wrong, but the wrong is in the heart's attachment to money and relying on it.

The place where you lay up treasure indicates the desire of your heart and your preoccupation; if your treasure is heavenly, your heart is directed toward heaven, and consequently your heart moves you to grow and become spiritually strong, and reach the Kingdom. And the opposite, if you are earthly, that is, your treasures are on earth, your end is perdition.

Overcome material things and their changes so that you do not rely on them, and so use them without attachment, content with what you have, whether much or little, giving thanks at all times for God's gifts, confident that what you have is your suitable need which God sent you. And if you want something else, ask Him, but with reliance and acceptance of His will; that is, if He sends it to you, thank Him, and if He does not send it, thank Him also, enjoying what is more important, which is your love for Him.

By the eye He means not only the outward eye but also the inward, that is, the heart. If it is single, that is, sees things as they are, as God sees them, and does not see evil, that is, sees all that is good, and does not seek excuses for faults and keeps away from them, then the body, that is, the works, becomes full of light, that is, good.

If we look at faults in order to condemn them, we are exposed to falling, and thus our works are wrong, that is, dark. The eye is the entrance of good things into the body, that is, it is what sees God in the things around it, and so leads the body to works of good. But if the eye itself is evil, it will bring new evils into the person, and his sins become very ugly.
Ask yourself how Christ would look at matters if He were in your place, so that you can see them as they truly are without personal aims or wrong thoughts, and do not mislead yourself.

Seek everything good in what is around you and thank God for it, and if you see faults in others, pray for them that God may set right what is in them and make up their shortcomings, and thus you see only God in those around you, whether good, which is from Him, or evil, which He sets right.
By money here He means all the possessions in the world, of food and clothing and anything material that we use and buy with money.

And although money is a blessing from God, attachment to it makes us enslaved to it, and we are separated from the worship of God. It is impossible to combine the two loves, so either we love God, or we love the world and the material things in it. When we love God, we use all our energies for the glory of His name, but if we love money, our whole life is directed to gathering it and delighting in it.

God shows us the importance of life with Him, so that we do not lose our life and direct it to acquiring food and clothing, but on the contrary, we are content with the least possible of them, to be free for life with God and to enjoy it in His hands, offering proof of this, which is that our life itself is better than these passing material things. And God, who gave us this life and this body, is of course able to give us what is less important, which is its needs.

God calls us to rely on Him, and offers a second proof, which is looking at the birds of the air, which fly off singing His praise, without worrying about their bodily needs and storing for the future, for God feeds them day by day.
And of course man, the head of creation, is cared for by God, who gives him his needs if he relies on Him.

Then He offers a third proof, which is: what have those concerned with material things gained, have they been able to add one cubit to their stature (about 50 cm)? For God is the one who gives the length of the body and its form, and preserves it if we rely on Him.

God gives us a fourth proof calling us to rely on Him, which is meditating on the lilies of the field, that is, the various kinds of flowers that have very beautiful forms, which man tries to imitate in the shapes of his clothes, but does not reach their beauty, for Solomon the king, despite his greatness and abundance of money, his clothes did not reach the beauty of these flowers, though they are merely grasses that grow for a few months and then wither and are burned with fire in the oven. So what is the value of man in God's sight? ... It is far greater, and God cares to clothe him and supply his needs. If he believes in God, however few his resources or works, God will provide his needs, as He gives beauty to the flowers that cannot dig or spin, so He gives them an embroidered beautiful appearance, better than all the garments spun by human hands.

In conclusion, do not be anxious about your material needs as the rest of mankind does, but be assured that God, your heavenly Father, knows your needs and will provide them for you, and care only to seek that God reign over your hearts and that you enjoy fellowship with Him, confident that the rest of the matters are very easy for God to provide for you, better than you providing them by your much preoccupation; though we must carry out our duties and not be lazy.

It is concluded from this that we should do our daily duties, and not be occupied with the future and its troubles (that is, its evil), so that the heart is free to enjoy God today, and He will arrange tomorrow.

See how much time you spend caring for material things, and how much time you are occupied with being with God? Do not forget that your goal is God, so arrange your day so that God is the priority, indeed in everything you do, see that it is pleasing to God, and likewise your words and thoughts.

And let you have spiritual ambition and constructive thoughts, confident of God's provision for your needs and His protection of you. The Sermon on the Mount continued; Not judging; Acting on the commandment

Our Lord Jesus Christ warns us not to judge others, that is, to be distressed by their faults, forgetting that we are sinners like them, and deserve that God should judge us. But by humility we receive God's forgiveness. For when we find excuses for others and show them mercy, God also has mercy on us and forgives us our sins.
So judging is not only a lack of repentance and a lack of love for others, but an encroachment on the authority of God the Judge, for we take His place and judge others.

It also carries pride in the heart, and contempt for the sinner. And not judging does not mean not discerning; rather we must discern the sin, and pray for the sinner, and love him, and find an excuse for him, and have compassion on him as a father, but we keep away from his sin and rebuke it as far as we are able, so we separate between the sin and the sinner, that is, we hate the sin and love the sinner.

"Measure": it is a vessel for measuring the volume of grain, and what is meant here is the vessel that we fill with judgment and pour out upon others, which is poured out upon us also with the same vessel, as judgment from God, and in many cases He permits us to fall into the same sin for which we judge others, until we repent and are humbled.
"Mote": a small straw or chaff, and it signifies a small sin.

"Beam": a piece of wood much larger than the mote, which blocks the sight, and signifies a great sin. Christ likens the sin of the other to the mote in his eye, but my sin to a beam in my eye, so repentance is first necessary to remove the beam from my eye, so my life is purified, and consequently I am able, by love and the work of the Holy Spirit, to see the mote that is in the other's eye, that is, his sin, and help him to be rid of it.

But my neglecting the beam in my eye by not repenting, and then presuming to judge others, pretending in hypocrisy that I want to help them remove the mote, which is a very small straw, from their eyes, is unreasonable, for how can the one whose eyes the beam blocks see a small mote in the eyes of others?!
The truth is that it is pride that drives us to judge others and not repent of our sins.
In conclusion, care for your repentance every day and pray for others if they err, and find an excuse for them.

The meaning of simplicity and love in dealing with others, so that we do not judge them, is not that we speak about the holy sacraments in the Church and the works of the Holy Spirit before unbelievers who do not appreciate their importance. In ancient times the Church used to close the doors after the catechumens were sent out, so that only the faithful remained who would partake of the Mysteries.
"Dogs": they signify attack, so they represent those who resist the truth.
"Swine": in their lack of understanding, they trample and defile everything because of their filthiness, so they signify contempt for the truth.
That is, simplicity is joined with wisdom in dealing with others.

Among holy things also are personal spiritual experiences, which are not told except to the father of confession, or without mentioning the name, so that we keep our humility, and do not expose these divine dealings to the lack of appreciation of others. You need to discern between truth and falsehood, and between the righteous and the wicked, but you say the suitable word at the suitable time, so do not speak to beginners about high spiritual matters that make life with God difficult. You have the right to ask and understand everything for the growth of your spiritual life, but speak only of what benefits you and benefits others.
God, in His fatherly love, wants to give us everything. But He gives only to the one who appreciates the gift, and this appreciation appears in asking for it from God.

God gives general gifts to all mankind, such as the sun, the air, the water ... and so on. But, in His love, He wants to give more than this. So if He finds us neglectful of praying to Him, He stirs us to ask Him, so that we receive from Him ... and if He delays in answering to test our faith, we ask from Him and press Him, and so find our needs in Him. And if God's door remains closed and He does not answer, we knock until He opens to us, and we are confident that He will surely answer all who pray to Him, as long as their prayers are according to His will and for their good.

Christ offers us a logical proof of His fatherly love. Human fatherhood cares for the requests of the children, and cannot give them the opposite of their requests, as long as the need is real, necessary and beneficial. No father gives his son a stone instead of bread, or a serpent instead of fish, to eat.
If fatherhood according to the flesh has this love, how much more God, the source of fatherhood and love, who gives good things to His children who trust Him and ask their needs from Him?!

"Evil": all mankind, because they fall into evil, but by instinct they care to give good gifts to their children. "Your Father which is in heaven": showing that God is the source of fatherhood and tenderness.
"Good things": that is, good gifts that His children need.
"To them that ask him": those who hold fast to their prayers in faith and persistence, and rely on God.
Do not listen to the devil's doubts if God delays in answering your requests, but press Him, confident of His love, and that He gives you at the suitable time what is for your good.

In order that God may answer our requests, we must do good to others. If we want them to do good to us, let us begin first to do so; for love of others is the fulfillment of the commandment and the Law. When you meet any person, put yourself in his place, and think what he expects from you, so that you offer him the love he needs, or the care and sympathy and support he awaits. And if someone wrongs you, do not hasten to answer him or judge him in your heart, but feel his circumstances so as to find an excuse for him and be tender toward him, even if only with a prayer in your heart.

"False prophets": they are those who teach doctrines foreign to the Church, and deceive people with their pleasant appearance, but their hearts within are savage and harsh. They think inwardly of what is for their own benefit, and not for the glory of God as they claim; so Christ warns us to keep away from them and to remain steadfast in the Church. "Sheep's clothing": that is, they are wolves with the appearance of lambs, meaning their pretending to piety and virtues in order to deceive the simple, and draw them away from the Church and its gatherings, and make them attach themselves to foreign gatherings, and deceive them that this is the right interpretation of the word of God.

To know the truth about these prophets, we look at their "fruits", that is, their character and deeds, because if the heart is harsh, however much it pretends, its harshness will be exposed in some situations.

"Thorns": they represent the absence of blessing and the wronging of others, so they make no sacrifice (which is signified by the grape that is pressed and yields wine, that is, joy), for the selfish, harsh person does not care to give of himself for others. "Thistles": a dry plant resembling thorns in its smallness, which cannot give figs.
The fig fruit: it is made of small seeds united together in love inside a single covering, so it signifies unity and love.

The person who is isolated in selfishness alone cannot be united with others in a oneness of love. So it is natural that the good tree, that is, the heart that loves God, will give good fruits. And the opposite is true, for the evil person will do evils.
So the heart must be changed by repentance, that the fruits may become good.
"Is cast into the fire": just as it is customary to burn useless trees, so these false teachers have nothing awaiting them but torment in the eternal fire.

If these wicked persist in their misleading teachings, their end will be perdition, that is, the eternal fire. So we must be careful before following any person, and be certain of his conduct and virtues, and that he is a son of the Church and submissive to the spiritual fathers.

Be discerning toward those around you while keeping your love for them. Do not be led after teachings foreign to the spirit of the Church, or attend gatherings that do not have the official character and church affiliation, or host people you do not know on the pretext that they will speak to you about God. Remain steadfast in your Church and your holy sacraments and your spiritual gatherings, and so you grow in the knowledge and love of God.
Christ concludes His Sermon on the Mount by affirming the importance of acting on His commandments, and not merely hearing them and admiring them.
"Wise": that is, he examines his life and is careful in his conduct.

The one who acts on the commandment He likens to a man who wanted to build a house to live in, so he dug in the ground and deepened the digging until he reached the rock, and laid the foundation of his house on it, then built it and raised it into the air; and when the sky rained violent torrents, and the torrents rushed like rivers and struck this house, accompanied by stormy winds, they could not shake it, because it was founded on the rock.

"The rock": it points to Christ, since He said of Himself that He is the chief cornerstone (ch. 21:42), and the Apostle Paul said that Christ is the foundation on which the spiritual house is built (1 Cor 3:11), so the foundation must be laid on Him, that is, faith in Him, for building our spiritual life, steadfast in the Church, His body, and united with Him in the holy sacraments.
"The rain ... the floods": they signify material desires.
"The winds": they signify temptations and the wars of Satan.
If these rise against us, they will not be able to shake our life, because we obey the commandments of Christ.

"Foolish": he does not want to understand or to labor in caring for the salvation of his soul. The one who is content with knowing Christ, and does not want to labor in carrying out His commandments, is like one who does not want the labor of deep digging, that is, he refuses to carry the cross, and to go deeper in the knowledge of God and the carrying out of His commandments, since he is a lover of appearances.
"Sand": it signifies weakness of faith, and likewise the false speech of heresies, which promises people salvation without striving.

Since they refuse the labor of carrying out the commandment, if temptations and the devil's wars rise against them, their whole spiritual building falls, and they go far from God, and their end is eternal perdition.
"Great": that is, a complete collapse of the person, and eternal perdition.
Commit yourself to a specific spiritual discipline every day, so that the word of God which you read may be turned into practical action in your life.
Since the crowds were moved by His words, hearts were attached to Him, so they followed Him to hear more of His sermons.
And Christ welcomed them so as to work His miracles before them, and so establish their faith. And He walked on the plain beside the Sea of Tiberias on His way to the city of Capernaum.

The disease of leprosy appears in the form of spots on the skin, so it resembles the present disease of vitiligo, and also some of the affected parts can separate from the body, so it also resembles the disease of leprosy (Hansen's disease), and it signifies uncleanness, and whoever is struck by it must be isolated from people whatever his position, and must tear his clothes and cover his moustache and bare his head. And if someone approaches him, he cries: "Unclean, unclean", to warn him to keep away from him (Lev 13:45). This disease no longer exists at present.

And while Christ was coming down from the mountain (and this signifies Christ's condescension in love to heal our uncleanness and weakness), He cleansed this Jewish leper (an indication of the cleansing of the Jewish nation from foreign teachings) and its return to the commandments of God.
This leper met Christ outside the city, where he was isolated, because he had heard of His teachings and His power in healing diseases.
"Worshipped him": a declaration of his faith in Christ and his humility before Him.
"If thou wilt": a polite form in addressing Christ, and a surrender to His will.
"Thou canst": confidence and faith in Christ the Healer.
Believe in God's power to forgive your sin, and ask His help, and He frees you from it, and gives you the feelings of repentance and confession, however great your weakness.
Christ commanded the leper to be cleansed, and joined His word with action, and touched him, and he was healed immediately, and the color of his skin changed and returned to normal.

Christ touched him to teach us to join our words with deeds, and to declare His authority and His purity, which is not affected by touching the unclean, but cleanses them, because He is God, who is able to cleanse.
And so too, if we live in purity of heart, we are not defiled by evil if circumstances compel us to face it in the world.
"Tell no man": because Christ does not seek honor from people, and because His aim in the miracles is to establish His teachings and not to dazzle the crowds.

And Christ declared that He does not break the Law but fulfills it by sending the leper whom He healed to offer a sacrifice according to the Law, after the priest examines him and makes sure of his healing, and so that this might be a proclamation to the Jewish priests to believe in Him, when they see that His authority is stronger than theirs in the power to heal.
"The gift": which the Law commanded, which is two birds (Lev 14:4).

entries.section: (2) The healing of the centurion's servant

paragraphs.text: "Came": it appears from (Lk 7:3) that he sent elders of the Jews to Christ, to ask in his name for the healing of his servant, and the coming is attributed here to the centurion because the elders were delegates for him.
"A centurion": in charge of a Roman unit of a hundred soldiers, found in large cities such as Capernaum. He was a pagan man, but devout and loving the Jews.

Jesus then entered the city of Capernaum, a large city in Galilee, and a centurion came to Him and asked Him to heal one of his servants who was afflicted with paralysis and lay at home; and this shows the tenderness of this centurion and his care for his servants.
"Grievously tormented": some kinds of paralysis are accompanied by severe pains, or he may have been tormented in spirit by being laid on his bed and unable to move and do what he needs.
This signifies the Gentiles' turning to Christ, to save them from the spiritual paralysis into which they fell by their worship of idols, and their souls were tormented by it.

entries.section: (2) The healing of the centurion's servant

paragraphs.text: Jesus showed His love for the Gentiles as for the Jews, and His readiness to enter their houses and heal them, for He does not despise the Gentiles; and in humility, He is ready to go to them, because He became incarnate for the salvation of the whole world. "I will come and heal him": this declares His complete power to heal.

entries.section: (2) The healing of the centurion's servant

paragraphs.text: "I am not worthy": despite the position of this centurion, and the Romans' habit of despising the Jews, this centurion showed unexpected humility before Christ.

"Under my roof": because the Jews do not enter the houses of the Gentiles, Christ would not be embarrassed if he invited Him to heal his servant. The centurion said humbly to Christ that he was not worthy that He should visit him in his house to heal his servant, and declared his faith that one word from Christ is able to heal. For he is a commander and has authority over his soldiers, so how much more Christ, the great God, has authority over everything.

"Under authority": that is, under the authority of commanders in the army greater than I, or under the authority of the king, yet I am able to command my servant and he obeys me, so how much more You, who are able to do all things?!

entries.section: (2) The healing of the centurion's servant

paragraphs.text: Christ marveled at this faith and praised it, declaring that it was greater than any faith that appeared among the Jews. For God is just and gives every person his due honor.

entries.section: (2) The healing of the centurion's servant

paragraphs.text: "From the east and west": that is, from the Gentiles, and this is a clear declaration from Christ that His Kingdom includes the Gentiles also like the Jews.

He added that many of the Gentiles will believe and precede into the Kingdom where Abraham and the Fathers are, and at the same time many of the Jews, whom He calls "the children of the kingdom", since God chose them as His special people, and gave them His commandments, and was born among them to save them, will refuse to believe, and so will be cast into eternal torment outside the Kingdom, which He expresses as "darkness" where the light of Christ is not found.
"Gnashing of teeth": it represents torment, anger and despair.

entries.section: (2) The healing of the centurion's servant

paragraphs.text: Christ granted healing by His word from a distance, and the servant was healed immediately, and the centurion enjoyed joy because of his faith, and this shows two important things:
(1) Christ's power to heal immediately.

(2) The importance of intercession in God's sight, by Christ's answering the centurion's request for his servant. If someone asks you for a service, have compassion on him and hasten to help him, indeed may you have compassion on the weary around you before they ask you, and be ready to spend all effort to help them, giving up your dignity for their comfort, confident that this is the greatest thing in God's sight, that is, the work of mercy.
"Peter's house": he had a house in Capernaum, although he was originally from Bethsaida.

"His wife's mother": this means that he was married, and his marriage did not hinder him from following Christ and serving Him. "Laid, and sick of a fever": it appears from this that the fever was severe and deprived her of the ability to move and work.
"He touched her hand": to proclaim to the people in a tangible way His power to heal, and that He is the source of the health that the sick woman would receive.

And Christ here cares for His servants; if they have followed Him and relied on Him, He cares for all their affairs, and heals their diseases and those of their families; Christ takes special care of His children who serve.

In this miracle there is also concern for women and a welcome of their service, since when He healed her, she arose and ministered to them. And from the spiritual side, the fever signifies the spiritual diseases that hinder the soul from its life with God and its service of Him. But when we take refuge in Him, He heals us and we regain our first strength.

The news of Christ's miracles spread throughout Capernaum. And because the day was a Sabbath, as our teacher Mark the Apostle mentions (Mk 1:21), they brought the sick to Him in the evening, that is, after the end of the Sabbath day on which they do no work (Mk 1:32). They were sick with various bodily diseases, or demons dwelt in them and caused them diseases such as madness, and He healed them all by His love and tenderness. For He came to take away our diseases, and He bore all our sufferings on the Cross and redeemed us, as Isaiah prophesied (Isa 53:4). God seeks the weary, and goes to them to heal them, as He became incarnate to take away our troubles. Therefore let us be encouraged and take refuge in Him in all our needs, confident of His fatherhood and love, and also His power to solve all our problems. Let us not rely on our minds and abilities or the abilities of those around us, for all are of no use unless they are in God's hand; and in this our heart is always assured of His being with us, and we do not worry about anything that may happen in the future.

The great crowds followed Christ to enjoy His sermons and see His miracles, so He told His disciples who were close to Him to cross from the western shore of the Sea of Galilee to the eastern shore, which is about six miles, that is, it takes about two hours by ship, so that there might be an opportunity to preach in other places, and also as rest for His body and His disciples, and so as to escape from the Jews who wanted to set Him up as an earthly king who would free them from the Romans, because His Kingdom is greater than this, being the Kingdom of Heaven.

As He was going to the shore, one of the scribes came to Him, who are an advanced group among the Jews, knowing the holy Scriptures, because they were concerned with copying them, and consequently knowing what is in them. This scribe asked to be a follower of Christ in every place, after seeing His authority over diseases, so that he might have a position in the new kingdom which the Jews thought He would set up on earth.

Christ's reply to him was that He was poor, having no dwelling to live in like the rest of mankind, or even the animals such as the foxes which have dwellings, that is, holes called dens, nor like the birds which have dwellings that are their nests, that is, their roosts, but He used to spend the night in any place where they hosted Him, or sometimes slept in the boat, and at other times spent the whole night praying in secret.
And Christ's reply shows that this scribe's aim was to obtain a material position, and not love and seeking discipleship to Him.
Ask yourself in your following of Christ: is it for love of Him or to obtain material requests? And do you grumble if God does not answer your prayer, or delays in answering?

Try to understand God's purposes, because His aim in all His dealings with you is the salvation of your soul and your drawing near to Him, even if this requires you to pass through some tribulations, or to lack some material things.

Another person came forward from the followers of Christ and those who were being discipled at His hands, but not one of the twelve disciples, declaring his readiness to continue following Him without any material purpose, unlike the scribe who asked to follow Christ in the previous verse, but he asked Christ's leave to bury his father. What is meant is not merely the burial of the body, but the ceremonies of burial and condolence which took a long time, and procedures for dividing the inheritance might be connected with them, and they also attach the heart emotionally to many griefs that could occupy it from the salvation of its soul.
Christ said to him that he must concentrate on following Him, and not be occupied with the customs of people and their many worldly concerns.

"The dead": he means those alive in body but dead in spirit, that is, who do not believe in Christ and do not care for the salvation of their souls. These are the relatives and friends of the dead man who will be occupied with the ceremonies of burial and condolence. This disciple's attachment to passing material things would hinder him from God, so let him leave the spiritually dead to be occupied with material things, but let him be free for God.

It is understood from this that Christ does not mean merely the burial of the body of the dead, but not being hindered from following Him by any excessive emotional attachments, and not ordinary emotion in the burial of the dead, or love of those around us; on the contrary, we carry out our duties toward our parents and all our loved ones for God's sake, and our goal is clear before us, which is the salvation of our souls.
Christ entered the ship to cross the Sea of Tiberias, that is, the Sea of Galilee, to the eastern side, and slept inside the ship.
"A great tempest": the Sea of Tiberias was far below sea level, and surrounded by mountains, and consequently exposed to sudden winds that stir up its waves.

"Asleep": besides the fact that Christ's sleeping confirms His humanity, and His need for sleep and rest, it was a deliberate sleep so as to test the faith of His disciples, and from another side, their helplessness appears, despite their experience in fishing and sailing the sea, so that they feel the need for God the Savior.
The ship faced violent winds, and the waves rose until they covered it, and it was about to sink.

The winds signify temptations, and the waves the troubled world, and the ship our life in which Christ dwells, but He is asleep, that is, not working in us, because of our not taking refuge in Him, and our reliance on our own strength, whose helplessness appears before the cruelty of the devil's wars.

At last, when the disciples were certain of their helplessness, they took refuge in Christ, declaring that they were perishing, because of their weakness before the violence of the winds and waves, asking Him to save them.

Before Christ showed His authority over nature, He rebuked their little faith. For after they had seen His miracles, they should have trusted and believed in His divinity, and not feared the waves; then He commanded the winds and the waves and they grew calm. "O ye of little faith": they have faith and therefore they took refuge in Him, but it is little, as is proved by their fear and lack of trust in His complete power to save them.

"Rebuked": a declaration of the divinity of Christ and His authority over nature, as though He were commanding a person and he obeyed Him. "A great calm": it shows the power of the miracle in the stilling of the winds and waves at once and completely.
If a temptation meets you or you fall into sin, hasten to awaken the Christ who sleeps in you with a prayer of supplication and humility, and He will save you and restore your peace to you.
Before Christ's authority over nature, and the appearance of the power of His divinity, the disciples marveled, and their faith began to grow, and their knowledge of Christ the true God increased.

entries.section: (6) The two madmen in the country of the Gergesenes

paragraphs.text: "Unto the other side": Christ reached by ship the eastern shore of the Sea of Galilee.

"The country of the Gergesenes": a village situated among the lands of the Gadarenes, on the eastern shore of the Sea of Tiberias. Two madmen who lived in the tombs of this city ran quickly toward Christ. It seems that one of them was more violent than the other, so our teachers Mark and Luke mentioned him (Mk 5:1-20; Lk 8:26-39), and omitted mentioning the second madman. Because of their great violence, they blocked the way for passers-by, so people feared to pass along this road.
And the demons dwelt in these two madmen and deprived them of their minds, and they no longer enjoyed the natural peace that belongs to human beings.

This is the action of the cruel demons upon careless human beings, when they go far from God. Indeed more than this, they, by their violence, prevented others from passing along this road, for Satan tries to hinder people from passing along the way of God.

entries.section: (6) The two madmen in the country of the Gergesenes

paragraphs.text: The demons could not bear to see Christ, and cried out in weakness and fear of His authority not to torment them. A large group of demons dwelt in these two madmen, and not one demon, therefore they spoke in the plural.
"Before the time": that is, before the day of judgment.
"To torment us": to destroy us and cast us into eternal torment.

entries.section: (6) The two madmen in the country of the Gergesenes

paragraphs.text: Near the city were hills on which herds of swine were feeding, numbering about two thousand (Mk 5:13), and the demons asked Christ, if He wished to cast them out of the two madmen, to permit them to enter the swine. This shows clearly Christ's authority over the demons, for they do not move without His permission, and it also shows the wickedness of the demons, who wish to kill the swine to stir up their owners against Christ and prevent His preaching.

entries.section: (6) The two madmen in the country of the Gergesenes

paragraphs.text: Christ permitted them to enter the swine, and they rushed from the shore into the sea and all were drowned.

This shows the cruelty of the demons who want to destroy us, but Christ did not permit them to destroy the two madmen, and permitted only the destruction of the swine, because swine are forbidden among the Jews, so raising them was against the divine Law. And this shows that the violence and madness in the two madmen was not a nervous disease, but the work of the demons. "A steep place": that is, from the foot of the mountain to the edge of the sea.

entries.section: (6) The two madmen in the country of the Gergesenes

paragraphs.text: The herdsmen were greatly disturbed by the power of the miracle, and grieved over the loss of their wealth, and told the Gergesenes, the inhabitants of the city, who went out and saw Christ, and feared His power, and grieved over the loss of the city's possessions, which were these swine. And in hardness of heart, they did not care about the healing of the two madmen, because their attachment to material things blinded their eyes, and they did not see the divine grace with which they could have been blessed by Christ, but feared losing something else material, so they asked Christ not to enter their city.

Christ left them because of their attachment to material things, although at the same time He sent the two healed madmen to preach in His name "in Decapolis" (Mk 5:20), which are the cities surrounding their city.

The love of money and material things blinds your eyes to understanding the works of God, and even makes you reject the work of His grace in you, so you lose Christ's dwelling in your heart. Therefore try to feel for those around you and strive to serve them, and sacrifice some of the material things you have, so that you become alert and your eyes are opened, and you see the work of God offered to you.
The healing of the sick; the casting out of demons; the raising of Jairus's daughter

After the Gergesenes rejected Christ, He boarded the boat and returned to His city, that is, Capernaum, which He had taken as a place in which to perform His miracles and give His teachings. By returning to His city He shows us the importance of caring for our homeland, while our hearts are opened wide in love to everyone.

It appears here that Christ crossed from the west of the Sea of Tiberias to its east in order to heal the possessed men, and then returned immediately afterward to Capernaum. This shows how precious a single soul is to Christ, how He travels for hours to meet it and save it.

This man was struck with paralysis and the attempts to cure him failed. When his four friends heard that Christ had come to Capernaum, they hurried to carry him to Him that He might heal him. The two Evangelists, Mark (Mk 2:3-12) and Luke (Lk 5:18-26), tell us that they found a crowd around the house, so they went up on the roof, broke through it, and let the paralytic down on his bed before Christ, who was sitting among the crowds. When Christ saw the faith of these friends, and saw the cause of this man's illness, which was sin, He granted him forgiveness by the authority of His divinity, which is the greater grace, that is, the healing of the spirit before the healing of the body.

Seated around Christ was a group of scribes, who were those who knew the Law, and religious leaders of the Jews. Instead of doing their work as servants of this people, and presenting them to Christ that He might heal them and forgive their sins, they thought evil in their hearts, saying: How does this man speak blasphemies? For, being a man, he speaks as God who has authority to forgive.
"Blasphemeth": he claims for himself an authority that belongs to God alone.

Jesus knew their thoughts without hearing them, and this confirms His divinity, because none knows the inner thought except God. He rebuked them for their evil thoughts, and this makes clear that an evil thought is sin, and not only the deed and the word.

Christ asked the scribes which is easier: the forgiveness of sin or the healing of the body? They did not answer, because they feared Him, since He knew their thoughts without their having spoken them... The answer, of course, is that the easier is the healing of the body. So God, who has authority, gave what is more important, namely forgiveness. Then, as a proof of His divinity, He gave bodily healing, and said to the paralytic: "Arise, take up thy bed (thy couch), and go unto thine house."

Taking up the bed: this proclaims the strength of the paralytic's health. The bed reminds a person of the pains of illness, so when he carries it he feels the power of the miracle, remembers his former weakness, and thanks God.
The house: it is his former life, and signifies his return to the Church and his relationship with God after being healed of the spiritual illness.
"The Son of man": what is meant by it is Christ incarnate.
"Power on earth": that is, the authority of God who is in heaven, in forgiving sins and healing the sick, and the ability to do anything.

When the crowds saw the greatness of the miracle, they marveled greatly and glorified God, because He had given such great authority to one of men, namely Jesus, since they were not yet able to believe in the Incarnation and divinity of Christ. Praise every good work you see, and do not doubt everything and think evil. The more humble you are, the more you are able to see the virtues of others, and you will judge no one, and will always glorify God.

Matthew, the writer of this Gospel, worked as a tax collector, and this profession was associated with cruelty, injustice and the love of money. For the tax collector first paid the Roman authority the tax required for the village or place entrusted to him, and then collected it with the help of the Roman soldiers, so he collected more than he had paid, however poor the people were.

But when he saw Jesus and heard His word, his feelings were moved, so he obeyed His call, and left all his work, his money and his sins, relying on Him, and he did not consult his relatives and loved ones lest he be hindered.

Here the love and humility of Christ appear, in calling His disciples from among fishermen, or from among the wicked such as Matthew the tax collector, known for cruelty and violence, in order to purify them and fill them with His Holy Spirit, so that the glory is to Him and not to human strength.
"The receipt of custom": most likely a large tent, set up on the road for collecting money in it under the guard of Roman soldiers.
"Follow me": he may have heard of Christ before and seen Him, so he was ready to obey Him at once when He called him.
The tax collectors and sinners: because of the greed and cruelty of the tax collectors, their name became linked with sinners, and they were rejected by Jewish society.

After Matthew followed Christ, his heart rejoiced greatly, so he longed that his fellow tax collectors and sinners might enjoy the knowledge of Christ. So with spiritual wisdom he made a feast for Christ, to which he invited all his friends that they might hear and repent of their sins. And Christ accepted the invitation, because He came for the salvation of sinners and not the righteous.

But the Pharisees, who held to the outward appearances of the spiritual life and not its essence, and who criticize others with pride, reproached the disciples of Christ because their Teacher sits and eats with sinners. They paid attention to the appearance without seeking the reason for His presence at the feast, that is, His concern for the salvation of these souls.

"When Jesus heard": the Pharisees' words were addressed to His disciples, because they were afraid to speak to Him. But He, with power, declared to them their error in keeping away from calling sinners to repentance under the pretext of not being defiled by mixing with them, and Christ showed them the reason for His Incarnation, which is the calling of sinners to repentance. And this is logical, for the physician goes to the sick and not to the healthy; so it is natural for Christ to care for those who are far off, that they may repent of their sins.

Jesus rebuked them gently, requiring of their hearts mercy toward sinners, which is more important than offering sacrifices without understanding, because the sacrifice is a symbol of Christ's sacrificing His life on the Cross so that He might have mercy on sinners, and these words were declared before by Hosea (Hos 6:6). ("The righteous": in their own eyes, because there is no righteous man, but all are sinners in need of the redemption of Christ. "Sinners": that is, those well known for their sins, such as the tax collectors.)

Care for those who are far off so that you may call them to Christ, and pray for them, and look for ways to draw them to God, if not by direct speech, then by indirect speech, such as speaking with others in their presence, or offering encouraging words or works of love that soften their hearts, until they turn back from their rejection of God.

"The disciples of John": some of them followed Christ and became His disciples, and some did not join Him, holding only to John's teachings of repentance and asceticism; so these speakers are not disciples of Christ. "Oft": the Pharisees imposed fasts other than those the Law prescribes, and the disciples of Christ, like most of the Jews, did not keep them.

The disciples of John and the Pharisees complained against Christ because His disciples do not fast. This means that they felt the burden of fasting, as an ordinance difficult for them, from which they wanted to be freed, or whose hardship they wanted others to bear along with them; that is, they had the outward form of fasting but did not feel its spiritual blessings.
"The children of the bridechamber": the close relatives and friends of the bridegroom.
"Mourn": because fasting is linked with humbling oneself, tears and repentance.

Christ answered that His disciples, who are the children of the bridechamber while He is their Bridegroom, ought not to fast until after the Bridegroom is taken away; therefore they will fast when Christ ascends to heaven. But during His life on earth they rejoice in Him, and fasting is postponed because it is a sign of humbling oneself and of spiritual striving; and the Apostles did in fact fast after the Ascension of Christ.

Christ addressed the real problem, which is the understanding of fasting: it is not a compulsory ordinance, but a love offered to God. If the whole of life is not changed by repentance, we do not benefit from any spiritual practice, because it will be superficial, and will even harm a person since he becomes proud through it.

Christ likened this harm to putting a piece of new cloth on an old garment, so that its fabric, being stronger than the old fabric, tears it because of its weakness; thus the new patch does not benefit the old garment, but harms it and tears it.
"Old garment": that is, an ancient garment, a symbol of the life of the Pharisees who refused to believe in Christ and who loved pride and various evils.
The new patch: it signifies fasting which, if it is not placed in a life renewed by Christian faith, will harm, that is, it will add pride to the Pharisees.

And this is a second reason for the disciples' not fasting, since what matters first for them, and for all people, is to believe in Christ and repent of their sins; only then are their worship and fasts accepted.

"Bottles": vessels of skin, that is, (waterskins), in which wine or water or any liquid is put. Also, new wine is strong and the old bottles cannot bear it, because the products of fermentation are stronger than the thin skin of the old bottles, so they burst and the wine is spilled. Therefore new wine needs new bottles, whose skin is thick.
"Old bottles": that is, old vessels, a symbol of the life of the Pharisees and of John's disciples who did not yet believe in Christ.
"New wine": it signifies fasting, which is a spiritual worship that rejoices the heart of God.
"New bottles": this is the life renewed in Christ by faith, which bears and is adorned with all spiritual practices such as fasting.

May your fasting be joined with repentance and partaking of the Holy Sacraments, and reading the Holy Bible and meditating on it, so that it becomes a spiritual fast that stirs your feelings with love and mercy toward the needy, and you rejoice and long for fasting, because it is a strong means that brings you near to God and delivers your soul from many lusts.

entries.section: (4) The healing of the woman with the issue of blood and the raising of the daughter of Jairus

paragraphs.text: A ruler of one of the synagogues of the Jews came to Christ. These were places spread throughout Judea in which prayers and the reading of the Holy Scriptures were held, while sacrifices were offered only inside the Temple in Jerusalem.

This ruler, whose name was Jairus (Mk 5:22; Lk 8:41), came with faith and humility, worshipping Christ, asking Him to raise his daughter, who had died, by coming and touching her, and he believed that she would rise. This is great faith, but the faith of the Gentile centurion is greater, for he said to Christ: "Speak the word only, and my servant shall be healed" (ch. 8:10); he did not need Christ to come to him, but it was enough that He command, and the illness withdraws.

The age of the girl, the daughter of Jairus, was twelve years (Lk 8:42), and she points spiritually to the nation of the Jews, which had twelve tribes. She died on her bed, and so she signifies the sin of the inner thought, and Christ is able to raise from this sin.
So Christ responded with great love as was His custom, and went to the house of Jairus, and His disciples followed Him to see His miracles and hear His teachings.

entries.section: (4) The healing of the woman with the issue of blood and the raising of the daughter of Jairus

paragraphs.text: The woman with the issue of blood had for twelve years been trying to be cured without avail, so she points to the spiritually sick soul, which tried by human means to cure sin and did not succeed.

"Behind him": she did not appear before Him, either from shame at her illness, or because the Jews regarded a woman's issue of blood as uncleanness (Lev 15:25-26), and therefore they would not allow her to touch Christ.
This woman resorted to Christ to meet Him on the way, like the soul that meets Christ on the road of life through the events of the world, and believes in Him and is healed of its troubles.

She believed that merely touching the hem of His garment would heal her, and she did this and was healed. And Christ wanted to glorify the faith of this woman, so He made known what she had done before the crowds, and assured her that she had been healed completely.

entries.section: (4) The healing of the woman with the issue of blood and the raising of the daughter of Jairus

paragraphs.text: Christ reached the house of Jairus and found the relatives and loved ones weeping, and even those whom they had hired, the pipe players with their sad tunes, giving forth loud sounds that stir the emotions. So He reassured everyone that the girl was asleep and not dead, although she had in fact died. But by the power of His divinity He is able to raise her; for in His sight the rest of death is like the rest of sleep.
But they did not believe and mocked His words, since they could not believe in His power to raise from the dead.

entries.section: (4) The healing of the woman with the issue of blood and the raising of the daughter of Jairus

paragraphs.text: Christ put out the unbelieving crowds, and took with Him the girl's parents and a few of His disciples (Mk 5:40), that is, those who believe in His power. Then He took the girl by the hand and raised her, and her family and all the crowds rejoiced and glorified God who raises the dead.
And this is one of the many clear proofs of the divinity of Christ, who commanded death and it departed, and the girl arose, and the report spread in the lands surrounding Capernaum.

If you have faith, you will behold the great works of God. So do not be troubled if matters become complicated and it appears that there is no solution for them, for your God shows miracles in every generation and in ways that never cross your mind; only rely on Him, confident of His love and care.

entries.section: (5) The healing of the two blind men

paragraphs.text: As Christ was walking along the road, two blind men followed Him, asking healing from Him. They represent the Jews and the Gentiles who fell into the darkness of sin and needed Christ the Savior to enlighten their lives. Christ let them cry out all along the way, to test their faith. And when He reached the house to which He was going, He asked them: Do you believe in my power to heal your eyes? So they declared their faith in Him as the awaited Messiah, the Son of David, who is able to open their eyes.

entries.section: (5) The healing of the two blind men

paragraphs.text: "According to your faith": God is rich and ready to give much, in proportion to what you believe of Him.
Then Christ touched their eyes, and commanded, and they regained their sight.

"Straitly charged them": that is, He forbade them to speak of the miracle, out of humility on His part, because He does not need the praise of men, in addition to His concern not to stir up the jealousy of the scribes and Pharisees, and lest they think of Him as an earthly king who would give them their material needs by freeing them from slavery to the Romans.
And He told them, in humility, not to tell anyone of this miracle.
Learn not to speak of your works in order to receive the praise of men, but do as Christ did, and God who sees you in secret will reward you openly.

entries.section: (5) The healing of the two blind men

paragraphs.text: When they saw the love and humility of Christ, they met His love with love also, so they went out proclaiming this miracle to everyone, since they wanted all to enjoy faith in Him, although it would have been better for them to obey Christ in not speaking of the miracle, because obedience is better than everything.

entries.section: (6) The healing of the dumb and possessed man

paragraphs.text: Satan entered a man, and made him lose his mind, and prevented him from speaking. He represents the man subject to sin, whom Satan causes to lose his mind, and makes preoccupied with base lusts, and prevents him from speaking the word of God.

"They brought to him": this man needed people to lead him because he does not speak, in addition to having lost his mind. They brought this man to Christ, and He commanded Satan, by the authority of His divinity, to come out of him. And immediately he came out, and the man's mind returned and he spoke. So the crowds rejoiced and glorified God who had sent them a prophet who heals their diseases and saves them from the power of Satan.
"It was never so seen": that is, no prophet appeared in the history of the people of Israel who had this authority over demons and performed all these miracles.

entries.section: (6) The healing of the dumb and possessed man
