paragraphs.text: But the Pharisees, the leaders of Jewish society, did not believe in the divinity of Christ or His authority over demons, but in their pride saw Him as a rival to them in leading the crowds, so they accused Him of having a relationship with "the prince of the devils," and that this is why He casts them out.

Pride makes you lose your understanding of matters, so that you do not see the works of God with you and in you. So be humble, and accept people's guidance for you, and seek God's direction every day, and submit to the word of your father of confession.

entries.section: (7) Preaching in the cities and villages

paragraphs.text: Christ took care to visit the cities and also the villages, that is, the rich and the poor, and He did not center Himself in Capernaum or Jerusalem or only a large city, to show the importance of visitation. His preaching was the nearness of the Kingdom of Heaven and preparing for it by repentance. And He used to confirm His word with miracles, that people might believe His preaching.

entries.section: (7) Preaching in the cities and villages

paragraphs.text: The tender heart of Christ appears toward His children, whose leaders the Pharisees were too occupied to draw them to repentance, so He Himself took care to shepherd them.
"Troubled": this is the disturbance that accompanies falling into sin and being far from God. "Cast down": that is, exposed to the attacks of the devil and to falling into his sins.

entries.section: (7) Preaching in the cities and villages

paragraphs.text: The Lord directed the gaze of His disciples to the need of souls for someone to shepherd them, and likened them to stalks of wheat waiting for someone to reap their ears; but the reapers, that is, the leaders of Jewish society, were too occupied to serve because of their concern for their own dignity. And He did not tell the disciples to reap, but to ask God to send servants to shepherd His people, so that they might understand that it is God who calls servants to service, and not merely their own emotion or conviction about it; that is, they should pray, and God will move their feelings to care for souls, and then God sends them to His service. May you care for the salvation of the souls of those around you, so that you have compassion on all instead of being troubled by their many faults, and pray that God may move their hearts, for all are His children and created in His image, and He wants their salvation... And God either sends you to them, or sends them someone who brings them back to Him.
The calling of the disciples and their preaching in Judea

Christ chose twelve of His followers to become His disciples, and this calling came in stages. The goal was that they should be discipled at His hands, so that He would hand over to them the spiritual life and the teachings that they were to convey to the world and preach.

And as they went out to preach repentance and the Kingdom of Heaven, He strengthened them with authority to cast out demons and heal diseases, to help people believe their words, since the devil who dominates them is driven away from them, and they are relieved of their troubles, so that their hearts are more ready to receive the good news.
Offer your love to people, and their hearts will open and respond to your words.

The number of the disciples was twelve, that is, three times four, and it signifies the work of the Holy Trinity in the whole world with its four directions, and that they might preach to the twelve tribes of the Jews.
"Simon, who is called Peter": that is, a rock, or Cephas, and he was the first of the disciples and the eldest in age.
"Andrew": the brother of Simon Peter, and both of them had been disciples of John the Baptist.
"James the son of Zebedee": the first of the disciples to be martyred.

"John": the brother of James, and the two were sharp in temperament, so Christ called them "Boanerges," that is, sons of thunder. John was distinguished by his intense love for Christ, and he used to lean on His breast.
"Philip": from Bethsaida, and he is not Philip the evangelist, one of the seven deacons. He called Bartholomew, who is also called Nathanael, and who was from Cana of Galilee.
"Thomas": who is called the Twin.
"Matthew": who is called Levi, and Matthew called himself the publican out of humility, because the tax collectors were known for their sins.

"James the son of Alphaeus": or James the Less, to distinguish him from James the son of Zebedee, who was older in age; he was a cousin of Christ on His mother's side, and he became bishop of Jerusalem.
"Lebbaeus": who is surnamed Thaddaeus, and is also called Judas; he was the son of Alphaeus, the brother of James, and he is the writer of the epistle known by his name (James).

"Simon the Canaanite": that is, the Zealot, and it does not mean that he was from Cana of Galilee. The Zealots were a group of Jews who held fast to their nationalism against the Roman authority, and were ready for acts of sabotage in defense of their Jewish homeland.
"Judas Iscariot": which means "man of Kerioth," one of the towns of Judea; he is the one who sold Christ to the Jews and delivered Him to them.

It is to be noted that Christ chose His disciples from ordinary people, and not from the eminent, so that their works would be ascribed to the power of God working in them and not to their personal strength; He is ready to accept and work through any person, however weak he may be.

And He chose them with differing temperaments: among them one who collaborated with the Roman authority, such as Matthew the tax collector, and also one who defied this authority, namely Simon the Zealot; among them the poor, such as Peter and Andrew, and the rich, such as James and John the sons of Zebedee. So He gathers all in His Church with one love.

God is ready to work in the least and weakest of people, so hold fast to your spiritual relationship with God, however weak you are before your sins, or however few your resources, because God is able to work through you, so that you serve Him, and the glory is to God through your thanking Him at all times.

Christ sent them to the land of Judea to preach in it, and not to Samaria, that is, the part split off from the Jews and mixed with the Gentiles and pagan worship. He likewise forbade them to go to the Gentiles, that is, the pagan lands, because Christ is the Messiah awaited by the Jews, who came for their salvation, so that everyone who awaited the divine promises and prophecies might believe in Him, and then the rest of the world would be evangelized. He came for the salvation of all, but He begins with the Jews, for they were supposed to be the first to respond to His good news, so that He might gather those of them who had strayed from the truth, then the Samaritans as a link between the Jews and the Gentiles, then the Gentiles; that is, in the end He offers salvation to all, and this is what happened after His Ascension (ch. 28:19).

The subject of the Apostles' preaching is the same as that preached by John the Baptist and by Christ Himself, namely repentance in preparation for the Kingdom of Heaven, because through repentance a person rejects his sins and begins the new life with Christ, who then reigns over his heart, as a pledge of his enjoying the eternal Kingdom with Him.

Christ gave His disciples the means for preaching, which is authority to heal diseases, even difficult ones such as leprosy, which represents uncleanness. Indeed He gave them authority to raise the dead, and to cast demons out of the weak in soul; that is, He gave them authority over everything, even what seems impossible, in order to rescue His children from the hand of the devil, and to prepare them to receive the good news about Him.
And He required of them that their service be free of charge, as love without return, just as He gave them everything freely, so that they too might give to others, and hearts would be drawn to them.
And this is a principle that still holds in service to this day, namely that servants offer spiritual service without payment.

Gold, silver, brass: money at that time was made of these three metals, so what is meant is any kind of money or any pieces of these metals that have monetary value. Since Christ strengthens them with His power, they do not need to take money with them, or food in their scrips, that is, the bags that they carry on a journey, and they do not need clothes or shoes, or a staff to lean on, because Christ is their support; and if they need these things He will provide them through those to whom they preach, because, although the service is free, the servant's necessary needs can be provided by God for him through the gifts of those he serves.

What is meant here is that the disciple should be content with the necessary needs that he uses, and not take with him anything extra as a precaution, because if any of them is lost, God will provide it for him.

Christ charged them that, if they entered any place to preach in it, they should look for those who respond to the word of God or are ready to hear the word; these are the ones worthy to receive the good news, so that they repent and amend their lives. And He told them to keep staying in that responsive house, so that they might complete the persuasion of the responsive ones until they draw them to Him; they should not move quickly from house to house, but complete the persuasion and care of each person. On the other hand, they should not be occupied with hospitality and seek after it in different houses, because their aim is preaching, and the house in which they stay is merely a place to lodge, from which they set out to serve souls.

"Salute it": offer greetings, love and sufficient care to the people of the house, for preaching is not a dry work, but is accompanied by feelings of love; and the importance of expressing feelings in order to draw people appears here.

Christ commanded them to proclaim His peace to all hearts, and to offer their love to all. If some respond, they will enjoy the salvation of Christ, and benefit from the peace offered to them. And if they refuse, the disciples should not grieve, for their peace and love return to them, while those who refuse lose the grace of God.

"Shake off the dust of your feet": shaking off dust was a well-known custom, signifying the clearing of responsibility, since the Apostles had done what was upon them, and those who refuse are therefore held accountable for their rejection of the word of God. It also signifies taking nothing material from these who refuse, not even the dust on the feet.
"The day of judgment": it is the last day of judgment.

But those who reject the good news of Christ at the hands of the Apostles will lose their opportunity to reach the Kingdom and the redemption of Christ, and will be cast into eternal torment, and their torment will be harder than the torment of the people of Sodom and Gomorrah, who were known for their wickedness in ancient times, to the point that God burned the two cities (Gen 19:24), because in the Old Testament they rejected the words of the men of God. But in the New Testament they rejected Christ Himself.

Take care to express your love for those around you every day, and for all whom you serve and wish to draw to Christ, for expressing love in word and deed is the necessary preparation for opening hearts to obey the word of God, since they see Him in you and so submit to His word that is on your lips.

entries.section: (3) The world's persecution of the disciples

paragraphs.text: If one wolf among the lambs terrifies them, although it will devour only some of them, how great would the terror be if we placed lambs among many wolves? But so that the power of God may be manifested in the weak lambs, they are placed among the wolves and overcome them, and strip them of their savage nature. And even if the wolves devour the lambs, the blood of the lambs will run in the veins of the wolves and turn them into lambs, as St. John Chrysostom says.

And this is what actually happened during the preaching of the Apostles, who endured violent persecutions and changed many hard hearts, just as the martyrs drew to faith those who were tormenting them.

And Christ calls His disciples to be adorned with the simplicity and innocence of the dove, because it is known for not harming others. And at the same time, to be marked by the wisdom of serpents, which are known for their great caution against danger, so that we keep away from all evil in order to live with God.

entries.section: (3) The world's persecution of the disciples

paragraphs.text: "Beware": be on guard against the wicked whom you are preaching to, and do not throw yourselves into their hands without need; but if preaching requires it, do not be afraid.

"Councils": these are either the local councils of the elders of the Jews found in every village to pass judgments on wrongdoers, or the supreme council in Jerusalem, which is the "Sanhedrin" (ch. 5:21-22). "Their synagogues": they were spread throughout all the land of Judea, and in them the Holy Scriptures were read and preaching was given, and in them there were three judges from among the elders who had the right to pass sentences of flogging on offenders.

"They will scourge you": they used to scourge offenders with forty lashes, and as a precaution, lest they err, the Jews fixed it at 39 lashes, since the whip is made of three strands, so the offender was lashed 13 times, which equals 39 lashes.
"Governors and kings": who tried the Apostles, such as Felix the governor (Acts 24), and Agrippa the king (Acts 26), who both tried St. Paul the Apostle.
"A testimony for them": that they might believe, as Paul tried with King Agrippa (Acts 26).
"To the Gentiles": that is, all the crowds who listen to their trial, as many of them believed during the trial and torture of the martyrs.

Here Christ speaks in detail about the kinds of persecutions that will meet the Apostles, or the children of God in every generation: instead of honoring them in appreciation of their preaching, they will arrest them and try them, and torture them with scourging and with many kinds of torments, and this will be a proof of the faith of the servants and their steadfastness in Christ.

entries.section: (3) The world's persecution of the disciples

paragraphs.text: Christ reassures us in these confrontations that the Holy Spirit will give us what to answer them, so that we persuade them or silence them, because the power of the Holy Spirit in us is stronger than all human wisdom. "The Spirit of your Father": it shows the tenderness and care of God, who makes His Holy Spirit support the Apostles and servants in every generation.

entries.section: (3) The world's persecution of the disciples

paragraphs.text: Persecutions will come, not only from those who are far off, but from the nearest people, such as father, child and brother, and it is strange that religious fanaticism abolishes natural love between the nearest of the near, but this is what has happened and does happen to this day.

entries.section: (3) The world's persecution of the disciples

paragraphs.text: "All men": most of the people who do not believe in Christ.
"For my name's sake": for your holding fast to the faith and to preaching.
"Endureth": persecution does not mean killing only, but mostly insult, torture and deprivation of rights, and so it requires the patience of the servants and the believers.
"The end": the end of the persecution or the end of life.

Tribulation may reach the point where a person finds everyone around him hating and persecuting him for the sake of Christ, and God will allow this to prove our faith. And by patience and endurance we gain the salvation of our souls, and even an eternal reward that cannot be expressed, with the assurance that the Holy Spirit supports us so that we may endure these persecutions.

entries.section: (3) The world's persecution of the disciples

paragraphs.text: Christ counsels His Apostles not to enter into confrontations with the wicked, if they refuse to believe, but to flee to other lands, and complete their preaching. This fleeing is not weakness, but busyness with completing the preaching, as proved by the fact that in the end they accepted martyrdom for the sake of Christ with joy; all the disciples were martyred except John, who endured many torments and was exiled and died in exile.

And Christ gives them the good news that they will not complete their preaching until He comes and reigns over the hearts of people through their faith in Him, that is, until the preaching spreads in the whole world.
Likewise the Temple was destroyed in AD 70, as a proclamation of the end of Jewish worship and the spread of Christianity as the new Israel.

Hold fast to your principles of self-giving love like the lamb ready for slaughter, of simplicity and not harming others like the dove, in addition to wisdom in offering this love at the right time and in the right way, so that you may show Christ to everyone you meet, confident that the power of God in you is stronger than the world and its evil: love overcomes hatred, and simplicity overcomes cunning, because the God who is in you protects you and guides you, so that you go forward toward all hard hearts and soften them and bring them back to God.

"The disciple is not above his master": the disciples of Christ are not better than He; if Christ was subjected to insults and the Cross, it is natural that they share His sufferings by enduring persecutions. "Nor the servant above his lord": it appears that these sayings were well known at that time, and Christ took them to point to His meaning; the servant means the believers, and the lord is Christ.

"Beelzebub": he is the god of the Ekronites (the people of a city in Palestine), a land neighboring the Jews (2 Kgs 1:2), and his original name is Baal-zebub, that is, the god of flies, because they believed he drove the flies away from them, and the Jews called him Beelzebul in contempt of him.

"They of his household": that is, the disciples and those who believe in Christ, who are His children and members in His Church, which is His house. Christ reminds His disciples that the world will persecute Him, and will say of Him that He is the prince of the devils, and consequently they will persecute them because they are His disciples, and their carrying of the Cross is a proof of their following Him.
"Covered... hid": these are all the teachings of Christ that they learned in the house with Him, or that only the Jewish people knew.
"Revealed": appears and reaches all the Gentiles.
"Darkness": quiet places with dim light, or the sittings of Christ with His disciples in secret during the night.
"Light": it means open proclamation and preaching before all.
"Ear": what the disciples heard in private sittings with Christ.

"Housetops": what is meant is teaching and preaching from pulpits, or high places, so that all may hear it. Christ warns them not to fear people's accusations against them, because their service and their love of righteousness will appear and be made known in time before all, and their preaching of Christ will reach all the earth, and by this He gives the first reason for not fearing enemies. And He encouraged them to preach everywhere with boldness and power, and what they heard from Him in quiet sittings, they should proclaim to people in a loud voice from the housetops everywhere, and thus the preaching spreads so that all may believe.

Christ gives a second reason for not fearing people, which is that the most that the authority of men can reach is to harm the body, but the spirit they cannot harm. But the One who deserves to be feared is God, who has authority over both spirit and body; if we fear God, we will not fear people.
The farthing: the smallest known Jewish coin.

Here He gives the third reason for not fearing people, which is God's care for us and His concern for all creatures. The sparrow, one of the smallest birds, whose price is half a farthing, God cares for its needs, and it does not die except by His permission. How much more does God care for man, the head of all creation, and even for the smallest thing in man, which is his hair, which is not only numbered but counted by God, that is, every hair has a number with Him and does not fall except by His permission.

Rely on God and go forth in His service, assured that He protects you and keeps you and arranges your whole life, for He is responsible for you, and Satan is afraid to come near you because of the God who supports you.
"Confess me": shows My name in his words and conduct, holding fast to the commandments, and rejecting sin by repentance.

"My Father which is in heaven": I cover him with My mercy and intercede for him with My blood and bring him into the heavenly glories. For our entering into the divine justice, which is the Father, is through the mercy of the Son. The fourth reason for not fearing is the heavenly reward: everyone who stands firm in his faith and preaches in His name, confessing Him before the world, He will declare His care for him in heaven. But whoever rejects Him on earth and keeps away from Him, God will reject him in heaven.

"A sword": that is, the conflict between good and evil, or the persecution of the followers of Christ by unbelievers, so there is no outward peace, but God grants them His inner peace during persecutions.
"The daughter in law": the wife of the son.
Christ declares the suffering that a person endures in order to hold fast to the faith, that is, the Cross that he bears for the sake of Christ.

And He also called it a sword, since because of faith problems occur inside the one family, so the father persecutes his son because he believed in Christ, and likewise the pagan mother persecutes her Christian daughter... and so the Christian finds hostility from the members of his household; and for the sake of Christ he endures all these pains.

If human affections are strong within the one family, our love for Christ is greater than any affection. So if the faith of those close to us conflicts with our faith in Christ, we must obey God, otherwise we do not deserve to have Him as God, and we have no place with Him in heaven; for God must be obeyed rather than men.
Whoever wants to be a follower of Christ must endure pains for His sake, and give up much as a proof of his love for Him.
"He that findeth his life": that is, he is busy with the lusts of the world, and finds his pleasure in them.
"Shall lose it": that is, he takes it away from God, so it finds no place in heaven, but in eternal perdition. "Loseth his life": he gives his life in the toils of worship and service.

"Shall find it": he receives peace and consolation and fellowship with God on earth, then the eternal reward in the heavens. Christ asks us to give up our comfort and our bodily pleasures for His sake, and whoever gives them up finds true rest in Him, and even receives complete rest in eternity.

Look at what you have left for the sake of Christ as a proof of your love for Him, and hold fast to His commandments even if you lose some material things in which others delight, for being with Christ is better than evil pleasures or laziness and ease.
"Him that sent me": that is, God, for receiving the teachings of Christ on earth is receiving the God whom the Jews know.

"In the name of a prophet": that is, as being a prophet, and not for his person. For a person may be ordinary, but the gift of prophecy raises his rank, like the honor of the priest, however weak his person and his former standing were before the priesthood. "A prophet's reward": that is, God's blessing for the prophet or for whoever honors the prophet.
"Righteous man": a believer who lives in godliness and spirituality.

As encouragement from Christ to His disciples in the face of persecutions, He declares their dignity, and that honoring them is honoring Him personally, and receiving their word is receiving Him, and consequently everyone who receives them is rewarded with a divine reward.
"Little ones": the servants who endure many toils in serving Him and conveying His word to people.
"A cup of cold water": that is, the least refreshing drink, which helps the servants to continue their service.
"In the name of a disciple": as being a disciple, or as a follower of Christ.
"In no wise lose his reward": that is, he has a heavenly reward.

Christ shows the importance of the smallest service offered to the servants of God, even if it is a cup of cold water, for whoever offers it will receive his reward from God. For if the servants or priests or bishops give spiritual care to their people, then the flock ought to show its love for God in their persons, by working for their comfort, or providing their needs, as a declaration of their love for God, who, in His humility, offers Himself to them through these servants. If someone offers a cup of water to the servant, considering him a disciple of Christ, God will surely reward him in heaven, and even in his life on earth.

Do not belittle your love which you offer to God in gladdening those around you, however small it seems, such as words of encouragement or material help and psychological support, for it is precious in God's sight, and He will reward you for it. If you find an opportunity to serve, do not neglect it, and look for what you can give to everyone you meet, especially those close to you.
The discourse about John the Baptist, the rejection of faith

entries.section: (1) John sends two disciples to Christ

paragraphs.text: After Christ had explained to His disciples how to preach, He presented Himself as a practical example in carrying out what He had commanded them, for He began to teach what He had taught them in the synagogues spread throughout Galilee.
Take care to carry out what you teach others, so that your words may be effective.

entries.section: (1) John sends two disciples to Christ

paragraphs.text: King Herod arrested John and put him in prison. And as John felt that his end was near, he wanted to attach his disciples to Christ, so he sent two of them with a question to Him, saying: Are you the awaited Messiah or not? John was not doubting this, because he had known Him and had bowed down to Him while still in his mother's womb, and when he baptized Him, he testified that He is "the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world" (Jn 1:29), that is, that He is Christ the Redeemer; but he wanted to establish the faith of these two disciples in Christ, so that they would preach to the rest of their companions, John's disciples, so that all would follow Christ.

entries.section: (1) John sends two disciples to Christ

paragraphs.text: "The poor": not only the poor and the weak, but rather the poor in spirit, that is, the humble.

Christ's answer was His miracles, which these two disciples had seen, and they were varied, and included the healing of diseases however difficult, even if they signified uncleanness, like leprosy, or deprived a person of life through death, for He is able to deliver a person from them. Consequently, they conclude from this that He is the Christ. Make your good conduct an example that preaches your Christ, especially when speaking about Christ is not possible, for deeds are stronger than words, and words without deeds are not enough.

entries.section: (1) John sends two disciples to Christ

paragraphs.text: Christ cautions the two disciples, lest they stumble or doubt Him, because some of John's disciples were jealous for him, since a better teacher than he had appeared, and many crowds were following Him (Jn 3:26); so He calls them to believe in Him, for He is the Messiah for whom John prepared the way.
"A reed": that is, a stalk of cane, and these reeds or canes were abundant at the Jordan River, where John used to baptize.

After the departure of John's two disciples, Christ spoke about him, not intending flattery, but to give true testimony to John, who prepared the way for Him, and He said: Was John a reed shaken by the wind? The reed is hollow, so it points to the person who is empty of the grace of God, and "the wind" signifies the evil thoughts of the world. So the person who has a shining appearance like the reed, and is inwardly empty of God, is affected by the winds of temptations and evil thoughts. This is not John, but he is a man full of God, preparing the way for Christ by calling people to repentance, and firm in his principles however much evil surrounds him.
Christ asks: Was John's clothing of soft garments? No... because these pampered, luxurious people sit inside the palaces in the cities.

And these garments signify the body pampered with lusts and ease, but John was ascetic, his clothing rough and his food bare, because his heart was occupied with God and His service, and he lived austerely in the wilderness. Therefore Christ declares the greatness of John and his steadfastness in the faith, and that his sending his two disciples to Him was to bind his disciples to Him, and not for his own sake.

John the Baptist was greater than all the prophets of the Old Testament, because they longed to see Christ, and did not see Him, but only prophesied about Him. But John prophesied about Him and then beheld Him, and even baptized Him, for he is the messenger who prepared the way for Christ (Mal 3:1).

John is the greatest of men, but Christ, who is younger than he by six months, is greater than he. There is another opinion, that John is the greatest of the men of the Old Testament, but the least believer in the New Testament is greater than he in respect of his enjoying the Holy Sacraments in the Church and all the blessings of the New Testament.

Christ shows here the importance of spiritual striving for obtaining the Kingdom of Heaven: in proportion to the grace of the New Testament which John the Baptist prepared, spiritual striving is required to hold fast to it. Indeed the necessity of using force appears, that is, that a person compels himself and does not pamper his body, in order to leave his sins and hold fast to his prayers and his relationship with God, and also to seize every spiritual opportunity to draw near to God and enjoy fellowship with Him.
"Until John": because he is the last of the prophets of the Old Testament.
"If ye will receive it": if you had faith you would receive what I am about to say now.

If the aim of all the prophets was to prepare for the coming of Christ, then John is the forerunner who prepared the way for Him directly, and he came in the spirit of Elijah, so this is the fulfillment of the promise of the coming of Elijah, but in a spiritual way and not a bodily one, as will happen at the end of days (Mal 4:5-6), when Elijah comes in his body as he ascended in his body to heaven, to proclaim the voice of God before the last day of judgment.

And because of the importance of these teachings, Christ says: He who has inner ears in the heart to hear and believe, let him hear, because many of them were doubting, and did not believe that John is the one coming in the spirit of Elijah to prepare the way of the awaited Messiah, for if they believed this, it would mean their believing that He is the awaited Messiah; so He calls them to intense listening, understanding and faith.

In order to be strong in proclaiming the truth and holding fast to the commandments of God, you need detachment like John the Baptist. So do not pamper yourself with many lusts and ease for the body, and you will have a strong will in your spiritual striving and your worship, and then in your service and your proclaiming the name of Christ.

"This generation": He means the scribes and Pharisees and chief priests who refused to believe in Christ. "Children": that is, weak in their understanding and grasp of spiritual meanings and the word of God, and fickle in their opinions. "The markets": the place where the children gather to play.

Christ likens the leaders of the Jews, the scribes and Pharisees and others, who refused to believe in the call of John the Baptist, and likewise to believe in Christ, to a group of children playing in the markets of the villages and divided into two groups; one group of them plays the pipe and makes joyful, amusing movements, and the other group was not affected and delighted; then they began to mourn and show signs of grief, and the second group was not affected so as to mourn and beat the breast; that is, they failed to change their expressions.

What is meant by this likeness is that John the Baptist's call to repentance came with rebuke and grief over sin, and they refused to respond to him. Then Christ came proclaiming love and healing the sick to rejoice hearts, and they refused also.
"Neither eating nor drinking": that is, ascetic and detached, content with the least food.
"He hath a devil": because of his conduct, withdrawn from people in the wilderness, they supposed that, with his strange life, he dealt with demons.
"A gluttonous man, and a winebibber": an exaggeration by the elders of the Jews in accusing Christ, although He eats and drinks like the rest of people.

John the Baptist was an ascetic living in the wilderness, and instead of learning asceticism from him, they accused him of having a devil. But Jesus Christ lived among people eating and drinking like them, to make it easy for them to fulfill the commandments in ordinary life, and they accused Him of being absorbed in eating much and drinking wine, and this of course is not true, and they accused Him also of being a friend of tax collectors and sinners, because like them He loves gatherings of eating and drinking; whereas Christ sat with sinners to draw them to repentance, as He drew Matthew and Zacchaeus the tax collectors.
The leaders of the Jews are like children, that is, spiritually immature. But the disciples of Christ and His followers are the spiritually mature.

The children of Wisdom: those who believed in the call of John and the good news of Christ, for the righteousness of Wisdom appeared in her followers, that is, the followers of John the Baptist, and then of Christ, the Eternal Wisdom, and they believed His word; that is, the power of Wisdom and her righteousness appear in those who believe in her, and they are the disciples and the believers.

Do not be hasty in judging others lest you err, and do not be biased lest people's virtues turn into sins in your sight, but on the contrary, look for God in the virtues of others, to learn and be discipled at their hands, so that you love all, and grow in your life with God.

entries.section: (4) The punishment of those who reject faith

paragraphs.text: After He had explained the faith to His hearers, and called them also by miracles, He rebuked them for the hardness of their hearts in refusing the faith, especially the cities in the region of Galilee, because He had performed many miracles in them. So He declared that the fate of Chorazin (a city in Galilee near Bethsaida and Capernaum) and Bethsaida (a city on the Sea of Tiberias) would be dreadful in eternal torment, because the clear teachings and miracles, which easily call people to faith, if they had been done in the ancient cities of Tyre and Sidon which were on the Mediterranean Sea (in present-day Lebanon), they would have repented long ago, using the signs of humbling oneself, such as wearing rough clothes like sackcloth, and putting ashes on the head.
And by this He shows how hard the hearts of the inhabitants of Chorazin and Bethsaida were, in refusing to believe in Christ.

entries.section: (4) The punishment of those who reject faith

paragraphs.text: On the last day of judgment, the punishment of Tyre and Sidon will be lighter than that of Chorazin and Bethsaida, because the latter two refused a great faith offered to them by Christ Himself.

And the meaning of this verse is that there are degrees in eternal torment, and that those who reject the good news of Christ and life with Him will have a punishment more severe than those who did not know Christ and lived in sin, such as the pagans. A person will be held accountable according to the divine graces that were declared to him, therefore you must live and apply what you have heard in your home and your church, so that these teachings may support you on the way of salvation, and not judge you on the day of judgment.

entries.section: (4) The punishment of those who reject faith

paragraphs.text: Christ speaks about Capernaum, which became the center of His preaching in Galilee, and He performed many miracles in it, which should have saved it so that it would find a place in heaven, but sadly its people became proud, and felt they were better than those around them, as if they were in heaven and the other cities lower than they, on the earth, and they refused to believe in Him; so the fate of this city is to descend to hell.
And the measure of the work of God's grace in Capernaum, had it been done in Sodom long ago, it would have repented and the divine judgment of burning would not have been carried out on it.

entries.section: (4) The punishment of those who reject faith

paragraphs.text: Then He affirms that the torment of Sodom on the day of judgment will be lighter than the torment of Capernaum, which rejected Him; both will perish, but the severity of the torment increases for Capernaum because of its rejection of Christ; and likewise everyone who today rejects the faith and the Christian way of life will have a greater punishment.
"At that time": that is, after His words about the pride of the cities to which He had preached and which rejected Him, and a severe punishment awaits them.
"Answered": it appears that some had put a question to Him about the fate of the students of the Law found in these cities, so He answered with a prayer:
"I thank thee": as a man, He offers thanks to God for His wisdom and His ordering of things.
"The wise and prudent": the scribes and Pharisees, wise in their own eyes, and proud of their knowledge. "Babes": the disciples, weak in their knowledge, but humble and obedient to His word.
"Even so": a confirmation of the preceding answer, that the grace of God is granted to the humble.
"Good pleasure": God's joy in granting His grace to the humble.

In this great conversation between the Son and the Father, Christ confesses and declares an important truth, which is that the knowledge of God is granted to the simple and humble, and those who are wise in their own eyes, that is, the proud, are deprived of it, for God does not give His glory to another.

"All things are delivered unto me of my Father": that is, the Son received the complete authority for the redemption and salvation of mankind, and the meaning of "delivered" is not that He did not have authority and then received it when He became incarnate, but it is a declaration to us as human beings that the Son has all the authority of the Father; for the Jews know God in the Old Testament, and so Christ, who appeared in the New Testament, makes known to them by Himself that He is God, who has all authority, because He is one with the Father in essence.

"No man knoweth the Son": that is, all human beings, however great their faith, will not know the whole essence of God, because they are limited and their knowledge is limited, so only God the Father is able to know the Son, because He is equal to Him in essence. "Neither knoweth any man the Father": just as all the human beings who believed in God in the Old Testament cannot know God the Father with perfect knowledge, so the only One who knows the Father is the Son, who has the same essence as the Father.

"He to whomsoever the Son will reveal him": these are the saints whom Christ makes to know more about God by His Holy Spirit, not everything, but more than other human beings, and that is because of their humility and their longing for the love of God. No one knows God except His own essence, because He is higher than human comprehension. So the Son knows the Father and the Father knows the Son, that is, God alone is the One who knows Himself. But God in His love revealed Himself to us through the Incarnation of the Son, who makes us know God in proportion to our humility, and these humble ones are the chosen, who enjoy the knowledge of God.

"Come unto me": a call to all human beings who feel their troubles and their need for salvation. But those immersed in the world and content with its lusts do not feel their need for Christ. "All ye that labour and are heavy laden": with the burden of sin, the reproach of conscience, the problems resulting from their sins, and all the pressures of life and its fears.

"I will give you rest": He did not promise human beings the prevention of afflictions, but promises them rest during them, since He bears them with them and for them, so they do not feel their weight, and are comforted and rejoice in fellowship with Him.

Christ became incarnate to bear our toils and our sins on the Cross, so His arms are open to lift from us our sins and all that results from them, so that we find our peace in Him, and He is able to order all the affairs of our life.

"My yoke": the yoke is the piece of wood placed on the necks of the animals that pull agricultural implements such as the plow, so bearing the yoke means bowing the neck, that is, humility, and enduring pain for the sake of Christ, and these are the marks of the followers of Christ.
"Learn of me": Christ is an example for us in all His conduct on earth, and He is the highest ideal for mankind. "Meek": He keeps His peace and inner calm, and is not stirred by any gain or loss.
"Lowly": He puts Himself beneath all, giving up all His glory.
"Rest unto your souls": meekness and lowliness are the way to obtaining salvation.

The Lord reassures us that His yoke is easy and light, because He bears it with us, and if two carry one load, the weight falls on the stronger. So if God, the stronger without limit, carries with us, He carries everything for us, so we feel no weariness at all, but enjoy fellowship with Him all along the way of our life, and behold His work in us and in the souls we deal with and serve.
Humble yourself under the feet of all, and you will know God and enjoy fellowship with Him...
Accept pain for God's sake, and you will see Him beside you encouraging you, and gladdening your heart, and lifting from you every pain and suffering, because He supports you in everything.
The purifying of the heart produces mercy and defeats the demons

entries.section: (1) Plucking the ears of corn on the Sabbath

paragraphs.text: "The Sabbath": the day of the Lord among the Jews, for God commanded that it be set apart for worship, but the elders of the Jews forbade even necessary works on it. The glory of Sunday surpassed the glory of the Sabbath, because on it the Lord of glory rose, so it is considered the Lord's Day in the New Testament.
"Through the corn": Christ wanted to be alone with His disciples, so He went with them to the fields.

"Plucked the ears of corn": the hungry were permitted to pluck some ears and rub them in their hands and eat them to satisfy their hunger. It is understood from this that the disciples were poor and needed necessary food, since they had no food.

"That which is not lawful to do": they forbade some works on the Sabbath, among them the plucking of ears of corn. The Law did not state this, but it was among the mistaken excessive interpretations that they added, and it conflicts with the necessary needs of man.

Christ was walking with His disciples on the Sabbath through the cornfields, continuing to teach them. After a while they became hungry, so they plucked some ears to eat, and this was permitted in the Law and is not considered stealing (Deut 23:25). But the Pharisees considered it a harvesting of wheat, and work is forbidden on the Sabbath day, so they objected to Christ, because He did not prevent His disciples from doing it.

Though work is forbidden on the Sabbath day so that they may be free for the worship of God, necessary works such as eating are not forbidden, so this was a vain accusation from the Pharisees, since they counted the disciples' satisfying their hunger as a harvesting of wheat, and this shows their ill intent and the narrowness of their interpretation of the concept of rest on the Sabbath day.

entries.section: (1) Plucking the ears of corn on the Sabbath

paragraphs.text: "The house of God": the Tabernacle of the congregation.

"The showbread": twelve loaves that were placed on a table in the Holy Place on the right, and none entered the Holy Place except the priests, so only the priests ate it, as a symbol of the special grace of the sacrament of the priesthood in the New Testament. Christ reminded the disciples of what David did on the Sabbath day, when he and those with him were hungry, for they entered and ate of the showbread, which it is not lawful to eat except for the priests, but out of necessity, and so that they would not faint from hunger, they ate of it.

And King David is very honored, and a point of reference for the Jews from whom to learn, so David's understanding of the spirit of the commandment, and not its letter, appears here; he did not intend to break the commandment, but the matter requires an understanding of the spirit of the commandment, that is, flexibility in carrying it out.
This is the first proof that the disciples did not err in plucking the ears of corn on the Sabbath day.

entries.section: (1) Plucking the ears of corn on the Sabbath

paragraphs.text: "The Law" (the Torah): the five books of Moses, and what is meant is specifically the book of Numbers, where it mentions the offering of sacrifices on the Sabbath day.
"Profane the Sabbath": that is, break the rest imposed on this day.
"And are blameless": because they obey the Law by offering the services required in the Law.

Christ gave a second proof, namely the works that the priests do on the Sabbath day in the Temple, for they do not intend to break the Sabbath, but these are works of service connected with the worship of God, that is, the offering of sacrifices. What is meant is abstaining from ordinary works and material gains, and devoting oneself to spiritual work, and being content only with the necessary needs of man.

entries.section: (1) Plucking the ears of corn on the Sabbath

paragraphs.text: If occupation with the Temple permits any work or service that it needs, then before us is Christ, the Lord of the Temple, who is greater than it; indeed the Jewish Temple signifies Him, for He is the One who will offer Himself as a sacrifice on the altar of the Cross. Therefore the disciples ate some ears of corn to satisfy their hunger, and to remain occupied with hearing His teachings and serving Him, and this is the highest purpose.

entries.section: (1) Plucking the ears of corn on the Sabbath

paragraphs.text: "The guiltless": the poor disciples who needed to satisfy their hunger, for they are guiltless of any fault.

Christ pointed to the words of God in Hosea the prophet (Hos 6:6), that He desires mercy and not sacrifice, that is, that what is meant is that the work of mercy is more important than literal adherence to sacrifice while the heart is empty of love and given to accusing and condemning others.

How did they not feel the hunger of the disciples, and their necessary need to eat?! It is hardness of heart on the part of the Pharisees, and so the righteousness of the disciples and the wickedness of the Pharisees appeared.

entries.section: (1) Plucking the ears of corn on the Sabbath

paragraphs.text: "Lord of the Sabbath": that is, the One who laid down the law of the Sabbath, and who alone may permit what He sees fit, and add what must be attended to, so He added the sanctification of Sunday, and it became the Lord's Day through His Resurrection on it. Christ affirms that He is the giver of the Law, which includes the sanctification of the Sabbath day, so He of course does not want to break the commandment, but its spirit must be understood and applied well. And this is a third proof in defense of the disciples for their plucking the ears of corn, since they have with them the Lord of the Sabbath, who is able to permit what He sees fit.
Do not judge by appearance and condemn others, but make excuses for them, and be merciful to sinners as God has compassion on you and has mercy on you.

entries.section: (2) The healing of the man with the withered hand

paragraphs.text: "Accuse Him": bring a complaint in their local councils that He is a transgressor.

After He had passed through the fields, He went to one of the synagogues of the Jews as was His custom to teach there, and all the sick were following Him that He might heal them; and a man came whose hand was paralyzed, hoping that Christ would heal him. The Pharisees noticed that the man would ask Christ for healing, so they hastened to ask Him, not out of inquiry but with malice: Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath day? They considered that healing is one of the worldly works, being the work of a physician who treats the sick, and not a miracle and a mercy that Christ offers to the needy; and this shows their ill intent and their mistaken interpretation.

entries.section: (2) The healing of the man with the withered hand

paragraphs.text: Christ answered their question with another question, namely: If someone has a sheep and it falls into a pit on the Sabbath day, will he not hasten to rescue it and lift it out of the pit so that it does not die? This work is not permitted, but it is excepted as a work of mercy to rescue the sheep, so how much more is a sick man more important than a sheep? Consequently, healing is lawful as a work of mercy on the Sabbath day. Then Christ, by His divine authority, commanded the man with the withered hand to stretch it out, and he obeyed in faith, and it was healed immediately.

It is to be noted that Christ only commanded and did not touch him, and the man stretched out his hand, and stretching out the hand is not forbidden on the Sabbath. Thus He healed him, and did not violate even their narrow, mistaken teachings, so they found no charge against Him.
How great is the obedience of this sick man: although his hand was paralyzed, he believed the word of Christ, and when he tried to stretch it out it moved with him, and he was healed immediately.

May you obey the commandments of God however difficult they seem, and accept the teachings of the Church and the guidance of your father of confession, confident of the power of God that supports you, so that you find nothing impossible before you, because Satan makes you imagine your weakness and your inability to be freed from sin and acquire virtues, so do not believe him, and be sure that obedience brings you out of his authority and grants you all blessings.
"That they might destroy him": this is the first attempt to kill Him.
"Great multitudes": of Jews and Gentiles, as appears in (v. 21).

When the wickedness of the Pharisees appeared before the righteousness of Christ and His mercy to His disciples and to the sick, they were greatly enraged and tried to kill Him, and He did not resist them using the power of His divinity, but fled from their presence, because He was occupied with completing the preaching and healing the needy, and also to teach us not to resist evil with evil, but to flee from it, so He charged the crowds to hide Him among them, in order to continue His teaching and doing good for all the needy, and because He was humble and did not seek earthly glory.

Christ showed this in a manner that appeared weak, contrary to what the Jews expected of the awaited Messiah, that He would be strong, establish a kingdom for them and free them from the authority of the Romans. And this of course is a mistaken interpretation by the Jews that God did not intend, but what matters is that He free them from sin, and reign over their hearts, and not the earthly kingship they claim, and therefore St. Matthew cited the prophecy of Isaiah about Christ (Isa 42:1-4), which shows His meekness and His not resisting evil with evil.
"Whom I have chosen": Christ alone is the One chosen by God and able to redeem mankind, and no angel or man can do this work.
"In whom my soul is well pleased": as the Father declared from heaven at His Baptism in the Jordan, for He is the object of the Father's pleasure because He accomplishes our salvation.

"I will put my spirit upon him": a declaration that the Holy Spirit is in the Son, as He appeared in the form of a dove at His Baptism, but He is united with Him from eternity because He is His Spirit, so it is a declaration to us as human beings that we may believe that He is God. "The Gentiles": a clear proof that salvation is offered to the whole world.

The Father speaks about the Son saying that He puts His Spirit upon Him, and He is at the same time the Spirit of the Son, who is the Holy Spirit. Thus He declares the Holy Trinity, who appears in the Incarnation of Christ, who proclaims the truth to mankind with meekness and love, when He says: my servant and my beloved.
If you are united with Christ and become a member of His body, the Church, you will be beloved of God and He will be pleased with you.

Among the characteristics of the meek Christ is that He does not meet people's evil with another evil, so He does not quarrel with the wicked, and does not become angry with shouting that makes others stumble in the streets, because He is calm within with true meekness.

The love of Christ appears in His care for every person however weak or hopeless he may seem, like the reed that has been struck and was about to break, or the wick from which the fire has gone out and nothing remains but smoke rising from it.
For He supports the very weak person until he becomes strong and is filled with Him, and overcomes his sins and weaknesses, and has a place in heaven.
He supports the reed and kindles the wick and cares for it, until He completes His work of showing forth the truth in all hearts, so that they overcome sin and are freed from it.

By this love He gives hope to the whole world. For if the Jews reject the Gentiles because of their distance from God, Christ preaches to them and seeks their salvation however weak they are, so that they leave the worship of idols and return to Him.

It is a great hope offered to you, however much your sins dominate you, or your problems seem to have no solution, for Christ loves you, and He is able to save you from your troubles. Trust in Him, and arise, begin anew with Him.
Satan entered a man, and made him lose his mind, his sight and his speech. They brought him to Christ and He healed him, that is, He cast Satan out of him, so he returned sane, seeing and speaking.
Sin makes you lose your sound thinking, so you do not see God and do not speak His commandments. So hasten to repentance, that you may regain your humanity in Christ.
"Amazed": he wondered and was greatly astonished.
"Son of David": as God promised that Christ would come from the seed of David.
"Beelzebub": see the commentary on (ch. 10:24-25), and accusing Christ of a relationship with him is a kind of contempt for Him, and means that His power is from the devils and not from God.

When the Jews saw the power of the miracle, they said that He is the awaited Messiah, the Son of David. But the Pharisees, because of their pride and love of worldly positions, found Christ to be a rival to them, since He had become a spiritual leader of the Jews, and by this they would lose their standing, so they hastened to oppose the miracle by accusing Christ that, by a special agreement between Him and Beelzebub the prince of the devils, He made this demon come out, and the man returned healthy; that is, they accused Christ of sorcery and of dealing with demons, in order to turn people away from following Him and from being amazed at His divine authority.
"Jesus knew their thoughts": this shows His divinity and His knowledge of the unseen, and of what is inside people without hearing them.

Christ gave the Pharisees a logical argument for the falsity of their accusation, so that the Jews would not doubt but stand firm in their faith in Him and in following Him, namely that if division occurs in any kingdom it is laid waste, since each party opposes the other. So if this happened in the kingdom of Satan, it would mean that the prince of the devils sets free those of mankind who follow him, and this is against his plan, because he wants to harm human beings and turn them away from God. So Satan cannot work against himself, or his kingdom would be laid waste, and this is illogical. Consequently, the casting out of this demon is by the power of God, and not by an agreement with the prince of the devils.

Then He gave a second logical argument, namely His disciples, that is, the sons of the Jewish nation who cast out demons. It is known among the Jews that the disciples were simple and had no experience in dealing with demons, sorcery and divination. So the disciples' casting out of demons judges the Pharisees' accusation to be false, just as the Jews do not object to any of their own who cast out demons, such as the seven sons of Sceva (Acts 19:14), even if this was a mere claim and not a real ability. Why then do they object to Christ and accuse Him of sorcery, except that they envy Him, and try to cast doubt on His divine power?

Satan came out by the power of the Spirit of God, and not by sorcery, and this means that He is the awaited Messiah. "The kingdom of God is come unto you": that is, Christ has come to reign over hearts, so why do you oppose Him with your evil thoughts?

And Christ gave a third proof that He casts out Satan by the authority of His divinity, which is that it is not possible to seize the possessions of a strong person unless we are able to bind him first. Consequently, it is not possible to cast a demon out of a person unless we have authority over the demons to bind them, and so command them to come out. That is, Christ is stronger than the demons, and consequently can command them to come out of human beings.

Since Satan is not good nor a follower of Christ, and does not gather people to believe in Him, this is a proof that he is an enemy of Christ, trying to scatter people and turn them away from Him, and he enters into people to lead them astray and make them lose their mind and insight. And Christ, by the authority of His divinity, drives His enemies the demons away from weak human beings, for He came to save mankind from the authority of the devil, who controls them because of their weakness and their sins. And by the Pharisees' accusing Him, they try to scatter people and turn them away from Him, and by this they are followers of the demons and enemies of Christ. He presents by this the fourth logical argument that He is against the demons and not with them, to rebuke the Pharisees so that they repent of their enmity toward Him, because, by their wickedness, they become followers of the demons who try to turn human beings away from God. Examine your words and your conduct: do they help draw others to God, or do they make them stumble and turn them away from Him, so that you may know whether you are a follower of Christ or of Satan?
Christ showed the gravity of the Pharisees' accusation against Him, which is that He casts out demons by an agreement with Satan, and not by the Holy Spirit.

Their insistence on rejecting the work of the Holy Spirit, and on not believing in Christ, will not be forgiven them forever, that is, it takes them to eternal torment. So He warns them to repent and not to persist in their evil thoughts. Whoever sins by a word against Christ the Son and repents, it is forgiven him, but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit, and rejects His work in his life by insisting on not repenting, his fate is eternal perdition.

Christ rebukes the hypocrisy of the Pharisees, who pretend to be religious while their hearts are full of evil and pride, so He tells them that the good tree bears good fruit, and likewise the bad one bears bad fruit, and He requires them to keep away from hypocrisy, so that their words and works agree with the feelings of their hearts, and their thoughts are purified, that is, the inside becomes pure and likewise the outside, and if there is evil in the heart, it appears in speech or deeds, and that helps them to repent and reject sin.

The works of Christ, full of goodness and mercy, are good works that prove His righteousness and goodness, but the Pharisees, whose evil speech about Christ and whose pride prove that they are wicked; their bad fruits declare the evil of their hearts. And He rebukes them that this hypocrisy of theirs is like snakes in their cunning and outward smoothness, but they are full of poison and savagery and preying on others.
And by this He calls them to purify their hearts from the evils they have stored up inside them, which appear in their speech and their accusations.
"Idle word": that is, unprofitable, and what is meant here, most of all, is the evil speech by which we wrong others.

Christ shows the gravity of vain speech, that is, evil or unprofitable, since we will be held accountable for it on the day of judgment, so let us not take it lightly and speak words that are unprofitable or harmful to others. Our good speech justifies us on the day of judgment, and on the contrary, our evil speech, which shows that our hearts are evil, will lead us to perdition.
Examine your speech today: is it profitable to you or to others, or does it harm you or them, or is it of no use? And ask the help of God, and He will give you wisdom by His Holy Spirit.
"Master": the scribes and Pharisees said it, either in mockery or in flattery of Christ, that He might perform a new miracle for them.

Despite the many miracles of Christ, the scribes and Pharisees were still unbelieving, so they asked Him for a miracle that they might believe in Him, and this means that they were sunk in the doubts that obstruct faith.
"Generation": He means the Jewish nation, most of which is far from God by their evils, despite their appearing to be His people.
"Adulterous": the Jewish nation is the bride of God, and its departure from Him is spiritual adultery, for debauchery is a kind of adultery.
"Three days": a part of a day is counted as a day among the Jews, so in the death of Christ there was part of Friday, and the whole of Saturday, and part of Sunday.
"Three nights": what is meant is the darkness that occurred at His death on the Cross, and the night of Saturday and the night of Sunday.
"The heart of the earth": the tomb of Christ.

Christ rebuked the evils of their hearts and their persistence in pride and doubts, and told them that they did not need to see a new miracle of His miracles, but needed repentance, like the miracle of the repentance of Jonah the prophet, who repented in the belly of the whale after remaining in it three days, and died to the world, and returned to God, and then the whale spewed him out, and he returned alive. Just as Christ will die for the sins of the whole world, but by the power of His divinity will rise from the dead. They need to die to their sins by repentance, that they may believe in Him and rise from their evil, and begin the new life with Him.

"Nineveh": the capital of the Assyrian Empire, a city on the Tigris River in Iraq, near the present city of Mosul, and it was very great, its circumference 48 miles, and the height of its walls 28 meters, and it was destroyed in the sixth century before Christ.

When Jonah cried out powerfully among the people of Nineveh, after he had repented, his words had an effect on them and they repented. And now, before the Jews are words stronger than the words of Jonah, and great miracles, yet they refuse to believe. Therefore the repentance of the people of Nineveh will condemn the unbelief of those who reject Christ on the great day of judgment.
"The uttermost parts of the earth": that is, from a distance of about 1,000 miles from Jerusalem.

If the queen of the South and of Sheba, that is, Yemen, came from a distant place, when she heard of the wisdom of Solomon, and believed in the power of the Spirit of God in him, her faith also condemns the Jews who reject Christ, with His word and His perfect wisdom displayed before them.
"Dry places": Satan tends to dwell in the wastelands, where there is no water.
"Seeking rest": that is, seeking to do evil, because his rest is in turning people away from God.

When a demon entered a man, and by the power of God came out of him, he goes about seeking another person to dwell in. And since he finds no life for him for the good of people, he returns to see his old friend in whom he dwelt for a time, and finds his heart empty of all goodness, swept of all righteousness, indeed prepared and adorned with the evil in which he lives. For although he was delivered from Satan, he did not repent of his sins and live with God in goodness.

When he finds this man more prepared for his dwelling than before, he takes with him seven spirits (demons) and they dwell in him, to lead him into more evils, so his misery increases, and his end is perdition. So too the Jews, during the captivity they were bound to the worship of idols, and after their return they left it, but they were not bound to God in their hearts, and their hearts remained empty. And when Christ came to them and preached to them they rejected Him, and added to their sins the sins of hypocrisy and pride, so by this they prepare themselves for the work of the demons in them more than before, and their perdition becomes harder and their torment more severe.

When God delivers you from a sin, or removes its warfare from you and you rest a little from it, hasten to be bound to the Church and the Holy Sacraments, and keep on praying and reading, until your heart is filled with the love of God, and you become fortified against any new warfare from Satan.
While Christ was teaching among the crowds, His mother the Virgin Mary came, and the children of her sister Mary the wife of Cleophas, that is, the cousins of Christ on His mother's side.

In Jewish custom, cousins are counted as brothers. They came looking for Him, to enjoy sitting with Him and speaking to Him. And because of the great crowd around Him, they could not enter, so they told Him that outside the house were His mother and His brethren seeking Him.

Christ seized this opportunity to teach the crowds the meaning of spiritual motherhood and brotherhood, and He did not deny the importance of bodily motherhood and brotherhood, but wanted to direct the gaze of the crowds to a new meaning, which is that a person should have many mothers and brothers in the Spirit.
Christ showed that spiritual motherhood and brotherhood to Him are in whoever keeps His commandments and does His will; and the example of this is His disciples who follow Him.

For motherhood means self-giving and sacrifice, and brotherhood means fellowship and bonding. So whoever does the will of God must give up his personal desires, and strive to be bound to God and to the whole world in His love, and so he has spiritual motherhood and brotherhood toward God, and toward his brethren in the Church and the whole world.

Christ's esteem for you, and His calling you a brother, is a great honor that gives you boldness in prayer, and confidence in His help however much you fall into sin, that you may repent and return to Him.

And on the other hand, you keep yourself pure because you are a brother of Christ spiritually, and likewise you feel that all the believers with you in the Church are your brethren, so you love them and honor them with all care.
Thirteen. The parables of Christ; the preaching in His homeland
"By the sea side": it is the Sea of Galilee.

The crowds followed Christ as was their custom, to enjoy His life-giving teachings, and as their number increased, and He was near the shore of the sea, He entered one of the boats and moved a little away from the land in it, so that it became a pulpit for Him from which to speak, while the crowds sat on the shore to listen to Him.

How great is the simplicity of Christ and His humility! He teaches on the mountain, or on the shore, or stands in a boat which He regards as a pulpit for His teachings. For the most important thing to Him is to win the love of the crowds, and convey His spiritual teachings to them.

He went out of the house in which He was staying, which signifies the Church, from which He went out into the world to visit His people, and He entered the sea, which signifies the world, but He stood in a boat, which signifies the human soul in which He dwells, and shows Himself from it to others, as He does through His believing children who are the light of the world.

"Spake many things unto them": it is understood that He gave many examples, some of which are recorded in the Holy Bible. "Parables": an illustration of the spiritual truth by a practical, real story, to bring the meaning near to the mind of the hearer. "The sower": he is God.
The sower used the seeds, which are His word that He gives to the different soils, which represent the kinds of people, each differing from the other in his receiving of His word.

The sower went forth to sow, for God's work is goodness; He casts His word to all in the hope that it may bear fruit. Likewise the children of God, their work is doing good to all, regardless of how much others respond to this good.
The first kind of soil is the farm path that passes beside the fields, which is raised above them and hard and not prepared for planting, and is always trodden by the feet of passersby.
It points to the proud human soul that has not been prepared by plowing to receive the word of God, that is, self-examination and repentance.

And it is hard, so it points to hardness of heart and rejection of the word of God, and it is trodden by all, that is, all the lusts of the world enter it, for it has no walls to protect it, that is, it is not fortified by the Church; so when the word of God was cast into it, it rejoiced in it quickly but the heart did not receive it, and soon the birds of the air swooped down on it and ate the seeds. The birds point to the demons that steal the word, because the heart is affected temporarily, and quickly loses this effect, because of its pride and its not repenting of its various lusts.

The second kind of soil is the stony ground, but it has a thin surface layer of earth, so its appearance is as though it were good farmland, and its reality is that it is stones that refuse any planting in it.

It points to hardness of heart like stone, and to the worship of idols of stone, that is, the worship of the money and positions of this world, which are like idols to which a person clings, for although he has a surface soil in which the seeds grow a little, when the roots try to extend, they cannot because of the stones, and when the sun rises these little plants dry up and die.
It also signifies hypocritical souls, which have the appearance of good soil and the reality of stone.

And it signifies hearts attached to the world, which receive the word for a short time, and when trials come upon them, like the rays of the sun, they dry up quickly and the word of God dies in them, for they are hard, selfish hearts that do not love God from within.
The third kind of soil is good soil suitable for planting, but full of thorns, that is, the heart's concerns for the world and its lusts.

So when the word of God is cast into it, it grows, but the growth of the thorns and foreign weeds is stronger than it, so they crowd its roots in the ground and it finds no nourishment, and the thorns and weeds cover it from above, so the rays of the sun do not reach it, and they choke it and it dies.

It points to the danger of keeping the lusts of sin in the heart, because they hinder the work of the word of God, so that a person does not benefit from it. And the remedy of course is repentance and removing the thorns of sin, and then the word can have an effect on these souls.

The fourth kind of soil is the good ground suitable for planting, and if the word of God is cast into it, it grows and bears fruit. And the amount of fruit differs according to the fertility of the ground and its response to the word, for all are children of the Kingdom, but one star differs from another in how it benefits from and applies the word of God.
Christ affirmed the importance of hearing His word with the two ears, that is, the outer ear, and the inner ear which is the heart, in order to understand and apply the word.

God offers His love and grace to all people, but what matters is that you respond to it, so do not reject the word of God that He sends you, whether in the Holy Bible or the teachings of the Church and the guidance of your father of confession, or on the tongues of those around you.

Receive the word for yourself and not for teaching others, and try to apply it in your life, and trust that every striving to carry out the word of God is very precious to Him, and He supports you to complete it, and rewards you for it.
"Came": after the crowds departed, a few remained and came forward to Christ to ask Him.
"The disciples": they are the Twelve and another small group of those attached to Christ, as appears from (Mk 4:10), and they are like the seventy Apostles and the Marys.
"It is given unto you": a special grace given to those who care to know God.

"The mysteries of the kingdom of heaven": that is, how God reigns over the heart, for the knowledge of God is above the human mind, but God by His grace gives understanding to those ready to receive Him.

"Them": those who do not care about the word of God, because of their preoccupation with material things, so their knowledge is always superficial. Christ spoke to the crowds in parables close to their lives, that they might understand the idea and be affected by it, because in the hardness of their hearts they will reject direct speech, but the parables from their own lives they may accept, and so submit to the word of God. But the disciples, because of their readiness to obey Christ, He explained the parables to them in direct spiritual language, for whoever has spiritual readiness is given more and more knowledge of God. But whoever has no readiness and keeps rejecting, even the parable he does not understand and will reject it, and the little spiritual understanding he has he will lose through his pride and his attachment to the material world.

"Seeing they see not, and hearing they hear not": despite their seeing Christ and hearing His teachings, they do not grasp the depths of the words in order to apply them in their lives, but are content with superficial knowledge. And more than this, they may even reject the words and their spiritual meanings, because of their attachment to their material lusts and their pride. "This people's heart is waxed gross": that is, it became bound to earthly lusts, and was no longer tender and open to being affected by the word of God.
"Dull of hearing": that is, they became unable to understand the word of God, because lusts have deafened their ears, and they want to hear only what pleases them.
"That I should heal them": that is, I accept their repentance, and set their lives right so that they become spiritual.

Although these crowds have outward eyes, and ears that distinguish letters, their hearts reject God; they awaited the awaited Messiah according to the prophecies, and when Christ became incarnate and came to them, they rejected Him because of the hardness of their hearts and their pride, and their attachment to earthly kingship and honor, so they lost spiritual understanding, as their great prophet Isaiah prophesied about them (Isa 6:10).

Christ praises His disciples for their understanding of His word, and their enjoying the sight of Him, and their faith that He is the awaited Messiah, and He even declares to them that the honor they received of seeing Him was desired by many prophets and godly men in the Old Testament who did not see Him, but received only the honor of prophesying about Him, and awaited the promise of its fulfillment while their souls were bound in Hades, until He came and accomplished redemption for them and saved them.

This is what you behold today, my brother, in the Church, and even receive true Body and Blood, and enjoy hearing the word of God in the Holy Bible, which all the men of God in the Old Testament longed to behold, so enjoy it, that you may live by it and in it, and be careful to attend the Liturgies from their beginning, and to receive the blessing of confession and Holy Communion always.

entries.section: (3) The interpretation of the parable of the sower

paragraphs.text: "The word of the kingdom": the word of God which, if you understand it and apply it, makes your heart prepared for the reign of God over it.
"Understandeth it not": he refuses to understand the word of God, because of his preoccupation with material things.
"The wicked one": Satan.
"Catcheth away": that is, his being affected is very temporary, like an emotional reaction that passes quickly, and he applies nothing of what he heard in his life.

entries.section: (3) The interpretation of the parable of the sower

paragraphs.text: "Anon receiveth it": the quick being affected by the word of God, and the intention to apply it and begin to do so.

entries.section: (3) The interpretation of the parable of the sower

paragraphs.text: "Hath not root in himself": he has not striven in the way of God to carry out His word for a long time, that is, his being affected is emotional and superficial, and the heart is weak as a result of his life preoccupied with the world.

"Tribulation or persecution": that is, problems that try to prevent him from continuing to carry out the commandment. "Is offended": that is, he leaves the commandments of God and returns to his life bound to the world.

entries.section: (3) The interpretation of the parable of the sower

paragraphs.text: "The care of this world": anxiety and preoccupation with acquiring material things and various lusts. "The deceitfulness of riches": pride resulting from the material things a person possesses, so he feels he is better than others. "Choke the word": that is, there is no place in the heart for the love of God, because it is preoccupied with evil lusts. "Unfruitful": that is, no virtues appear in his life.

entries.section: (3) The interpretation of the parable of the sower

paragraphs.text: "Good": that is, the ground that has been plowed and then fertilized and watered, meaning a person's self-examination and repentance, as well as spiritual striving in using the means of grace, of sacraments and spiritual practices.
"Heareth the word, and understandeth it": that is, he cares for practical application and not only theoretical knowledge.

"Beareth fruit... an hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty": degrees of response and spiritual striving, from which virtues result, and indeed the grace of God increases for those who respond and strive, so this difference among them in holiness appears.

entries.section: (4) The parable of the tares of the field

paragraphs.text: "The kingdom of heaven": that is, the reign of Christ coming from heaven, to reign over the hearts of His children.
The man: He is God, who created all human beings in His image and likeness, to live with Him forever in His Kingdom, and to bear good works.

entries.section: (4) The parable of the tares of the field
