Stumbling blocks result from the love of worldly lusts, inflexibility, and little feeling for others, especially the weak such as children. Therefore it is a great crime, and whoever insists on causing others to stumble and does not repent must perish, and his perishing is expressed by "that a millstone were hanged about his neck", which is a heavy stone used for crushing grain by being turned over a fixed stone. And when a person tied to this stone is thrown, he will certainly drown in the sea.

So if stumbling blocks must exist because of the evil of people, Christ declares that woe awaits the one who causes the stumbling and fall of another, and he is condemned to destruction like one who drowns in the depth of the sea, which signifies worldly lusts, so that his falling into many sins is easy, and he goes away from God.

Be careful about your speech, your appearance and your conduct, so that you do not cause the simple to stumble and turn them away from God... for how can you make fall those for whom Christ died, how can you hand them over to sin by your carelessness?!
The one who causes another to stumble has had his heart hardened by the lusts of the world, and for this reason his punishment is very severe.
"Life": He means our life in the world.
"Halt ... maimed ... one eye": that is, to live without the person or thing that you regard as important, like a member of your body such as your foot, your hand and your eye.
"Hell fire": eternal torment.

After speaking of the gravity of causing others to stumble, He warns us not to stumble ourselves and fall into sin, and says that however important the matter, we should be rid of it as long as it causes us to stumble. And He gave comparisons with necessary members of the body such as the foot, the hand and the eye, which signify the important things in our lives; as long as they lead us to evil lusts, let us keep away from them, whether it be a friend or relative or place or a stumbling work or a hobby, or anything the devil uses to make us fall into sin. For it is better for you to live in this earthly life giving up something important, so that you are like the lame or the maimed or the one-eyed, than to hold to what causes you to stumble and makes you fall into sin, and so go to eternal torment.

Do not say, I will leave sin and hold on to the evil relationship, since I have already fallen; flee for your life from this relationship, because the salvation of your soul is the most important thing. Do not be careless and cast yourself into eternal torment.

Set it in your heart that you must live for Christ forever, so leave behind everything that leads to sin, even if wicked people mistreat you because of your distance from evil. For enduring anything, even death itself, is easier than eternal torment.

Here He speaks of caring for others and not causing them to stumble by our carelessness, affirming the value of their souls before God, and He declares an important truth of faith, that each one of us has a guardian angel. These children, or simple or weak ones, their souls have value before God, and they have angels who always pray for them in heaven. On the other hand, Christ came to redeem these despised ones, and the price of the salvation of their souls is His precious blood, which is the greatest thing in existence.

Beware of contempt, for if anyone falls because of your carelessness, this grieves God and His angels greatly, and God responds to the intercession of the angels of these people, and raises them from their sins if they repent.

"The ninety and nine": they signify the angels who did not fall. It may also be interpreted as those righteous in their own eyes, whom God leaves because they do not feel their need of salvation, and He seeks the one who fell and feels that he is wicked.
"Upon the mountains": where there is safety in the folds prepared for it.
"That which is gone astray": it is the one who has fallen into sin and feels his weakness. It also signifies all mankind who strayed from God, as distinguished from the angels who did not fall.

"He rejoiceth": because he was lost and dead, and he lived and returned to his true life in God by repentance. He shows God's love for those who stumble because of their weakness, by the parable of the man who has a hundred sheep and only one goes astray, for he is not occupied with the ninety and nine, but shuts them in the fold and goes out searching with care until he finds this lost one. For God cares for and seeks every person, however weak or lowly he may seem, until He saves him.
Be confident that you have a place in the heart of God that no one else fills, so if you fall, repent quickly, to return to your place and so rejoice and make Him rejoice.

entries.section: (3) Dealing with those who wrong us

paragraphs.text: "Thy brother": that is, any person.
"Between thee and him alone": privately, so that you do not embarrass him before others, or stir up his pride so that he tries to justify himself.
"Thou hast gained thy brother": you have restored your good relationship with him, and at the same time his heart was purified and his relationship with God returned.

Christ explains how to deal with one who wrongs you. The first thing is that you love him, and take the initiative to go to him to rescue him from persisting in the fault into which he has fallen. For he has not only troubled you, but has sinned against God and himself, so you go to him in love to reprove him, so as to show him what he has done wrong.

He did not say that you rebuke him, because the aim is not to show his faults and prove them against him, or to take your right from him, but the aim is that you win him to Christ, and bring him back to Him by your love for him and your concern for his salvation, so that your manner of speaking is the reproof of love, with gentleness and tenderness.

entries.section: (3) Dealing with those who wrong us

paragraphs.text: If he refuses to hear your reproof and persists in his fault, do not despair, but take with you one or two of the beloved, especially those known to him, that perhaps by their intercession he may be persuaded to restore good relations with you and remove the causes of the dispute. Then your reproof is not merely your personal opinion, but two or three, whose opinion has more influence. On the other hand, they will be two witnesses against the wrongdoer when the matter is brought to the Church, as Moses commanded in the Law (Deut 17:6).

entries.section: (3) Dealing with those who wrong us

paragraphs.text: If this second attempt at reconciliation fails, do not despair either, but tell the Church, that is, the priests and servants, so that they may try to persuade him to remove the dispute and restore love. And if he persists in the fault, treat him as you would treat the heathen man and the publican, that is, those far from the Church, so you love him and pray for him, even if relations between you are cut off because of his refusal, or your relationship is limited and not a friendship.

entries.section: (3) Dealing with those who wrong us

paragraphs.text: The Church supports you in your stand so that you do not blame yourself, for it has the right to bind him, that is, to prevent him from her membership and from receiving the Sacraments, because of his persistence in the fault. But if he returns and repents, it has the right to loose him, and he has communion in the Church, and in heaven also after the end of this life.
And here is a second affirmation of the authority of the priesthood in the sacrament of confession, not only for Peter as mentioned in (ch. 16:19).

entries.section: (3) Dealing with those who wrong us

paragraphs.text: He opens the door of hope for this sinner who persists in his fault, for despite the Church's excluding him, she asks you and everyone who loves him to pray for him until he repents.
And He encourages us that the agreement of two in love and prayer is great in the eyes of God, so He gives them their request for the return of this sinner and his repentance.

And He affirms the importance of common prayer by the gathering of two or three, for Christ dwells with a special blessing in their midst; He blesses everyone who prays, but there is an additional blessing and a special indwelling of Christ in common prayer, and the greatest common prayer is the prayer of the Divine Liturgy around the Body and Blood of the Lord, and, extending from it, the family's prayer at home, that is, the husband and wife and children, in which they ask for the needs of the home and its cohesion, and it encourages its members to the spiritual life and to love one another.

May your love appear, not only toward those who love you, but even more toward those who wrong you, so that you seek them in love to reconcile with them and win their souls. And if all your attempts fail, persevere in praying for them, having compassion on them, and the mercies of God toward you will increase.

entries.section: (4) The extent of forgiveness toward others

paragraphs.text: Peter asked Christ about the extent of bearing the faults of others and forgiving them: should he forgive seven times? And this number is not small, because the Jews in their book "the Talmud" say that forgiveness is three times. It is understood from Peter's question that forgiveness has limits, and he asks about them.

entries.section: (4) The extent of forgiveness toward others

paragraphs.text: Christ answered: "Until seventy times seven", that is, 490 times, and this is a huge number, and what is meant by it is forgiveness without limits, and not thinking about how sincere the wrongdoer is in not returning to the fault.

If God asks us to forgive without limits, this reassures us that His mercy is very wide, and His forgiveness is endless too, as long as we repent and return to Him, on condition of not being careless, so that we do not lose the spirit of repentance and leave God.

entries.section: (4) The extent of forgiveness toward others

paragraphs.text: Christ explains the idea of forgiveness without limits toward others, so He likened the Kingdom of Heaven, in which we wish to live, and whose beginning is the Church on earth, to a king (who signifies Christ the Judge) to whom was brought a servant, that is, a sinful person, who owed an enormous sum, ten thousand talents, and to know how huge this sum is, we say that the gold used in the temple of Solomon in all its splendor was eight thousand talents. What is meant is that man's sins against God are enormous, indeed without limit, because God is unlimited and the punishment for a fault against Him is unlimited.

entries.section: (4) The extent of forgiveness toward others

paragraphs.text: The helplessness of this servant appeared, that is, of each one of us who sins against God, and consequently the king's (God's) judgment on him was that he be sold, with his wife and his children, that is, his body and his gifts, perhaps they might pay something of what he owed, but they would be of no use before this very huge debt. By this the weakness and evil of each one of us appears before divine justice.

entries.section: (4) The extent of forgiveness toward others

paragraphs.text: This servant worshiped, asking for patience, that he not be sold, that is, handed over to Satan and eternal torment. And here God's forgiveness of him appears, for He forgave him and released him with his wife and his children, and what is meant, as we mentioned, by his wife is his body, and by his children his gifts. That is, by the blood of Christ the Redeemer our sins were lifted from us, and He gave us renewal for our bodies, our spirits and all our gifts.
For God in His tenderness did not only grant the servant's request, which was for patience, but removed the debt from him, because He knows his inability to pay it however much time was given to him.

entries.section: (4) The extent of forgiveness toward others

paragraphs.text: After this servant was freed from his debts, he found a fellow servant, that is, a person who had sinned against him, who owed him a hundred denarii, a very small sum that has no comparison with the ten thousand talents (it equals one to a million and a quarter).
"Ten thousand": the number ten signifies the fault of the cruel servant against the Ten Commandments, and the number thousand signifies eternity, that is, that he deserves eternal punishment.

And despite the second servant's pleading with the first to have patience with him, the first servant was cruel, and did not forgive or pardon his brother, but threw him into prison, that is, he wanted the destruction of his own soul and his eternal torment.

entries.section: (4) The extent of forgiveness toward others

paragraphs.text: When his fellow servants saw this, who represent the Church, they were greatly grieved, so they prayed for the second servant who was thrown into prison.

And the king, that is, God, heard from the Church, and summoned the first servant and rebuked him severely for his cruelty, and for not appreciating the divine forgiveness granted to him, and his cruelty in not forgiving his brother. And he commanded that he be thrown into prison, to pay all that was due until the last farthing of all his debts. What is meant is that he remains in prison, that is, in torment forever, because of his not forgiving the one who sinned against him, since he will not be able to pay this unlimited debt.

entries.section: (4) The extent of forgiveness toward others

paragraphs.text: Christ affirms at the end of the parable that what is meant by it is God's not forgiving the one who does not forgive others. And He said "my Father", because the one who does not forgive others does not deserve to call God his Father, so He did not say "your Father". Offer your repentance every day before God, confident of His forgiveness, so that your repentance is joined with much thanksgiving. And as you strive to correct your faults, God supports you and your thanks to Him increases, and then you will be compassionate toward those who wrong you because they are sick like you, in need of divine forgiveness and the healing medicine from it. So do not be troubled by them, because your sins against God are greater, but pray for yourself and for them, and the mercies of God will embrace you all.
Marriage, virginity, detachment
"Beyond Jordan": it is the region lying beside the river Jordan, called Perea, and anciently the tribes of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh dwelt in it, and it is now called the Golan.

After His teachings that Matthew the Evangelist mentioned in the previous chapter, Christ left the region of Galilee, which lies in the north, where He had spent about three years, and moved to Judea, which is the southern region and contains Jerusalem, passing by the river Jordan, and He did not head quickly to Jerusalem, but moved about quietly in this region before reaching it.

Christ spent in this journey, from Galilee to Jerusalem, a period of about six months, during which many things happened that Luke and John mentioned, whereas Matthew mentioned a few events of them in this chapter and the one after it.
And Matthew mentioned that great multitudes followed Him, and He taught them His spiritual teachings and healed their sick as was His custom.

Here is clear teaching about the sacrament of marriage, which Christ established by His presence at the wedding at Cana of Galilee at the beginning of His ministry. The motive for it was the Pharisees' question to Him about the permitted reasons for a man to divorce his wife: for any cause, or are there specific causes? They knew, from His Sermon on the Mount, His opinion that divorce is not permitted except for the cause of adultery (ch. 5:32). Therefore, this question of theirs was not to know the truth, but to catch Him in a word, because if He forbade divorce He would be regarded as breaking the law of Moses which permits it (Deut 24:1 and 3), and to stir up Herod against Him because he had divorced his wife and married Herodias.

And Christ cited the words of Moses in the Torah, and took them back to the beginning of creation, when God created Eve from the side of Adam, and Adam declared in the spirit of prophecy that when a man marries, he should leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife, "and they twain shall be one flesh" (Gen 2:24), and so God joined them together in the sacrament of marriage, so how can we permit the separation of what God has joined?!
So divorce is a breaking of what God has done, and it is against it.
The Pharisees objected to the words of Christ, that Moses permitted divorce, so how does He forbid it?!

Christ replied to them that this permission was because of their low spiritual level, because after their mixing with the Egyptians they had become accustomed to divorce. So when they went out into the wilderness, He moved them gradually to the original law by narrowing the possibility of divorce, so that they would afterward leave it entirely, since the natural, sound state that God established in the Garden of Eden between Adam and Eve was the union of the two and the non-permission of divorce.

And Moses did not command divorce, but on the contrary, he commanded the one who wishes to divorce his wife not to be hasty, but to sit down and write her a bill of divorcement, to give him an opportunity to review himself and let his anger subside, so that he would reverse his decision if he thought that his wife would be with another, and that he would demolish his house and scatter his children.

After Christ's conversation with the Pharisees ended, He entered a house, as our teacher Mark mentions (Mk 10:10), and continued His talk with His disciples, affirming the law of the New Testament, which is that the only reason permitted for divorce in Christianity is the fall of one of the two parties into adultery, for by this he has separated bodily from the other, so the divorce has actually taken place bodily, and the writing of a bill of divorce is permitted.
But as for the one who wants to divorce his wife because of disagreements between them, the Church does not approve of that, for he is united with her in the sight of God.

But if this person resorts to trickery and obtains a civil divorce that the Church does not recognize and marries another, he falls into adultery. And whoever marries a woman divorced for a cause other than adultery, both of them fall into adultery.

The existence of differences in opinions and characters is not solved by divorce, but by taking refuge in God so that a person gives up some of his characteristics. By this he not only restores peace in his home, but his will also grows, so he is able to advance spiritually and control his desires and sins; and thus the affliction turns into a blessing, that is, the problems of marriage become a means of spiritual growth.

Since Christ did not permit divorce except for adultery, the hearers felt that this was beyond human endurance, and that it is better not to marry, because they did not understand the greatness of the oneness between the spouses, for divorce for any disagreements was easy in their view, and they were not ready to bear with one another.
Christ seized this opportunity to explain the difference between not marrying (celibacy) and virginity, and showed that there are three kinds of unmarried people:
The first kind: one who was born with sexual impotence, so he cannot marry, not out of love for virginity and being with God, but because of his inability to do so.

The second kind: those who wanted to serve in the palaces of the great and the kings, so they had an operation of removal performed on them, and became sexually impotent, in order to obtain a position or work in these palaces, where they would be trusted with serving the women without fear of assault on them. His not marrying in this case is for the sake of the desire for position and money, and to please people, and this is the worst kind.

The third kind: those who have risen above and sublimated the sexual instinct, and turned it into energy for the love of God, so that, although they are physically able to marry, they have turned their thought and their heart to the love of God as a heavenly Bridegroom, so they are in a spiritual marriage with God, higher than every human marriage.

This is virginity, whether serving in the world or in monasticism, and it is for some people to whom God has granted this grace and the inclination to be content with it, and not everyone can receive it, but it is very great if a person is fit for it.

"He that is able to receive it, let him receive it": that is, whoever has an inclination to virginity, it is good for him to live by it, and so enjoy the consecration of his thought and his heart to God.

If you are not fit for virginity, then at least be chaste from sin before marriage. And even after marriage, let your chief concern not be absorption in the bodily relationship to the point of disagreeing with your life partner, but give a greater place to the love of God in your heart, and to love of the other and appreciation of his feelings, so that you give up thinking about this relationship in order to please the other, or enter into this relationship, even if you are not inclined to it, also in order to please the other; do not seek your comfort but his, for this is true love.
Christ was blessing and healing the sick, and caring for teaching and solving people's problems. So some fathers brought their children to Him that He might pray over them and bless them.
But the disciples felt that their Teacher's time was too precious to waste on caring for children, so they tried to keep them away from Him so that He might attend to the affairs of adults.

Christ was not content with blessing the children and welcoming them, but declared an important truth, which is that these children are the children of the heavenly Kingdom, calling us all to imitate their innocence and simplicity. And although the child was neglected at that time in the prevailing religions, and in the earlier ages and kingdoms, Christianity cares for children, and even calls adults to learn from them, and to care for them and look after them.
"Of such": that is, of those who imitate them in innocence and simplicity.
A rich young man came to Christ (v. 22), and he was a ruler of one of the synagogues of the Jews (Lk 18:

18), and since he was accustomed to flowery speech, he called Christ Good Master, and asked Him a spiritual question, which was how to attain eternal life. Christ was concerned with his question, but before answering him, He directed his attention to not using words of praise without understanding, so He said to him: "Why callest thou me good? there is none good but one, that is, God." And the meaning of the question: do you believe that I am God, or do you say it as a mere compliment? And Christ is of course the Good Teacher, indeed the Good Shepherd as He said of Himself (Jn 10:11), and He is God without sin, as He said to the Jews: "Which of you convinceth me of sin?" (Jn 8:46). Then He answered the question that the way to eternity is keeping the commandments and carrying them out in life.

The young man asked Christ: "Which?" And Christ answered: "All the commandments that are on the two tablets that Moses received from God, whether those concerning the worship of God or dealing with others."

And Christ focused on the commandments of the second tablet, which concern dealing with others, because they cannot be fulfilled except by keeping the commandments of the first tablet, which are the worship of God and His love.
And Christ summed up at the end of His reply the commandments of the second tablet by saying: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself."

The young man answered hastily that he had kept these commandments from his youth. But Christ's intention was not keeping them literally, or applying them superficially, but with all their depths. Therefore Christ focused on treating the disease within him, so that he would understand the depth of applying the commandment, for his problem is the love of money, and He told him that he lacks one thing, that is, the treatment of the love of money (Mk 10:21).

Christ asked the young man to sell his possessions and distribute the price to the poor, and by this he would transfer his treasure from earth to heaven and his heart would be attached to it. And as an extension of this thought, he would follow Christ to walk in His teachings. † The actual application of these commandments is Christian perfection, and if a person cannot apply these words literally, as Anba Anthony the father of monks did, he should at least sell the love of material things from his heart, that is, be ready to give them up, and partly leave these possessions and give them to the needy.

Before the clear words of Christ, the weakness of this young man and his love of money were exposed, for he went away sorrowful, since he could not carry out the words of Christ, because his love of money was stronger than his love of God, and his great wealth helped his heart to cling to the love of money.

To be a child of the Kingdom, you must love God more than you love material things, and the proof of this is your offering of the firstfruits and the tithes however tight your financial circumstances, and that you be ready to give up material things to please those around you, and be content with everything.

Christ commented to His disciples on His dialogue with the young man after he left, explaining the danger of the love of money, and said that it is very hard for a rich man, who loves his wealth and relies on it, to enter the Kingdom of Heaven. And He likened that to a huge camel passing through the eye of a needle, and this is impossible, so likewise the rich man cannot enter the Kingdom. So he must first sell from his heart the love of money and reliance on it, and even if he has much money, it does not hinder him from entering the Kingdom because his heart is not in it.

The disciples felt the difficulty of carrying out these words, because their thinking was attached to the earthly kingship of Christ and the love of wealth and position, so Christ directed their gaze to the help of God which helps a person to do this, for what seems impossible in the eyes of man becomes easy with the help of God.

And this is what actually happened in the lives of many rich saints, who left their wealth and possessions, and lived in poverty in monastic life, or came forward to torture and martyrdom for the sake of Christ.

If you have any possessions and money, thank God for them, and do not compare yourself with others who are richer than you, but be content with what you have, and do not grieve if you lose some money, because it is changeable, but let this be a motive for you to cling to the love of God, for it is the only firm foundation and the unshakable support.

After Christ spoke of the importance of giving up the love of money so that a person may follow Him, Peter wanted to be assured for himself and the disciples, what would be their reward, since they had forsaken all for His sake? And what is meant is not only leaving the nets and possessions, because they are small, but even more the enduring of weariness and opposition from the Pharisees.

And the words of Peter may carry a kind of weakness of faith, so that he needs assurance of the reward from Christ, and may also carry a kind of feeling in himself that he has given. But he will discover after the accomplishment of redemption that everything a person gives is nothing before the perfect love in the giving of Christ Himself on the cross for the salvation of mankind.

Christ declared a great reward for His disciples who followed Him, indeed for everyone who follows Him, that in the regeneration, when the image of Christ changes from the weak human appearance to God the Judge in the Kingdom, His followers will be beside Him with a great standing, as proved by His saying: you shall sit upon thrones to judge the world, and this is by the faith of His followers and their preaching in His name, they judge the Jews who refused to believe, although they should have been the first to receive Him.

Christ affirmed the reward of the detached, and of one who gives up his attachment to possessions or loved ones in order to consecrate his heart to the love and service of God, which is that he receives a hundredfold in this life. And what is meant is not material compensation, but rather peace and love.

For example, the monk who leaves a father or mother and does not marry and beget children for the sake of God, God makes all people brothers and loved ones to him, and God becomes a father to him who cares for him and compensates him for all fatherhood of the flesh, and all become his children, and he finds his material sufficiency, and more than that. And some monks are chosen to become bishops, and all the money and possessions of the Church are placed under their hands, and they direct them with wisdom. Then what is better than that, the eternal reward in the Kingdom, which cannot be expressed.

God cannot be indebted to anyone, so what a person gives up, He will compensate him for in the present life, meeting the needs of His children, and then reward them with the greatest thing, which is the Kingdom of Heaven. And this is a clear truth that we observe, that those who love God and give up material things, He gives them favor in the eyes of all, and they are loved by many.

And so we find many great people in the world whose place in heaven is behind others, or who have no place in the Kingdom. And on the contrary, many of the despised and the least in the sight of men become great in the Kingdom of Heaven, such as the saints who renounced the world and lived in the wilderness, or the martyrs who endured many tortures. And likewise the first in their own eyes, that is, the proud, are preceded by the humble, that is, the last in their own eyes.

And there is another meaning, that those who were called first, like the Jews, may be rejected if they do not believe in Christ, and the Gentiles who were called after them and believed will have an advanced place in heaven.

Be confident that everything you leave on earth, you will receive in exchange for it peace and joy on earth, and manifold more in heaven. So do not be troubled if you lose something for the sake of Christ, or give up something to gain the love of others for the salvation of their souls. And on the contrary, you are the wiser the more you are able to give in this life, because this is a declaration of your love for Christ.
The parable of the laborers, seeking chief place
"An householder": he is God.
"His vineyard": it is the Church.
"The labourers": they are all people whom God calls to live with Him and to serve Him.
It is God who went out, that is, He is the One who takes the initiative in seeking man, and who begins with love, and He went out at dawn, at the first hour, seeking the hearts of His children.
The well-known Jewish hours are five, which signify the life of man, and they are (noting that the hour here is not 60 minutes, but a period of time extending to the hour that follows it):
The first hour: childhood.
The third hour: boyhood.
The sixth hour: youth.
The ninth hour: manhood.
The eleventh hour: old age.
These hours also point to the history of mankind: Adam, then Noah, then Abraham, then Moses and the prophets, then Christ.
And the meaning of this is that God seeks man throughout the history of mankind, and throughout his life, that perhaps he will respond and be saved.
"Even": it is the end of life, and the Day of Judgment.
"His steward": they are the angels.

"Those hired about the eleventh hour": when the lord reproached them for standing idle all the day, they said: "Because no man hath hired us" (v. 7), that is, they did not understand the call of God, so they remained without spiritual work all their lives, until they took notice at the end of life.
"A penny": it is salvation and eternal life.

So everyone, as long as he has believed in Christ and worked with Him even for one hour, receives eternal life. But one differs from another in the measure of his enjoyment, fellowship and attachment to God.

It may be that the call came at the end of life, and the person responded to it with all his heart, and so becomes like those of the first hour, indeed he may be better than they in proportion to his love for God.
And if someone says, I will wait until the eleventh hour, since salvation is given to all, and I do not want to be distinguished in the Kingdom of Heaven, this means:
First: that he does not know that his life may end at any moment.
Second: that he does not appreciate the value of fellowship with God and His love, and so he belittles his relationship with God on earth.

Those of the first hour signify the Jews, who thought that salvation was limited to them and not for the Gentiles, and that if non-Jews believed in Christ, they would be of a lower rank than the Jews who became Christians, and they spoke of those of the eleventh hour, saying: "These last"... But Christ spoke to them with love, saying: "Friend".

And in this murmuring was an interference in the work of God as Judge, for He gave each one what He had agreed with him, and then showed grace to another, without diminishing anything from the Jew or the murmurer.
"Thine eye evil": that is, selfish, thinking of good for yourself and refusing it for others, and envying others for what they receive.
"Many be called": God seeks the salvation of all. But only a few believe and live in love, and these alone are saved.
In sum, Christ gives salvation to everyone who believes in Him and lives with Him in His Church, whether he lived a life of repentance from the beginning of his life, or at the end of his days.
And this does not deny the existence of mansions and degrees in the Kingdom, but the talk here is only about entering the Kingdom.

Look at all people as the image of God, and that they may precede you into the Kingdom, and do good to everyone, especially to the weak and those far from God, that perhaps they will repent, knowing that they may increase in the love of God more than you.
"Then": after Christ's words about His coming sufferings.

"The mother of Zebedee's children": she is Salome, and her coming forward was at the urging of her two sons, so that she would support them in their request to Christ, and the proof of that is that Christ addressed the two of them afterward, and not the mother.
"A certain thing": out of courtesy on her part, and her sense of the difficulty of what she was asking and that it might be refused, she said to Him: I desire a certain thing of thee.
"What wilt thou?": Christ knew what she wanted, but He intended that she review herself one last time about what she would ask.

The mother of Zebedee's children came to Christ with her two sons, and worshiped Him in faith, and since she thought that Christ would have an earthly kingdom, as the rest of the Jews think, then out of love for her two sons she asked Him that they would have a distinguished place in this kingdom above the rest of the disciples, so that they would sit, one on His right hand and the other on His left, that is, that they would have chief place over the others.

Christ directed the attention of the two disciples to the sufferings that must be endured in order to reach the Kingdom, which takes place throughout life, to turn their eyes away from attachment to earthly positions, and to think in a spiritual way of the Kingdom of Heaven as love and fellowship with God, and not a search for positions or chief place. And He asked them a clear question: are you able to drink of the cup of sufferings and be baptized with the baptism of death? And they answered without deliberation and understanding and said: "We are able." And here Christ directed their attention to the fact that being in the Kingdom is a grace from God, so a person cannot by his will alone endure sufferings for the sake of Christ, but by the help of God.

"It is prepared of my Father": that is, for those who have completed their striving, and so deserve the grace of God. And although the will of the Son and the Father is one will, He said here "my Father", to raise their thinking from the earthly kingship with Him to the heavenly Kingdom, that is, with the Father.

The love of greatness stirred in the hearts of the disciples when they heard the desire of the two sons of Zebedee, James and John, for this chief place, and they were angered and troubled, for they feared that the two would obtain what they asked.

Christ warned them that striving for chief place is the thinking of the people of the world, and not of the children of God. And He declared clearly the importance of striving for humility in the form of serving one another, and each one's submission to the other, for this is what makes them great in the sight of God, and gives them a distinguished standing in heaven. That is, the world strives for chief place and domination, but the children of God for humility and service.
Christ gave Himself as an example of humility, for He did not seek a worldly position in which many would serve Him, but came to be a servant of mankind, and to die for it to redeem it.
Do you look for what service you can offer to others, and how to submit to them, or for your own standing and dignity among them? May you from today submit to all, to be raised in the sight of God.

entries.section: (4) The opening of the eyes of the two blind men

paragraphs.text: This is the last miracle that Christ performs before entering Jerusalem. As He was walking on the way with the multitude, there were two blind men sitting by the way, who seem to have been begging. When they heard the voice of the multitude, and learned that this was the procession of Christ who heals the sick, they believed in His power to heal, and cried out asking Him for that, confident that He is the awaited Messiah, the son of David.
Two blind men are mentioned here, whereas Mark and Luke mention one blind man, who seems to have been the one who spoke more than the second (Mk 10:46-52; Lk 18:35-43).

entries.section: (4) The opening of the eyes of the two blind men

paragraphs.text: By their much crying out they troubled the multitude, who tried to silence them so that they could enjoy listening to the words of Christ, but they kept crying out with insistence, declaring their faith and their great need of healing, seizing this opportunity that could not be replaced.
Press on God in asking, for this shows the extent of your faith, and do not be hindered by the thoughts of people that keep you from God.

entries.section: (4) The opening of the eyes of the two blind men

paragraphs.text: Jesus stood still and called the two blind men, for He cares greatly for the one who seeks Him, although He waits a little, to show the extent of his clinging and persistence in prayer. Then He asked them what they wanted, that they might show their need of healing, and they declared it. And then His tenderness appeared and He healed them. And from the excess of their joy, they followed Him, to enjoy like the others listening to His teachings and seeing His miracles.

God is ready to grant you spiritual insight, that is, discernment and understanding, if you ask for them with persistence, for His tenderness toward you is unlimited. And if He grants you wisdom and discernment, follow Christ in all your steps so that your faith is not theoretical, but you enjoy fellowship with Him every day more than before.
Christ's entry into Jerusalem, the parable of the husbandmen

From this chapter begin the events that took place in the last week of the life of Christ on earth. And the Holy Bible mentions them in detail, because they concern the accomplishment of salvation for the whole world. Christ drew near to Jerusalem (on the morning of Sunday), and to the village of Bethphage, which lies east of it at the Mount of Olives. So He sent two of His disciples, saying to them: when you enter the city, you will find an ass (a female donkey) and a colt (the young donkey), so loose them from their tying, and if anyone objects to you, say, The Lord hath need of them, and he will let them go with you.

And this was by divine arrangement, or the owners of the ass and the colt were informed, in a way not mentioned in the Holy Bible, that two would come asking for them for the Lord, and so they gave them to them.

"An ass ... and a colt": they signify people, that is, the Jews and the Gentiles, who have become as dull as the donkey because of their distance from God, whether by material preoccupation or by the worship of idols.
And see how great was the humility of Christ, who says that He has need of them, although He is the Creator of everything!
And thus He shows His need of the souls of His children, that they may return to Him and live with Him.
He is the giver of all gifts and perfect in Himself, but it is His love and humility that make Him ask.

And see the tenderness of God riding on the colt, but, so as not to tire the colt, He also rides on the ass a little, then on the colt a little, for He has compassion on His creation, and how much more on mankind.
And no one had ever ridden the colt, and this signifies not being subject except to God.

And He gave authority to the two disciples, that is, the priests of the New Testament, to loose mankind from its bonds, and this is the authority of loosing and binding in the sacrament of confession which is given to the repentant.
"The daughter of Sion": one of the names of Jerusalem.

As is the custom of Matthew the Evangelist, he declares that in Christ the prophecies are fulfilled. For Zechariah the prophet prophesied (Zech 9:9) of Christ's entry into Jerusalem in humility and meekness, to reign over hearts, and not as an earthly king, and therefore His procession is simple, riding on weak animals like the ass and the colt.
The two disciples of Christ carried out what He commanded them, and brought to Him the ass and the colt, that He might ride on them and enter Jerusalem.

Taking off a garment and giving it to another means, in Jewish custom, submission to him as a chief, for a person gives up what is necessary for him in order to submit to the other. And they put them humbly on the animals that Christ would ride, to be blessed by His sitting on them, and they even cast them on the ground for the same reason.
Take off your material concerns by fasting and detachment, and you will enjoy the blessing of God to whom you submit, and He will fill you with His grace.

The multitude also put their garments on the ground to be blessed, and they cut branches from the trees and spread them in the way, for Him to pass over them on the ass or the colt, so that the ground was clothed with greenness, that is, goodness, because He is the maker of good things.

"Branches from the trees": they point to the prophecies that were spoken about Christ, and are now fulfilled in Him. They also point to everything that is lofty, which is at His feet, because He is the Creator of all.

All the multitudes who went before Him to spread the way for Him, and who followed Him, declared their faith in Him that He is the awaited Messiah, the son of David, who comes in the name of the Lord to save them.
"The multitudes that went before": they point to the men of God in the Old Testament.
"And that followed": they signify the faithful in the New Testament, who believed the message of the Gospel, for all seek their salvation in Christ.
"Hosanna": its meaning is save us, for He is the Savior who lifts them to the heights in the Kingdom of Heaven. It also comes in the sense of glory.

It was a simple popular procession but a mighty one, for hearts were attached to Christ who loved them and cared for them, and the leaders of the city and the priests asked, Who is this procession for? and learned that it is for Jesus the Nazarene who teaches the multitudes, and heals their sicknesses and takes care of them.
Be concerned to win the love of others, and not to be raised above them by your position and authority, for all this passes away.

Connected with the temple was a group of open halls or courts in which the people gathered. And in them the merchants sold what those coming to the temple needed of animals or birds to offer on the altar.
And the Jews from different countries came at the feasts, so the priests arranged for money changers to change currencies into Jewish currency, and they had great financial gain from this trade.
And so people's preoccupation turned from concern for worship to buying their needs, and there may have been other goods they sold that had no connection with worship.
For if it was necessary to provide some needs related to worship, their sale should be outside all the courts of the temple, so that all the places of the temple remain for worship and teaching.

The zeal of Christ for the house of God appeared when He made a scourge (which signifies the Holy Spirit who rebukes us for our preoccupation with material thoughts inside the Church) to drive out with it the animals and birds and the large gatherings for trade inside the temple (Jn 2:15), declaring that the house of God is consecrated for prayer and worship only, as Isaiah said (Isa 56:7), and not for commercial gain, for the priests and their followers had become lovers of money like thieves who steal to heap up much wealth. For by this trade they turned the temple into a cave where thieves gather their material possessions. And Christ drove the sellers out of the temple on Monday, that is, the day after His entry into Jerusalem, but Matthew is not concerned with the order of events.

After the cleansing of the temple, there was quiet and an opportunity for spiritual work, so He healed the blind and the lame that they might be enlightened with the knowledge of God and hasten on the way of the spiritual life.

And those coming to the temple felt that Christ is the awaited Messiah, and perhaps they had been with Him in the procession of His entry into Jerusalem, so they repeated the acclamations they had said to Him, especially the children among them, who had memorized these phrases from their much repetition, saying: "Hosanna to the Son of David", and the chief priests and scribes were troubled by these acclamations because they are a clear declaration that He is the awaited Messiah, the son of David, as the prophecies said, and they said to Him: "Hearest thou what these say?"
Christ answered them with what is written in the prophets they have, that God prepares praise for Himself, which rises from the mouths of children (Ps 8:2).

After this, Christ went to the village of Bethany, whose meaning is "house of affliction", and which lies east of Jerusalem, where the house of His friend Lazarus whom He raised from the dead was, and He lodged there to return the next day to Jerusalem.

Your heart is the temple of God, so do not let the thoughts of the world occupy it, because God created it in you that prayers may be raised from it. So set aside sufficient time for your prayers before your occupations; and also during your work, lift your heart with short prayers to enjoy fellowship with God.

In the morning, Christ set out walking from Bethany, returning to Jerusalem to teach in the temple, and He was hungry, and this is a proof of His humanity. And on the way, He saw from afar a fig tree full of green leaves, so He came to it to eat figs, but when He reached it He found no fruit on it, so He said to it that it would never bear fruit, and it withered and died, and this is a proof of His divinity.

It is to be noted that Matthew the Evangelist was not concerned with the order of the time of events like Mark, because the fig tree was cursed by Christ on Monday morning, and the disciples noticed that it had withered on Tuesday morning as Mark the Evangelist mentions (Mk 11:14 and 20), whereas Matthew mentioned the cursing of the fig tree and its withering together.
And Christ did this to declare the seriousness of superficiality in the spiritual life, like the Jews who have the appearance of knowing God, but have not the fruits of love for others.
And every person who has the appearance of piety but not its depth is rejected by God, and condemned to death, for people come to him to know God, and they find no spiritual fruit in him.

"A fig tree": it signifies the Jewish nation and its temple. And because they rejected Christ, the destruction of the temple took place in the year 70 AD. And the withering of the fig tree is a prophecy of the destruction of Jerusalem.

And we find that the miracles of Christ declare His mercy, and this is the only miracle that declares the justice of God, so that our view of Him may be complete, and we remember His mercy and His justice at the same time, that we may repent and enjoy His mercies.

The disciples marveled at the fig tree's withering at once, so Christ seized this opportunity to show them the power of faith by which they can do everything, even the mountain, they can pluck it from the earth and cast it into the sea, if they have faith.

And the mountain points to the many lusts that reign over the heart, so if a person has faith and holds fast to God, he can cast this mountain into the sea, which represents the world, that is, he is rid of worldly lusts. Prayer with faith and persistence gives us everything we ask, on condition that it is in accordance with the will of God. So do not slacken, but ask God with faith for all your needs, and press upon Him, for He loves to hear your voice and give you all good things.
The chief priests and elders tried to catch Christ in a fault, because He is not of the tribe of Levi, which is responsible for teaching, but of the tribe of Judah.

And since they noticed His driving out of the sellers and the power of His teaching, they asked Him by what authority He teaches and works miracles, and who gave Him permission and allowed Him to do this: was it with the permission of the high priest?
They did not ask to know the power of God in Him, but perhaps He would err in some expression, and they would regard Him as breaking the Law and the order of the temple.

If the chief priests used human craftiness and cunning, Christ, the true wisdom, answered them with a question, and His intention was not to evade answering, because His question answers them. That is, if they had believed the call of John the Baptist, they would have believed his words about Christ and His authority. And Christ's question was about the source of John's baptism: was it from heaven, and God sent him, or from men, that is, a mere human claim?

So they reasoned among themselves, if they admitted that it was from God, He would ask them why they did not believe him and were not baptized by his hands? And if they declared their rejection of his baptism, they feared the people, because all knew that he was a great prophet, so they said: "We cannot tell", that is, their inability to answer appeared, because they feared declaring their true opinion, which was their rejection of John, for fear for their position and authority, and their unreadiness to repent. So Christ said to them: Neither tell I you by what authority I do these things.

And so He silenced them so that they would stop trying to catch Him in a fault, and would turn to their weakness, and mend it by accepting the call of John the Baptist, that is, repentance from their sins.
Do not be biased in your speech with others, but look for what benefits you, and learn from everyone, and offer love to all.

entries.section: (5) The parable of the two sons and the vineyard

paragraphs.text: The vineyard: it is the opportunity of life on earth in which we strive in holy worship of God, or waste it in the lusts of the world.
In the face of the refusal of the chief priests and elders to repent at the call of John or at the preaching of Christ, He gave them a parable about a father, who is God, who had two sons:

The first son: he signifies the Gentiles who refused to work with Him in His vineyard, that is, the Church, but afterward repented and worked in the vineyard. He also signifies the tax collectors and sinners who lived their lives far from God, but believed in Christ and repented and became saints.

The second son: he signifies the Jews or the scribes and Pharisees, who declared in words their submission to God and their following of Him, but refused to live with Him, that is, to believe in Christ and cleave to His Church.

entries.section: (5) The parable of the two sons and the vineyard

paragraphs.text: Then Christ asked: Whether of them twain did the will of his father? They said: The first. So He declared to them clearly that those far from God, like the tax collectors and harlots, that is, those immersed in every sin, can believe and repent, and so precede into the Kingdom those who call themselves believers, like the Jews, but do not do the will of God in love and doing good. So the far ones are the true children of the Church, that is, they are the believers in Christ, and not the rejecting Jews.
"In the way of righteousness": John the Baptist declared to you the truth of the necessity of repentance and returning to God.
"Ye repented not afterward": that is, you are still insisting on not repenting, content with formal worship, and your hearts are evil.

If God calls you to repentance through the Holy Bible or the teachings of the Church, or by any remark from those around you, or through the events of life, do not postpone your return to God, and do not promise Him with your mouth, then become occupied away from Him with the circumstances of life, but hasten to your father of confession, and partake of the Holy Mysteries to receive strength, and begin your spiritual striving and fellowship with God.
Christ summed up the history of the Jewish nation in this parable.
"An householder": he is God who planted a vineyard, that is, the people of the Jews, the descendants of Abraham, and hedged it round about, that is, the commandments and the Law by the hand of Moses.

"A winepress": it is the enduring of sufferings for the sake of holding fast to the word of God and serving Him, which the Jews were unable to do, so Christ completed it by His cross, and trod the winepress alone (Isa 63:3).

"A tower": the leaders of the people and its elders, responsible for watching over the people and the attacks of enemies from above the tower, to warn them of that. And they include the heads of the tribes and clans and the teachers and all the leaders of the people. "Husbandmen": they are the priests of the Jews responsible for the care of the planted vineyard so that it may bear holy fruits, that is, virtues and a pure life, in the hearts of the believing Jews.

"And went into a far country": that is, after He had revealed Himself clearly like a great fire on the mountain in the days of Moses, and the fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, He disappeared from the eyes of the people because of their absorption in sins, so they no longer saw Him, as though He had traveled.

"His servants": whom He sent to receive the fruits, and they are the prophets and men of God sent to His people throughout history, to reap a life full of virtues from the believing Jews, but sadly the priests of the Jews and their leaders opposed them and tortured them, and scourged some, killed some, and stoned some, that is, they rejected their teachings which are the voice of God to them.

And God lengthened His forbearance (patience) toward them, by sending other servants also, more than the first, that is, a great number of prophets, and the priests opposed them and rejected them like the first.
The last opportunity and the greatest work that God offered to the Jewish people is the incarnation of His only Son, as was told them in the prophecies of the prophets, to save them.

And in the parable, the husbandmen knew that he was the son of the owner of the vineyard and the heir of all that is in it, so instead of submitting to him and giving him the fruits, they rose against him and killed him.

And the chief priests, for their purposes of chief place and material things, refused to understand that Jesus is the awaited Messiah. And instead of believing in Him, they opposed Him lest He take their position, and they crucified Him on the cross. And so pride and the love of chief place appear, which blinded the eyes of the priests, to the point of rejecting the awaited Messiah, the Son of God.

Christ asked the scribes and Pharisees who were listening to Him about the fitting action of the owner of the vineyard toward the wicked husbandmen, and they said to Him: He will destroy them, and let out the vineyard to other husbandmen better than they, who will render him the fruits in their seasons.
This is the fate of the priests of the Jews who refuse to believe in Christ, that is, eternal torment.
"Other husbandmen": the disciples and Apostles and the Christian priesthood.
"The stone": it is Christ, and the building is the Church, and the chief builder who chose this stone is God.

"Marvellous in our eyes": according to the limited human view, Christ appears to be from a humble family, and has no wealth or material position, but He is God who humbled Himself for our salvation, and we need faith to receive Him.

Christ reminded them of what is written in (Ps 118:22) about the stone that the builders think useless, and then discover in the end that it is the most suitable stone to be the head of the corner, that is, joining the two walls together. And this stone signifies Christ the Savior of the Jews and the Gentiles, for He is the One whom God sent, and the priests did not understand that.

And Christ states clearly to the chief priests that the Kingdom of God which He promised His people will be taken from them because of their unbelief, and given to the Gentiles who believe in Him, and He means that the unbelieving Jews will be replaced in the Church of Christ by the believers from the Gentiles.
And whoever opposes Christ falls on the stone to break it, and he is himself bruised, that is, he meets troubles.
But if he repents and believes, God receives him.
But whoever remains refusing to believe in Him, He will judge him in the end and condemn him to destruction, that is, the stone will fall on him and grind him to powder.

The chief priests and Pharisees understood that the parable was about them, and instead of repenting, they were enraged at it and tried to arrest Him, but they feared the people, because in their view He was a great prophet. If others expose your faults to you, do not resist them, but hasten to repentance, for their words are a message from God. The parable of the wedding, the beliefs of the Sadducees, the greatest commandment

entries.section: (1) The parable of the wedding feast

paragraphs.text: As was Christ's custom, He presented the spiritual meanings in parables so that they would be close to the understanding of His hearers, because of the hardness of their hearts and their inclination to reject His teachings that were deep spiritually.
"A king": the Father.

"A wedding": the Church, in which God rejoices in the union of His people with Him, by partaking of His most holy Body and Blood, as they receive salvation from sin through Baptism, confession and Communion.
"For his son": Jesus Christ.

entries.section: (1) The parable of the wedding feast

paragraphs.text: "Sent forth his servants": the Fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the prophets, and all the men of the Old Testament who made God known to mankind.
"Other servants": the Apostles and disciples, and the priests and servants of the New Testament, who call mankind to faith and to life in the Church.
God respects the will of man, so He calls him to His Church and does not force him. He has prepared everything, and He offers us His love, and it remains for us to respond to Him.

"They would not come": that is, the Jews rejected the teachings of the prophets, kept away from repentance, and did not believe in Christ. "My oxen and my fatlings are killed": this refers to the sacrifice of Christ on the Cross, which the sacrifices of the Old Testament were a type of, and which is the sacrifice of His Body and Blood on the altar every day.
It also signifies the word of God, which satisfies the soul.

Likewise it signifies the life of the martyrs and the saints, who offered their lives as a sacrifice of love for God after the example of the crucified Christ, and whose lives satisfy the believing soul with the love of God put into practice in their lives.

entries.section: (1) The parable of the wedding feast

paragraphs.text: Sadly, the response of those who were invited to the one who gave the wedding was bad, for they were absorbed in material desires, which are expressed by the farm and the merchandise. They signify the Jews, who had the promises and the call to life with God, but were absorbed in material things; and more than this, they mistreated His prophets who carried His invitation to them, and they insulted them and killed them.

entries.section: (1) The parable of the wedding feast

paragraphs.text: "The king": he is God. He was angry at the evils of those who were invited, and issued his command to destroy them, that is, eternal torment for their refusal to believe, as well as the destruction of their city, which indeed happened in AD 70, when the Romans destroyed the city of Jerusalem.

entries.section: (1) The parable of the wedding feast

paragraphs.text: "The highways": where people throng.
"As many as ye shall find": the invitation is for all mankind.

The Jews rejected God's invitation, though they should have been an example of faith before the Gentiles, so God directed His invitation to the whole world through His servants the disciples and Apostles. They went out into the ways of the world calling everyone to faith and to the feast of Christ, that is, His most holy Body and Blood.

entries.section: (1) The parable of the wedding feast

paragraphs.text: "Bad": their past life was full of evils that were visible before people.
"Good": they have virtues known before others.
But all need faith in Christ and His redemption, and repentance from their sins.

The disciples called all the Gentiles, whether the bad among them or the good, however great the sins of the bad, provided they were ready to repent. So they believed and left their past life, and entered the Church believing in Christ, to be satisfied by Him.

entries.section: (1) The parable of the wedding feast

paragraphs.text: "A wedding garment": clothes that the giver of the wedding provides to the invited. Here it signifies the Holy Sacraments, especially Baptism, confession and Communion. If someone neglects these garments and relies on his own righteousness, that is, does not continue in confession and Communion and in walking in the new life with God, he is stripped of the wedding garments, and his end is destruction.

So when the Gentiles believed and entered the Church, they had to keep their lives pure in God by continuing in a life of repentance, so that they would have the pure life, which is the garment fitting for the wedding, that is, being in the Church on earth and then extending in it forever.

entries.section: (1) The parable of the wedding feast

paragraphs.text: Then the hour of judgment comes, and the king, that is, God, asks the negligent among the believers: how did you not abide in His love and the love of others, especially enemies? How did you make light of sins and not repent of them? Then these wicked ones fall silent, because there is no longer time for repentance.

entries.section: (1) The parable of the wedding feast

paragraphs.text: The negligent person binds his life with sin, and so receives his recompense, which is to be bound to it forever for torment, because he rejected the freedom of the Spirit and the enjoyment of God.

The severity of the torment, and the body's sharing in it with the soul after it has been changed into a spiritual body, is expressed by "weeping and gnashing of teeth", and this means very severe pains.

entries.section: (1) The parable of the wedding feast

paragraphs.text: Thus God calls everyone to faith, but those who believe and remain steadfast in faith are few, and these are the chosen for eternal life.

† The opportunity of a lifetime allows you to take part in the Lord's supper, that is, to partake of the Holy Sacraments. So do not let the engagements of life distract you from it, and do not excuse yourself from it because of the multitude of your sins, for the sacrament of confession forgives you everything, however hard it was or however long it has dominated you for many years.

So do not be negligent, forgetting your sins, but take care to put on the wedding garment, so that you may eat of the king's supper. Persevere in that, and you will rejoice in fellowship with Christ and live with Him forever.

"The Herodians": a group of Jews who sided with the family of Herod, which was of Edomite origin, that is, not Jewish, and who hoped that a member of this family would be governor of Judea on behalf of the Roman authority, and who were concerned with submission to the Roman state and the collection of tribute.

The Pharisees continued in their evil toward Christ. Although they despised the Herodians because they followed the Roman authority, while they themselves resisted the Roman occupier, they united with them in order to catch Christ in some error. In hypocrisy, they praised Christ, saying that He was a teacher of truth, and provoked Him by their praise of Him that He fears no one, so that He would refuse to pay the tribute. Then they asked Him: is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar according to the commands of the Roman state? If He said it is given, He would be cooperating with the occupier, and they would stir up the Jews against Him. And if He said no, He would become a resister of the state, and He would have to be arrested and tried.
"Caesar": the name of any Roman emperor, like the title Pharaoh for any king in ancient Egypt, and the Caesar at that time was Tiberius.

God, who searches the hearts and knows the unseen, knew their thoughts, and said to them: "Why tempt ye me?" He warned them of their sin, which is hypocrisy, that perhaps they would repent and believe in Him as God who knows the unseen, but sadly they were not moved, because of the hardness of their hearts.

"Shew me the tribute money": this is one of the kinds of money with which the tribute is paid, such as the Roman denarius. By presenting this denarius, the Pharisees declared their submission to the authority, contrary to what they proclaim, that their submission must be to the Temple only. They did not have only Jewish money, such as the shekel, but Roman money as well. So He showed them that they proclaim what they do not practice, out of fear of the authority.

Christ asked them for one of the coins, and they showed Him a denarius that of course had the image of the Roman Caesar and his name. He asked them: whose is this image and superscription? They said: Caesar's. He said to them: render to Caesar what is his, which is the tribute and all the political duties required of a citizen of the Roman state; since the state provides services to its citizens, it deserves to receive this tribute. But what is more important, which is the spirit, give to God, because money is the lowest and least important, whereas the spirit of man is the most important thing in him. They marvelled greatly at His wisdom, because He did not fall into an error that they could hold against Him, but sadly they did not believe and repent.

You are the image of God, so give Him your heart and your life, and do not be an image of the devil by loving evil desires and pride. Repent and cleave to God, so that you may regain His image in you.

The Sadducees were a wealthy aristocratic sect of the Jews, who did not believe in another life after this world, or in a resurrection of bodies after their decomposition, and most of the high priests were from among them.

The Sadducees referred to Christ to a part of the Law of Moses, namely that if a man married a woman and died without having children, his brother or nearest kinsman would marry her after him, so as to raise up seed in the name of the dead man, to inherit his land and preserve it, and the firstborn son would be ascribed to the dead man (Deut 25:6), and that was a symbol of preserving our eternal inheritance.

They composed a story and asked Christ about it, since they saw it as a dilemma with no solution. It was of seven brothers, one of whom married a woman and died without children, so the second married her and likewise had no children, and so on until the seventh brother, and he had no children, and then the woman died. Their question was: if there is a resurrection and eternal life, to which of the seven will this wife belong, to live with him in eternity, since she had been the wife of all of them on earth, and bore no children, so that no one could answer them that she would be the wife of the one by whom she had borne children.

Christ pointed out to them their lack of care and their lack of understanding of the prophecies of the prophets, for they always took them in the material sense, because their thinking was immersed in material things, though the speech is clear about a spiritual life in heaven, and no need for bodily relations or any material work, but all will be spirits attached to God, gathered by feelings of love without distinction of bodily kinship, for they have risen above it by their deep spiritual sense. And because they are immortal, they do not need marriage and procreation; they know one another as spirits, without need of bodily feelings.

Christ gave them another proof besides the prophecies of the Holy Scriptures, namely God's saying to Moses and to the prophets that He is the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob (Ex 3:6 and 15). Would God ascribe Himself to dead men who have come to an end and no longer have any worth?!
Of course not. For the great God ascribes Himself to spirits alive with Him in heaven who are His children, whom we knew in the body and who now live by the spirit in heaven.

He brought this proof from the books of Moses because the Sadducees rely on them and neglect many other books of the Old Testament. For God did not say "I was the God of Abraham", but He is their God at present. And this was in His speaking with Moses many years after their death, which means that their spirits are alive in heaven, and He is their God; spirits do not vanish with the death of the body, as the Sadducees proclaim.

Because of the loftiness of Christ's teachings, His wisdom and the power of His words, the hearers were astonished, and the Sadducees were silenced before His argument. The multitudes were not only of the Sadducees, but also of the Pharisees and ordinary Jews.
Think of the greatness of heaven and the glory of the spirits there, so that you may not be immersed in material desires, but reject your evils and care for your spiritual life.

The Sadducees lost the ability to catch Christ in any error, or even to converse with Him, because of His strong argument. So the Pharisees, who hold fast to the Law, gathered together to tempt Christ and make Him fall into some error.
The power of God that is in you silences the wicked, however great their evils or their schemes, because God who is with you is stronger than all the demons who stir up evil in men.

A Pharisee among them, who was a lawyer, that is, one of those exacting in keeping and expounding the commandments and the Law of Moses, asked Christ: which is the great commandment? So that if Christ singled out one of them, He would be in error, because all are commandments of God. Perhaps they had heard of His Sermon on the Mount, in which He completed the meanings of the commandments, so that they might accuse Him of saying that the Law is deficient.
Are you innocent in your speech with others, or do you try to show your own distinction or their weaknesses?

Christ summed up the Ten Commandments in two commandments, and did not single out one above the other. The first commandment speaks of man's relation to God, that he love Him with all his being, that is, with his heart, soul and mind, and this is the most important thing, namely the love of God, and from it necessarily results the second commandment, which is love of the neighbor, that is, all mankind, and it is proof of man's love for God.

True love is a person's love for the other as for himself, not merely some concern, and then the love of the New Testament grows greater, so that loving the other becomes more than loving oneself, as Christ did on the Cross, for He loved us and gave Himself for us.

Not only this, but out of the overflow of the river of His love that never runs dry, and at the height of the sufferings, He asked the Father for those who crucified Him, saying: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do" (Lk 23:34).
By this love, all the Law and the commandments and the words of the prophets are summed up.

Christ was longsuffering toward the questions of the Sadducees, the Pharisees and the lawyers, some of which were mentioned in the preceding verses, and their attempt to make Him fall into any error. And He silenced them with His strong arguments. In the end, He was compelled to show them the error of what they were doing, for by this they were resisting the truth, and they were very weak before it, so He asked them a religious question from their study of the prophets and the Law, namely: what do the Holy Scriptures say about the expected Messiah, whose son is He? They quickly answered: "The Son of David", for there is no dispute about that, that He would come from the seed of David according to the prophecies.
David.
"Doth David call him": in (Ps 110:1), and the Jews were agreed that its writer was David. "In spirit": by divine inspiration.
"The Lord": God the Father.

"My Lord": that is, the master and God of David, and a man cannot call his son or grandson "my Lord". Christ said to them: if He is the son of David, how does David in his psalm call Him his Lord, when he said: "The Lord said unto my Lord, Sit thou on my right hand" (Ps 110:1)? And that is in a conversation between the Father and the Son after Christ completes redemption on the Cross, and all the demons become subject to Him, for He bound them with His Cross, that is, He comes to be in His divine majesty, which is indicated by the right hand.
How then can He be the son of David and the Lord of David at the same time?!

The Pharisees were bewildered and unable to answer, because they were absorbed in material thinking about Christ, though the answer is simple, understood by any Christian, namely that Christ is the son of David in the flesh, and is the eternal God at the same time, for He is God incarnate.
And since they felt their inability, they departed from Him in shame, and no longer resisted Him.
God wants you not to resist the truth, but to repent and love Him and live with Him; so obey the word of God and live in it. The twenty-third: the pride of the Pharisees; the formality of worship.
These are the last sermons of Christ to the multitudes. After that, all His talks were to the disciples.

Christ endured the opposition of the proud scribes and Pharisees, and used to answer their malicious questions, using that as an opportunity to teach them along with all the multitudes. But when He reached the last week of His life on earth, He wanted to expose their errors, that perhaps they would repent, and so that the people would not imitate them and fall into many sins.

God entrusted the scribes and Pharisees with teaching the people the commandments and the Law, and they taught everything with exactness, but lived a life utterly far from the commandments. So Christ instructed His disciples and the multitudes to obey the word of God that the scribes and Pharisees teach, with great caution, lest they imitate them in their wrong works, because the Pharisees neglected to carry out the commandments of God.

"They bind": He likens the commandments to loads that the Pharisees tie together and demand of the people. "Heavy burdens": He likens the people to beasts of burden, on whose backs the Pharisees place the commandments as heavy loads, until the beasts almost fall under them and lose the ability to move with them, that is, they are not able to carry them out. "With one of their fingers": they refuse to carry out the least thing of them.

Because the Pharisees do not strive to carry out the commandments, their words became theoretical, and their demanding that people carry out the commandments became burdensome, not because the commandment is heavy in itself, but because the expression and teaching of it is wrong, so they do not encourage people to carry it out, and they have no experience in how to progress gradually in applying the commandments and overcoming obstacles.

Do not teach another anything that you have not begun to carry out practically in your own life, so that you have benefited from it, and your words will be more effective. And on the other hand, you will have learned how to carry it out, and you will guide people with realistic, practical words suited to the circumstances of life surrounding you and them.

The Pharisees were not content with not carrying out the commandments, but sought honor and the praise of people. The Law commanded that the commandments be written in small script on pieces of leather and placed between the eyes, that is, to be always in a person's thought and before his eyes. But they made these bands broad, to pretend that they held to the commandments more than others. As for garments, God commanded that on their borders, that is, their hems, some blue threads be placed, that is, sky-colored, to remind them of the heavenly life. But the Pharisees made these borders large to show their piety more than others; and thus they refused humility.

The material bands dulled their minds and kept them away from the commandment, and the long, grand borders made them fall into pride, and hindered them from walking in the narrow way, that is, spiritual striving, and they even sought the grand, foremost place at feasts, banquets and synagogues. And when they pass through the markets crowded with people, they love people to give them greetings of praise and honor, and to call them by words of honor such as "my master", and by this pride they were occupied away from the love of God and carrying out His commandments.
Therefore Christ took care to be humble in all His conduct, whether at the wedding in Cana of Galilee, or His inclination to hiddenness, or His washing the disciples' feet...

In proportion to your humility, you see God and understand His commandments and love Him. On the contrary, if you seek the praise of people, you move away from His love, because you love yourself instead of Him.

Christ warned His disciples against love of leadership, authority and the praise of people, asking them to be humble, and to feel that all of the people whom they shepherd are their brothers, and that Christ alone is the Teacher and the Shepherd. The meaning is not the word "master" or "teacher" literally, but the spirit of pride and domination, because in different societies there are, of course, masters and slaves, or chiefs and subordinates, and teachers and learners.
